Title: Unlocking post-harvest value for rural farmers through solar cooling tech and a USSD-based food trading platform
Subtitle: Nampya Farmers Market is building a post-harvest chain platform that allows rural smallholder farmers to store, manage and monetize their produce
Problem Statement:
In most of the western world, the agricultural supply chain is intricately connected and integrated from farm to table, but the situation is quite different in Uganda and many other African countries.
The mostly smallholder farmers suffer a significant gap in connectedness and infrastructure and as a result, lose over 1.3 billion tons of produce a year to post-harvest spoilage. Add climate change to this scenario and the problems multiply because food spoilage process is often quickly expedited. This forces farmers to sell what they quickly can – and at huge discounts – or risk their produce rotting, keeping them trapped in a poverty cycle.
In addition, the urban population also finds it hard to access quality, safe and fresh food due to massive distribution delays and poor handling by third parties, leading to massive food waste - the cost of which is pushed on to end consumers who are paying high price points (often 200% on average) for semi-fresh food from retailers. Ironically, both producers and consumers are food insecure.

Furthermore, according to UNHCR, Uganda is a ground for refugees from East Africa and the neighboring regions. However, food shortage becomes serious for refugee settlements because 160,000 refugees, who flee from the civil wars, come to Uganda every year. Humanitarian agencies spend extensive resources on imported food aid for refugees, but 40% does not reach the intended beneficiaries. This is due to an inefficient and uneven food distribution system of the ground teams.

And after COVID-19 spread all over Uganda, the government formed a task force team to support vulnerable communities with relief food. Ultimately, due to the continued unequal distribution of food and embezzlement, the team lost public trust. It takes a lot of effort for aid organizations to procure food regionally, leading to high imports. Private donors hardly have any possibility to donate food aid because there’s a problem of ordering and distribution.
Solution Overview:
To protect food security, Nampya Farmers Market provides solar-powered micro-warehouses near farm clusters, making it easier and more affordable for smallholder farmers to store and insure their surplus harvest. We also run a USSD-based, tech-enabled food supply platform that connects rural farmers directly to urban food retailers, bypassing exploitative middlemen. This allows farmers to sell their produce at fair prices, promoting economic self-sufficiency and supporting sustainable food supply chains. With mobile money payments integrated into the system, Nampya facilitates smooth, direct transactions, helping greengrocers, hotels, and restaurants source better-quality, competitively-priced food straight from the farmgate to their doorstep.
Farmers use their simple, basic and feature phones to advertise their ready-to-harvest crops on the platform and the food retailers can conveniently order them from the platform via mobile app or a USSD short code. Nampya then delivers the crops directly to the food stores, hotels and restaurants through our distribution network. 
According to the UN Environment Programme, 500 million small farms provide up to 80% of food consumed in the developing world. However, they receive a very little share of the value generated by their production. Instead, most if it is captured by intermediaries in the supply chain between them and final consumer. These last years have seen an increasing demand from consumers for fresh and ethical products. Thus, there’s a very huge opportunity for developing transparent and fair distribution models which can put back farmers’ livelihoods at the center of the equation. Cutting out intermediaries and enabling a more direct access to market for smallholder farmers can directly increase economic security for rural communities to assure food production for local and global markets. This is exactly what Nampya is doing by connecting smallholder farmers to markets they could never attain on their own. In the process, we cut out several middlemen and redistribute this value to the consumer and the producer. The retailer's order of outstandingly quality and fresh produce is delivered with the story of the farmer’s region attached so they know exactly where food comes from.
Besides successfully connecting rural tenant farmers with urban food retailers, Nampya Farmers Market also operates a food donation service connecting relief donors and vulnerable groups. Donors can easily donate food to vulnerable groups via Nampya platform. They can make the order, and then Nampya delivers the relief food to the donor, donor-agent or directly to the beneficiaries. In this way, it becomes sustainably cheaper for donors to source food relief from the region.
Precisely, through the use of technology, Nampya Farmers Market is changing the food distribution landscape, enabling rural farmers to market profitably while end consumers can access the highest standard of quality produce. Farmers and consumers are benefitting from our next-day delivery service value offering. With our innovative mobile ordering solution that democratizes and makes the agricultural value chain process easy to exploit and navigate, Nampya is opening markets to several farmers that would not necessarily have access to markets and cannot scale as a result.
Solution Provider(s): With our business model, Nampya wants to create the following positive impacts for Uganda: First of all, Nampya Farmers Market wants to tackle the issue of poverty. While many smallholder farmers are paid less than $1 a day, Nampya’s objective is to increase it to $4 a day for 1 million smallholder farmers by 2040. In addition, the company stands up for gender equality, decent work and economic growth with our business. Furthermore, we want to encourage life on land by giving farmers ownership of their land. In order to achieve these goals, Nampya Farmers Market relies on the following key partners and resources: For our business idea, Nampya needs food retailers, farmers, transportation providers, Mobile Telecom Operators (MTOs), solar suppliers as well as internet providers. Therefore, the most important resource is the app and platform, where retailers and farmers can be connected. The company’s costs compose of transportation and logistics, advertising, wages, as well as the creation and maintenance of the application/platform and website. On the other side, Nampya Farmers Market aims to generate revenues with a commission on deliveries. The relationship Nampya has with its customers is at customer support via the application and website, during face-to-face outreaches as well as during pick-ups and deliveries. To summarize everything, at the heart of Nampya Farmers Market is the application/platform in order to connect all the relevant stakeholders.
Implementation location(s): So far, Nampya Farmers Market is headquartered and operational in Uganda
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Smallholder farmers are the back bone of food production across Africa, providing up to 80% of the continent’s food supply. Yet these farmers struggle to fully capitalize on their yields and labor. With over 120kg of food lost per capita in Sub-Saharan Africa annually, lack of storage and transparent market linkages squander immense nutritional and economic potential.  we plan to expand beyond Uganda to larger regions of East Africa starting with Tanzania by 2027.
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 15 (Life on Land);
Desired impact:
Nampya Farmers Market is poised to drive a massive positive impact on incomes, resilience, and food security across Africa’s predominant but underserved smallholder farmers. 
Across the continent, farmers face a myriad of challenges from low access to capital, to poor market linkages, to weak infrastructure and logistics. Aggregation and efficiencies are also difficult to achieve since most farms are small: in Uganda, 38 million smallholder farmers till fewer than 10 acres each. Furthermore, farmers are facing dramatic climate change impacts and environmental conditions, so yields are declining even as land being farmed increases.  
While many organizations are targeting on-farm productivity, few are addressing the post-harvest challenges that keep farmers’ income down. According to FAO, 37% (or 120-170 kg/year per capita) of food produced in Sub-Saharan Africa is lost between production and consumption due to lack of storage facilities and low access to liquidity. Those challenges also force smallholders to sell immediately after harvest when market prices are lowest, even as intermediaries can resell their produce at huge margins later. 
Nampya Farmers Market is providing the infrastructure for farmers to store their produce, connect them to markets, improve access to credit and secure better prices. We do build and lease solar powered micro-warehouses at close proximity to the farm clusters/communities making it cheap and easily accessible to smallholder farmers to store and insure their harvest. Using a USSD-platform, farmers are able to efficiently store and transparently trade their produce. By solar cooling, safely storing, and selling at optimal prices, farmers using Nampya’s micro-warehouses increased incomes by up to 90% while avoiding storage losses.
Thus, as Nampya Farmers Market rapidly scales up storage units across Central Uganda and beyond, we can exponentially increase impact. Just reaching 1% of Ugandan smallholders would impact 380,000 livelihoods directly. With robust measurement frameworks in place, quantified income improvements and post-harvest loss reduction for each additional farmer will clearly showcase Nampya Farmers Market’s value chain approach lifting smallholders out of cycles of poverty.

80% of Ugandan smallholder farmers and food retailers are women. With our integrated USSD-enabled food trading platform, Nampya is currently working with them to protect food security through their economic self-sufficiency. Agricultural productivity has improved amongst them as they're now able to put their agricultural produce for sale at a price of up to 40% higher than the wholesale price, thus generating a higher return on investment for the farmers, along with a direct linkage to consistent and better-paying urban markets. In addition, the Nampya delivery service saves food retailers' time, allowing them to focus on sales activities and efficient inventory management.
In terms of numbers, with only 6 storage units built, Nampya Farmers Market has successfully brought together over 9,000 smallholder farmers, overseen the cultivation of 17,000 acres of land and has delivered 46,200 tons of commodities with 502 food retailers involved, while saving 18,280 tons of food from wastage (post-harvest losses). As a pilot, Nampya Farmers Market has also successfully distributed over 120 tons of relief food to about 4,516 people in cooperation with local politicians, a relief organization, mosques and churches. In total, Nampya caused an amount of $2,626,400 in terms of farmer additional income thanks to Nampya's farm-to-market disintermediation platform and solar warehousing.

Environmental Impact – Food waste is a big contributor to climate change through gas 
emissions. By reducing waste through solar cooling, a well-organized and short supply chain, Nampya Farmers Market positively impacts the environment.
Key technologies:
Nampya Farmers Market is powered by solar cooling and mobile technologies (USSD, Mobile Apps, mobile money payments and internet). By solar cooling, safely storing and selling at optimal prices through our marketplace, farmers have increased incomes by up to 90% while avoiding storage losses. And by providing logistics to link farmers to the retailers and relief donors, ensuring that food quality meets buyer specifications and providing the retailers with the ability to trace the source of the crops they are purchasing while ensuring mobile money payments on pickup or after delivery of their crops, Nampya Farmers Market provides a reliable route to the food market using the internet as the vehicle instead of a passing truck. This has enabled rural farmers and food retailers to build confidence in the food market, gaining the ability to plan ahead and invest in improved production and more robust trades.
In addition, we have learnt that Uganda loses $38 million yearly due to aflatoxin-contaminated grain. Nampya Farmers Market intends to expand into grain post-harvest management by solar drying and establishing a grain processing facility with ozone technology embedded to remove carcinogenic aflatoxins and we will produce aflatoxin-free fortified flour for local consumers across East African markets.
Ozone technology is an emerging and effective method in food processing, offering benefits such as enhanced food safety, extended shelf life, and minimal use of harsh chemicals.
The Use of Ozone Technology to Control Microorganism Growth, enhances food safety and extend shelf fife. It is a Promising Food Decontamination Technology.
Unique Characteristics:
Nampya Farmers Market takes an innovative big-picture approach by bundling four interconnected solutions - solar warehousing, pricing transparency, farm-to-market logistics and embedded lending options. It’s this combination that we believe can holistically tackle root causes trapping smallholder farmers in cycles of poverty.
Many farmers lack access to any storage infrastructure, forcing distressed sales immediately after harvest when market prices tank. Private facilities are often only accessible to large commercial farms. Nampya Farmers Market’s distributed solar storage units overcome these challenges to minimize post-harvest losses for smallholders specifically.
However, building climate-resilient storage infrastructure alone is not enough. Smallholders also need more visibility and bargaining power in commodities markets. Nampya’s integrated USSD and tech trading platform cuts out exploitative middlemen by giving farmers more direct agency in selling to fair national markets through optimized logistics processes that guarantee market access for farmers and increase the value of food for retailers through proper handling.

The fourth and final piece of the puzzle is the access to finance. With our storage units preserving harvest quality over weeks to months, Nampya Farmers Market links receipts of banked crops to unlock credit for farmers to invest in inputs for increased yields.
This complete view addressing infrastructure, transparency, logistics and finance holistically makes Nampya Farmers Market’s model so innovative. As pioneers bundling physical and digital tools uniquely tailored for smallholder farmers' needs, Nampya Farmers Market is cementing an innovative business model linking underserved farmers to formal markets and finance.

Nampya’s competition today comes from brokers, but these do not supply based on demand and only provide 1 or 2 product lines without traceability in a market setting. Other players in the field include (1) Trutrade which is more of a value chain optimizer linking mostly grain farmers to big off-takers in Uganda and Kenya, (2) Bringo Fresh and (3) Akatale Fresh -these are more of smart brokers because they buy from farmers and resell to anyone and they have no function of supporting farmers’ growth for long-term business 
Besides providing infrastructure that transforms farmers price takers to price makers for their products, Nampya is a gamechanger in the following ways:
(1)	QUALITY - Food in our chain is more protected through warehousing and reliable, agreed and faster logistics. In addition, we ensure better quality with our daily quality standards and the future involvement of quality inputs providers. 
(2)	FAIRNESS - We ensure an optimal connection between of smallholder farmers and food retailers/social institutions through our transparent mobile money-powered platform. Fair prices towards farmers and resellers are a matter to us.
(3)	TRUST – We’re not a middleman. We work in trust and partnership with food retailers and smallholder farmers, helping them to improve their business model.
(4)	ACCESS – we offer smallholder farmers and food retailers access to optimized logistics that guarantee market access for farmers and increase the value of food through proper handling for retailers  
(5)	EFFICIENCY – Our integrated USSD and tech-enabled food trading platform not only allows smallholder farmers to sell at optimal prices and retailers/social institutions to stock at significantly low prices but also allows us to offer more efficient processing in the food market, which leads to less food waste and post-harvest losses.
Sustainable Change:
Poverty is a cyclical trap for millions of Africans with rural populations adversely affected, while food security remains an elusive goal for over a billion of the earth’s inhabitants. Further events like Tunisia’s Jasmine revolution demonstrates once more how important and affordable food is for stability and peace. And to face this globally pressing issue, it’s critical that the private sector plays a meaningful role.  However, merging business and social objectives requires ambition, strength of will and a dedication to business as unusual. And as agribusiness intersects a myriad of humanity’s greatest challenges, only by cultivating sustainable systems for its actors can lasting solutions be realized.   
The African continent is facing a food crisis greater than any other region in the world. Already affecting over 300 million people, the crisis is worsening due to climate variability, political instability, economic downturns, and other shocks. And the ensuing hunger and malnutrition puts communities at further risk of violence and exploitation. Both immediate needs and the root causes of food insecurity need to be addressed, urgently.

Through solar cooling & drying tech, mobile technology to make the movement of food smarter and more productive, along with ozone technology -a promising food decontamination technology, Nampya's long-term impact is to build a transparent, waste-free and self-sustaining agri-food ecosystem for East Africa.

For decades and centuries, farmers have been branded as un-bankable individuals simply because they’re dependent on agriculture - an activity in Africa without predictable cashflows. In Uganda particularly, because farmers can hardly market their hard-earned produce profitably, the following are pure facts among 80% of smallholder farmers in Uganda:
(i)	They lose 40% quality and volume to the environment
(ii).	They waste 30% of related inputs.
(iii).	They pay interest on loans
(iv).	They miss 40% marketing, and
(v).	They lack incentive to manage their land more productively.

The cooling intervention to allow farmers safely store and insure more of their harvest, is a maiden channel that attracts financial institutions and other value chain actors to this potential market.  Nampya Farmers Market allows crowding in other partners because Nampya’s food supply platform is built and established as open platform to enable authorized third-party systems (like banking, credit management and inputs management systems) to access farmers’ records for traceability, loan approvals, or any other prompted campaigns that could benefit farmers. The data collected on our food supply platform along the value chain presents an opportunity to scale. A web-based interface is already available, capturing production, sales records and credit analysis and reference for the smallholder farmers covering their KYC.

Our average greengrocers order their goods three times a week. So, we will give most of the greengrocers a 48-hour line of credit until the next delivery. This will not only allow them to sell more but also help them deal with their liquidity issues.
It is also part of our strategy to off-take the increased volumes through fresh food franchising. By this, Nampya plans to recruit young women without working capital from neighboring communities, prepare them and strategically place them in Prime Market Areas (PMAs) as greengrocers. And then Nampya will supply them with foods on credit and we shall share the profits with the women after selling the foods.
For the key change objective, Nampya Farmers Market seeks to provide the necessary innovative social work that can trigger comprehensive improvement in farmers’ livelihoods in Uganda and help to fill the country's food basket within which the poor can have the potential to increase the overall productivity and resilience of subsistence farming in the country, embracing its diversity of crops and fertile soils. Summary: Nampya Farmers Market is a Uganda-based agri-tech enterprise addressing post-harvest losses and food insecurity through solar-powered micro-warehouses, a USSD-based trading platform, and logistics that directly connect smallholder farmers to urban retailers and relief donors. Title: Agro-Digital Innovation for Rural Resilience
Subtitle: AgriPeace Idjwi connects women and youth to digital agroecology tools, skills, and markets—advancing climate resilience, local capacity, and inclusive rural livelihoods.
Problem Statement: Communities on Idjwi Island are trapped in a cycle of poverty and vulnerability due to critical gaps in digital access, climate-resilient agricultural knowledge, and economic inclusion. Women and youth key drivers of local development face systemic gender disparities and unemployment, limiting their ability to contribute to and benefit from sustainable growth. Simultaneously, outdated farming practices and significant food waste exacerbate environmental degradation and climate risks. Without urgent, innovative digital solutions that bridge these divides, the island’s social, economic, and ecological resilience will continue to deteriorate, undermining both local livelihoods and broader sustainable development goals.
Solution Overview:
AgriPeace Idjwi is a digital agroecology platform designed to empower smallholder farmers especially women and youth by providing access to climate-smart agricultural knowledge, digital tools, and inclusive market opportunities. The platform leverages mobile and web technologies to deliver localized training, real-time advisory services, and resource management solutions tailored to the island’s unique agro-ecological conditions.
How it works:
Farmers access the platform via smartphones or community digital hubs where they receive step-by-step guidance on sustainable farming practices, including soil health, water conservation, and crop diversification. The platform also facilitates the collection and redistribution of surplus produce to minimize food waste and improve food security. Additionally, it connects users to local and regional markets, enabling fairer prices and new income streams.
Methodologies and Technologies:
- Agro-ecological principles underpin all training content, promoting regenerative farming that protects biodiversity and builds resilience to climate shocks.
- Data-driven advisory tools use satellite data and IoT sensors where available to provide precise weather forecasts and soil condition monitoring.
- Mobile-first design ensures accessibility for users with basic smartphones and intermittent internet connectivity.
- Community digital hubs provide shared access points, training, and peer networking.
- Circular economy practices are integrated to reduce waste and optimize resource use.
Partnerships and Collaboration:
AgriPeace Idjwi works closely with local farmer cooperatives, women’s groups, and youth organizations to co-design and deploy the platform. Partnerships with agricultural research institutions and NGOs ensure content relevance and quality. Collaboration with local government bodies supports scaling efforts and policy alignment. Technical partners contribute with software development, data analytics, and digital literacy training, creating a multi-stakeholder ecosystem dedicated to sustainable rural development.
Solution Provider(s): Congo Peace Academy : A youth-led non-profit organization focused on peacebuilding, digital inclusion, and sustainable development in the Great Lakes region. Sector: Education, Digital Empowerment, Social Development.  Agroecology Cooperative : A local farmers’ cooperative specializing in agroecological practices and sustainable agriculture on Idjwi Island. Sector: Agriculture, Rural Development.  Idjwi Women’s Empowerment Network : A grassroots organization promoting gender equality and economic empowerment of women through training and advocacy. Sector: Gender Inclusion, Community Development.  B2R Foundation of Agricultural Sciences : Academic partner providing research, climate-smart farming methodologies, and data analytics support. Sector: Education, Research, Agriculture.  FFFoundation Green Solutions Ltd. : A technology company specializing in developing mobile platforms and IoT applications for sustainable agriculture. Sector: Technology, Digital Innovation.
Implementation location(s): The solution is currently being implemented on Idjwi Island, Democratic Republic of Congo.  Idjwi is a rural, climate-vulnerable island located in Lake Kivu, home to smallholder farmers and underserved communities targeted by the AgriPeace Idjwi platform.
Implementation timeline(s): The solution has been under implementation since January 2022 and is currently ongoing, with planned activities continuing through December 2026.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: The estimated duration to pilot AgriPeace Idjwi in a new geography is 12 to 18 months. This timeframe includes initial community engagement, capacity building, digital platform adaptation, training delivery, and monitoring & evaluation to ensure successful local adoption.
SDGs addressed: SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);SDG 13 (Climate Action);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives:
- Empower smallholder farmers, especially women and youth, with digital tools and agro-ecological knowledge to improve productivity and resilience.
-Reduce food waste through circular agroecology practices and efficient resource use.
- Strengthen inclusive rural economies by connecting farmers to markets and enabling fair income generation.
- Enhance climate resilience and environmental sustainability on Idjwi Island.
Key Achievements / Impacts:
- Engaged over 1,200 smallholder farmers (45% women, 40% youth) in digital agroecology training since 2022.
- Achieved an estimated 20% reduction in post-harvest food waste through improved handling and redistribution methods.
- Enabled the creation of 150 new local jobs in digital agriculture services and supply chains.
- Reduced greenhouse gas emissions by promoting regenerative farming practices and minimizing the use of chemical inputs (estimated 500 tons CO₂eq avoided annually).
- Improved household incomes by an average of 25% through better market access and diversified crops.
Key technologies:
Key Technologies Used:

Title: SmartSaha: Digital Traceability and Climate Tools for Inclusive Rural Supply Chains
Subtitle: Empowering smallholder farmers—especially women and youth—through traceability, climate data, and market access using a low-literacy-friendly digital platform.
Problem Statement: Smallholder farmers, particularly in rural Madagascar, face systemic barriers to inclusion in formal markets due to lack of traceability, limited access to climate data, weak digital infrastructure, and exclusion from finance and certification systems. Most operate informally and cannot meet buyer or regulatory requirements. Rural youth and women are underemployed, and digital tools are rarely accessible or adapted to their contexts. This results in low income, high post-harvest losses, and vulnerability to climate shocks—perpetuating cycles of inequality and economic exclusion.
Solution Overview:
SmartSaha is a digital platform that bridges the gap between smallholder farmers and formal markets by providing accessible tools for traceability, agroecological monitoring, and inventory management. It enables georeferenced mapping of producer plots, tracks harvest data, sends climate alerts (fire risks, rainfall), and manages batch-level traceability—all essential for certification and market compliance.

The platform is built using a mobile-first architecture with offline functionality, icon-based interfaces, and USSD/SMS options to accommodate low digital literacy. Its backend integrates with dashboards for cooperatives, NGOs, and buyers to monitor supply chains transparently.

SmartSaha works through partnerships with cooperatives, youth data collectors, and NGOs. Youth are trained to act as digital field agents who collect and input production data from farmers. Collaborations with agribusinesses, academic institutions (for R&D and data validation), and certifiers ensure traceability aligns with export standards. This multi-actor model reinforces digital inclusion, climate resilience, and rural economic participation.
Solution Provider(s): SmartSaha (digital agriculture platform, Madagascar), MAD’AROM (agribusiness and sourcing partner for valuable plants), ESSA – University of Antananarivo (academic partner in food sciences and digital R&D), NGOs (training and farmer inclusion programs, agroecology support and digital resilience), IMRA Laboratory (testing and product validation), ACQSDA & Ministry of Health Madagascar (food safety and traceability certifications), rural youth cooperatives and farmer groups (on-the-ground data and training implementation).
Implementation location(s): Vatovavy, Atsinanana, and Analamanga regions, Madagascar.
Implementation timeline(s): Pilot deployment began in Q1 2025 and is ongoing through 2025.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 5 months — including onboarding of partners, field agent training, georeferenced mapping, and live traceability testing with 50–100 producers.
SDGs addressed: SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 13 (Climate Action);
Desired impact:
SmartSaha aims to digitally transform rural value chains by integrating smallholder farmers,especially women and youth,into formal, traceable, and climate-resilient supply networks.
Objectives:
_Expand access to markets, certifications, and finance for smallholder producers and MSMEs.
_Generate decent digital and technical employment in rural areas, especially for women.
_Strengthen climate resilience through agroecological data, fire alerts, and early warning tools.
_Reduce post-harvest loss by improving planning and traceability.
Key Impacts to Date:
_2,000+ producers supported
_~30% reduction in post-harvest loss
_10 full-time digital jobs created for youth (≥70% women)
_50+ farms digitally mapped and monitored via SmartSaha
_Foundation for certification and export compliance digitized
Key technologies:
SmartSaha uses a combination of lightweight, mobile-first technologies adapted to rural connectivity and literacy constraints:
_Geospatial Mapping (GIS): For farmer plot registration and location-based monitoring
_IoT-Linked Climate Alerts: Fire detection and rainfall trends via remote sensors and satellite data
_USSD/SMS Integration: Ensures low-literate users can access services without smartphones
_Offline-First Mobile App: Enables data collection and syncing even in remote areas
_Digital Dashboards: Real-time monitoring and analytics for cooperatives, NGOs, and buyers
_QR/Batch Traceability System: Enables product tracking from farm to processing and export
Unique Characteristics:
SmartSaha is one of the few platforms built specifically for rural African value chains that combines traceability, climate risk monitoring, and digital inclusion in a single system. Key differentiators include:
_Designed with farmers: Developed in collaboration with local producers and youth cooperatives
_Low-literacy design: Icon-based interfaces and USSD for non-smartphone access
_Job creation built-in: Platform deploys trained rural youth as data agents and traceability officers
_End-to-end integration: Links informal farmers to formal systems (certification, market, export)
_Scalable & modular: Adaptable to new crops, regions, and markets
_Gender-forward model: Prioritizes digital employment for rural women in agri-tech
SmartSaha blends inclusive design, decentralized data collection, and climate-smart decision tools to address market exclusion at the last mile.
Sustainable Change:
SmartSaha addresses systemic rural exclusion by embedding digital tools into the everyday operations of smallholder producers, cooperatives, and agri-MSMEs. Its theory of change is built on enabling producers to move from informal, climate-vulnerable, and low-productivity systems to digitally traceable, market-integrated, and climate-resilient value chains.

By empowering rural youth, especially women, with tech jobs (e.g., data agents, field technicians), the platform fosters local capacity to manage traceability, certification readiness, and supply chain transparency. This shifts the power balance toward community-owned data and self-managed compliance systems.

Over time, SmartSaha contributes to system-level change by:
_Formalizing the role of smallholders in certified, export-ready systems
_Building a rural digital workforce that can scale beyond agriculture
_Creating data infrastructure for better policies and public–private partnerships
_Reducing environmental degradation through risk-based monitoring and early warnings
The platform becomes a catalyst for inclusive digital transformation, scalable across countries and sectors.
Funding Sources: SmartSaha has been self-funded by its founding team and supported through in-kind contributions from the associated agribusiness MAD’AROM. We actively seek project-based grants, innovation challenges, and competitions to support the development and scale-up of the platform. We are currently incubated in a national innovation program (Zafitody) and have applied to international opportunities to attract non-dilutive funding.
Further comments/feedback: We sincerely appreciate this opportunity to showcase inclusive digital innovations like SmartSaha. The questionnaire was clear and well-structured. We suggest including an optional upload section for brief demo videos or one-pagers to visually support the solution description. Thank you for supporting grassroots tech from emerging markets.
Primary thematic focus area: Stable and Resilient Digital Supply Chains
Summary: SmartSaha is a digital platform piloted in Madagascar that combines farmer traceability, climate risk monitoring, and market access tools for smallholder farmers. Built with low-literacy design, offline-first features, and USSD/SMS access, it enables georeferenced farm mapping, batch-level traceability, and climate alerts. Rural youth—especially women—are trained as digital field agents to collect and manage data, linking informal producers to formal certification and export systems. The platform is designed for scalability and inclusion, integrating cooperatives, NGOs, academic partners, and agribusinesses.

Title: A+ SmartTrade Hub: Digital Training & Business Support for MSMEs
Subtitle: A+ SmartTrade Hub empowers MSMEs in Plateau and Bauchi with digital skills, e-commerce tools, and business support to drive growth, sustainability, and inclusive economic development.
Problem Statement: The solution tackles the lack of structured business development support and low digital literacy among MSME owners in Northern Nigeria, particularly Plateau and Bauchi States. Most MSMEs operate informally, with limited access to digital tools, financial literacy, and structured markets, making them unprepared for investment and growth. These challenges hinder their ability to scale, attract investors, and compete in modern digital economies. The A+ SmartTrade Hub bridges this gap by providing digital training, formalization support, and market access strategies to build investor-ready, sustainable MSMEs.
Solution Overview:
A+ SmartTrade Hub is a blended digital and physical incubation model designed to empower MSMEs in Plateau and Bauchi States through structured digital skills development, business formalization, and access-to-market strategies. The hub provides a step-by-step support system to move informal MSMEs into the formal economy, making them investor-ready and digitally enabled.

Assessment & Onboarding

MSMEs undergo a baseline digital and business readiness assessment.

Customized learning pathways and business support plans are created for each MSME.

Digital Skills Training & Business Development Support

Practical training in essential digital skills: smartphone business tools, digital bookkeeping, social media marketing, e-commerce, and cybersecurity.

Business development modules: business structuring, branding, product pricing, investor pitching, and access to finance.

E-Commerce & Market Access Enablement

Training MSMEs to list their products on local and global e-commerce platforms.

Support with digital product packaging, mobile payments integration, and online store creation.

Investment Readiness & Mentorship

MSMEs are guided to create business plans, financial forecasts, and digital pitch decks.

Each MSME is matched with an industry mentor to provide coaching and connect with investors.

Certification & Continuous Support

Certified MSMEs gain access to periodic digital trade fairs, A+ partner marketplaces, and post-training incubation support for 6–12 months.

Methodologies and Technologies Used
Blended Learning Approach
Physical training at the A+ MSME Hubs in Jos and Bauchi, complemented by virtual modules via the A+ Online Learning Portal and WhatsApp-based micro-learning.

Digital Tools Integration

Microsoft 365 for productivity training

Google Business Profile setup

AI tools for business content creation

WhatsApp Business and mobile apps for marketing & customer service

Human-Centered Design (HCD)
All training and support services are tailored to the local context, language, and literacy levels of the participants.

Data Tracking & Impact Analytics

Digital dashboards to track MSME growth metrics, sales, and online visibility

Baseline and post-training surveys for monitoring outcomes

Partnerships and Collaboration Models
Local Government and MSME Agencies

Collaboration with Plateau and Bauchi State Ministries of Commerce and Digital Economy, SMEDAN, and BOI for MSME selection, endorsement, and post-training funding support.

Development Partners & Donors

Engagement with UNIDO, UNDP, and private donor agencies for technical assistance, visibility, and scaling support.

Private Sector Partners

E-commerce platforms (e.g., Jumia, Flutterwave Store)

Telcos for subsidized data packages for MSMEs

Local banks and microfinance institutions for access-to-credit schemes

Technology Providers

Partnership with Microsoft, Google for Startups, and local tech firms to provide tools, training licenses, and cloud hosting.

Academic and Incubation Partners

Collaboration with local universities, NBTE, and innovation hubs for curriculum validation, research support, and joint program delivery.

Title: Allo Docteur TV – Inclusive Digital Health Platform
Subtitle: Multilingual web TV and mobile platform delivering trusted health education, fact-checking, and e-health services to empower communities across Guinea and beyond.
Problem Statement: In Guinea, limited access to reliable health information, the proliferation of health-related misinformation, and low digital literacy contribute to high maternal, neonatal, and child mortality rates, preventable disease outbreaks, and poor health-seeking behaviors. Rural and marginalized populations, especially women and youth, face linguistic, geographic, and economic barriers to accessing quality health services. The absence of dedicated, trusted digital health platforms and localized content further widens the digital and health divide, undermining progress towards universal health coverage and inclusive development.
Solution Overview:
Detailed description of how the solution works
Allo Docteur TV is Guinea’s first multilingual, fully digital health education platform combining a web TV, mobile application, and social media channels to deliver accurate, culturally adapted health information. Content is co-created with health professionals, validated by official health authorities, and produced in French and key national languages (Pular, Malinké, Soussou, etc.). The platform offers diverse formats — interactive talk shows, documentaries, micro-learning videos, fact-checking segments, and community reports — designed to improve health literacy, counter misinformation, and encourage positive health behaviors. Users can access on-demand videos, live streams, and push notifications, and participate in community engagement through clubs d’écoute in rural areas.

Methodologies and technologies used

Multichannel access: Web streaming, mobile app (Android & iOS), Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp.

Inclusive design: Multilingual content, offline access options, IVR/USSD for basic phones.

Content validation process: Structured editorial workflow involving medical experts, public health authorities, and professional health bodies.

E-health integration: Online health directory, appointment booking, teleconsultation via partners, and localized health alerts.

Data and impact tracking: Analytics dashboard (audience, engagement, learning outcomes) and community surveys for continuous improvement.

Micro-learning pedagogy: Short, interactive modules with quizzes and certification badges.

Partnerships and collaboration models

Institutional partners: Ministry of Health of Guinea, National Public Health Institute, professional medical orders (doctors, pharmacists).

International organizations: Collaboration prospects with WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA for content co-development and distribution.

Private sector: Telecom operators for zero-rating and SMS/USSD integration; local SMEs for production, logistics, and translation.

Civil society & communities: NGOs, youth associations, and women’s groups to mobilize local “digital ambassadors” and host listening clubs.

Media partners: National and community radio/TV stations to amplify reach and adapt content for non-internet audiences.

Sector: ICT / Technology, Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene of Guinea – Government institution responsible for public health policy, health service delivery, and health promotion. Sector: Public Health / Government, National Public Health Institute of Guinea (INSP) – Specialized institution for epidemiology, disease surveillance, and health research. Sector: Public Health / Research, Order of Physicians of Guinea – Professional regulatory body ensuring standards and ethics in medical practice. Sector: ICT / Telecommunications.

Implementation timeline(s): Start date: January 2023 – Ongoing (initial deployment in Conakry, progressive rollout to other regions planned through 2025).

Desired impact:
Solution Objectives

Improve health literacy and access to trusted health information for all populations, especially women, youth, and rural communities.

Reduce misinformation in the health sector through a validated content and fact-checking process.

Facilitate access to health services via digital tools (directories, appointment booking, teleconsultation via partners).

Empower local MSMEs and media professionals through training, employment, and service contracts.

Strengthen community engagement in health promotion using multilingual, culturally relevant content.

Title: Inclusive Digital Hubs for Women and Girls with Disabilities in Conflict-Affected Regions
Subtitle: A mobile‑first, trauma‑informed digital inclusion model empowering women and girls with disabilities in post‑conflict Northeast Nigeria.
Problem Statement:
Women and girls with disabilities in post-conflict Northeast Nigeria face compounded vulnerabilities, resulting from systemic exclusion, prolonged insecurity, displacement, and gender-based violence. In the BAY states (Borno, Adamawa, Yobe), they are significantly underrepresented in digital spaces due to limited access to technology, assistive devices, digital literacy opportunities, and safe platforms for self-expression or reporting abuse.
Structural barriers including inaccessible infrastructure, stigma, and policy neglect, limit their participation in economic, social, and civic life. While digital platforms offer potential for empowerment, current models often fail to account for the realities of disability in conflict-affected, resource-constrained settings.
The solution addresses:
•	Digital exclusion of women and girls with disabilities in fragile, underserved areas.
•	Inaccessibility of digital tools and content, including learning platforms and reporting mechanisms.
•	Lack of safe, disability-friendly channels for GBV reporting and access to services.
•	Limited integration of assistive technologies in humanitarian response and recovery systems.
•	Absence of tailored digital capacity-building in post-conflict recovery efforts.
This model confronts these challenges holistically by combining mobile-first learning, trauma-informed digital hubs, assistive device distribution, and accessible GBV tech, positioning inclusion as foundational to digital transformation in post-crisis societies.
Solution Overview:
A. Description of how the solution works

The solution is a Post-Conflict Digital Recovery Model designed to foster the full and effective participation of women and girls with disabilities across the BAY States (Maiduguri, Damaturu, and Yola North). Building on a successful pilot in Michika and Madagali, it combines accessible digital learning, assistive device support, and safe reporting mechanisms into a cohesive empowerment ecosystem.
Key components include:
1.	Virtual Inclusion Hubs: Disability-accessible learning and support centers are established, equipped with assistive technologies and solar-powered infrastructure. These hubs serve as safe spaces for learning, peer interaction, and civic participation.
2.	Mobile-First Digital Literacy Training: Tailored digital literacy programs are delivered through smartphones and tablets, reaching women and girls with disabilities in hard-to-reach or mobile-only contexts. Training includes social media engagement, advocacy, job skills, and content creation.
3.	Trauma-Informed Approach: Programming integrates psychosocial support and uses healing-centered facilitation methods, acknowledging the compounded trauma from conflict and exclusion.
4.	Integration of SmartRR App: DKF has partnered with BigFamily360 Foundation to make the SmartRR GBV reporting app disability-friendly. The app is deployed as a confidential platform for reporting incidents and accessing survivor-centered services.
5.	Distribution of Assistive Devices: Based on individual needs assessments, the program provides hearing aids, wheelchairs, white canes, and other mobility or communication aids, ensuring equitable access to digital platforms and services.
6.	Capacity Building of Facilitators: Local facilitators, including women with disabilities, are trained to run hubs, support digital learning, and act as peer mentors, strengthening sustainability and community ownership.


B. Methodologies and technologies used.

1. Participatory Learning Methodology: The curriculum is co-designed with women and girls with disabilities to ensure contextual relevance and agency.

2. Mobile-first Approach: Leveraging Nigeria’s growing smartphone penetration, training is optimized for mobile access, with options for low-data or offline learning modules.

3. Assistive Technology Integration: Hardware and software include screen readers (JAWS), high-contrast displays, large-print keyboards, styluses, magnifiers, braille devices, and hearing support tools.

4. Solar-Powered Infrastructure: Ensures consistent access in areas with unreliable electricity.

5. Human-Centered Design (HCD): Both the digital training and SmartRR app are designed with feedback from persons with disabilities, ensuring usability and dignity.

C. Partnerships and Collaboration Models

Collaboration is central to the model's success and sustainability. Key partnerships include:
•	Disability Working Group (DWG): Ensures alignment with national disability standards and connects the program with government and humanitarian actors.
•	Joint National Association of Persons With Disabilities (JONAPWD): Co-leads community mobilization, beneficiary identification, and monitoring, ensuring strong representation and ownership by the disability community.
•	BigFamily360 Foundation: Technical partner for the SmartRR app, working with DKF to make it accessible and disability-inclusive.
•	Government MDAs (e.g., State Ministries of Women Affairs, Education, and ICT): Support policy linkages, provide technical backing, and offer infrastructure support.
•	Community Gatekeepers and Leaders: Support local buy-in, security, and identification of safe spaces for women and girls.
Solution Provider(s): Joint National Association of Persons With Disabilities (JONAPWD) – National umbrella body advocating for disability rights (Disability, Civil Society), Disability Working Group (DWG) – Humanitarian coordination platform for inclusive response (Humanitarian, Coordination), BigFamily360 Foundation – Developer of SmartRR app; tech-driven GBV solutions (Technology, GBV, Inclusion), State Ministries of Women Affairs (Adamawa, Borno, Yobe) – Gender and disability policy support (Government, Gender), State Ministries of Education & ICT – Technical/policy support for digital learning hubs (Government, Education/ICT), Local Government Authorities & Community Leaders – Grassroots engagement and mobilization (Governance, Community).
Implementation location(s): Nigeria, Adamawa State, Michika and Madagali Local Governement Areas
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 15 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives
1. Bridge the digital divide for women and girls with disabilities in post-conflict regions (Yola North, Damaturu, and Maiduguri), enabling full participation in education, economic life, and civic spaces.
2. Establish disability-inclusive digital ecosystems that empower beneficiaries with tools for digital literacy, entrepreneurship, and self-advocacy.
3. Integrate GBV protection services by scaling the disability-adapted SmartRR app to enhance access to support and reporting channels.
4. Foster systemic change through multi-stakeholder partnerships, including government agencies, CSOs, tech providers, and DPOs, driving policy shifts and inclusive development agendas.


Key Achievements /Impacts 

•	Reach at least 1,500 women and girls with disabilities across 3 states with digital skills training and support services.
•	Equip 600 individuals with assistive technologies that enhance access to information, mobility, and productivity.
•	Train 60 peer mentors and facilitators, strengthening local capacity and ensuring sustainability through community ownership.
•	Enable 400 users to access GBV reporting and referral services through the adapted SmartRR mobile platform.
•	Stimulate inclusive microenterprise growth, with at least 150 beneficiaries supported in launching or scaling digital or home-based businesses.
•	Support local and state-level policy engagement, targeting at least 3 government bodies for regulatory improvements and increased funding for digital inclusion.
Key technologies:
1. Mobile-First Digital Platforms - leveraging mobile devices as the primary access point for digital literacy, microenterprise, and GBV services—especially critical in low-resource, post-conflict contexts where smartphones are more accessible than computers.
2. Assistive Technologies -  includes screen readers (e.g., JAWS, NVDA), text-to-speech tools, hearing aids, mobility devices, and accessible keyboards/styluses adapted for individuals with visual, hearing, or mobility impairments.
3. Disability-Friendly Mobile App (SmartRR) - in partnership with Big Family360 Foundation, the SmartRR app was enhanced to support inclusive GBV reporting, service referrals, and real-time support tailored to persons with disabilities.
4.Cloud-Based Learning Tools - virtual learning modules and accessibility-focused digital literacy programs are hosted online and designed for low bandwidth environments.
Unique Characteristics:
What makes this solution unique is its positioning as a post-conflict digital recovery model specifically designed for women and girls with disabilities, an often excluded group in both humanitarian response and digital development. Unlike traditional digital inclusion programs, this solution is built from the ground up to be mobile-first and disability-inclusive by design, reflecting both the high smartphone penetration in the target regions and the complex accessibility needs of its users.
A key differentiator is the integration of the SmartRR app, co-developed with Big Family360 Foundation and adapted by DKF to ensure full accessibility for users with visual, hearing, and mobility impairments. This app connects survivors of gender-based violence to responsive services in real time, embedding protection mechanisms within a broader digital empowerment ecosystem.
Moreover, the solution combines digital skills development, assistive technology access, psychosocial support, and entrepreneurship pathways, bridging immediate needs with long-term resilience. It is anchored in a rights-based, collaborative model that involves government agencies, the Disability Working Group, and the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities (JONAPWD), ensuring both community ownership and policy relevance.
Sustainable Change:
How the Solution Creates Sustainable, Systemic Change
This solution creates sustainable, systemic change by establishing a disability-inclusive digital ecosystem that transforms individual agency, community roles, and institutional behavior—laying the groundwork for long-term inclusion in post-conflict environments.

Theory of Change Logic

Phase 1: Individual Empowerment
If women and girls with disabilities access adaptive digital tools, trauma-informed training, and GBV-responsive platforms like SmartRR,
then they build digital confidence, self-advocacy, and safe online navigation skills.

Phase 2: Economic and Civic Participation
If digitally empowered women access microenterprise opportunities and civic engagement platforms,
then they emerge as visible economic actors and community leaders, challenging stigma around gender and disability.

Phase 3: Institutional Influence
If government, DPOs, and private actors observe outcomes and participate in co-creation,
then they integrate inclusive design into policies, budgets, and service delivery systems.
Phase 4: Replication and Scale
If the model proves effective in Yola, Damaturu, and Maiduguri,
then it becomes a scalable reference for post-conflict digital inclusion in fragile settings.

Sustainability Pathways
Financial
- Peer trainer networks reduce operational cost
- State government partnerships embed hubs in public budgets
- Telecom collaborations sustain connectivity support
- Participant-run enterprises create economic ripple effects

Institutional
- Integration with state disability and gender strategies
- Strengthened DPO capacity for local ownership and continuity
- Inclusive service delivery norms institutionalized via training
- Replication enabled through toolkits and open documentation

Technical
•	Mobile-first design leverages existing infrastructure
•	Open-source tools reduce maintenance costs
•	Local tech capacity ensures updates and support are community-led

Desired Follow-On Effects (5–10 Year Vision)
Individuals
- Over 1,500 women and girls with disabilities sustain active digital and economic participation
- Over 300 peer trainers lead inclusion efforts across their communities
- Significant gains in income, civic voice, and service access

Institutions
-  BAY state governments adopt digital accessibility standards
-  DPOs and women’s groups embed digital empowerment in core programming
- Telecoms and digital providers adopt inclusive design across services
- Public systems (health, education, protection) integrate digital access requirements

Society
- Norm shifts evident in increased representation of women with disabilities in leadership
- Disability inclusion is embedded in national digital policy frameworks
- The model is replicated across other post-conflict regions
- A broader societal shift sees disability reframed as diversity, not deficiency

Systemic Change Indicators
-  Number of revised policies with accessibility clauses; % of services meeting standards
- Adoption of inclusive design by private sector; growth in disability-inclusive digital employment
- Social Capital: Inclusion in mainstream development agendas; increase in rights-based narratives and leadership roles
Funding Sources: Nigerian Humanitarian Fund(NHF) and UNWOMEN
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: A mobile-first, trauma-informed digital inclusion model empowering women and girls with disabilities in post-conflict Northeast Nigeria through digital literacy, GBV reporting, and inclusive technology.

Title: AKE: Māori-led digital platform for iwi services, data, and wellbeing.
Subtitle: AKE is a Māori-led digital platform directing social spend to iwi-run services, using data sovereignty and wellbeing models to improve outcomes and empower communities.
Problem Statement: Many indigenous and underserved communities face persistent digital, economic, and service access gaps. Current systems are fragmented, Crown-controlled, and slow to respond, leaving whānau without timely support. This results in poorer health, housing instability, educational inequity, and reduced economic participation. Without culturally grounded, data-driven solutions, the cycle of disadvantage continues.
Solution Overview:
The AKE solution works as an integrated, iwi-governed digital infrastructure that connects community members, service providers, and funders through a single secure platform.

1. Data Sovereignty & Digital Twin Engine

Iwi and communities own and control their data.

A “digital twin” model creates a real-time, dynamic profile of individuals and whānau, mapping needs, risks, and strengths.

Data is drawn from government, NGOs, wearable devices, and community inputs, with strict consent protocols.


2. Community Access Apps

Te Pou Hihiri: One-stop access to health, housing, transport, education, and financial support.

Te Poutama: Learning management with educational rewards.

Te Pouranga: Iwi-based rideshare and transport scheduling.


3. Outcome-Based Procurement Hub

Redirects government and social investment spend to iwi-vetted suppliers for food, fuel, devices, housing, and other essentials.

Tracks spend in real time and links it to measurable wellbeing outcomes.


4. Measurement & Reporting

Uses UN Sustainable Development Goals, He Ara Waiora, and iwi-specific wellbeing measures.

Dashboards provide live ROI and impact tracking for funders, iwi, and community leaders.


5. Funding & Sustainability

Supports Social Investment Bonds, enabling reinvestment of returns into community priorities.

Creates local employment in data management, wellbeing navigation, and service delivery.


In practice, this means a whānau member can request support through the app, the system identifies the most urgent needs, matches them with local iwi or partner services, funds the intervention, and tracks the outcome — all within a culturally grounded, data-secure environment.

If you want, I can now also create a one-paragraph plain language version of this so it’s easy for non-technical readers to understand.
Solution Provider(s): UNICEF, Ngati Kahungunu, Oranga Tamariki, Ngati Toa
Implementation location(s): Ngati Kahungunu in Hastings New Zealand
Implementation timeline(s): We are working through a Pilot, will have at scale production by November
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being);
Desired impact:
The AKE solution aims to lift whānau wellbeing by improving health, housing, education, and income; close the digital divide through universal access and skills; stimulate the Māori economy via local procurement and job creation; uphold data sovereignty and self-determination; and enable transparent, real-time impact reporting.

Aligned to UN Sustainable Development Goals, it supports:

No Poverty (SDG 1)

Zero Hunger (SDG 2)

Good Health and Wellbeing (SDG 3)

Quality Education (SDG 4)

Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 8)

Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10)

Sustainable Cities and Communities (SDG 11)

Partnerships for the Goals (SDG 17)
Key technologies:
Key Technologies in the AKE Solution

1. Digital Twin & Wellbeing OS – AI-driven models map real-time community needs, forecast risks, and guide interventions.


2. Predictive Analytics – Multi-source data analysis to enable proactive, not reactive, service delivery.


3. Data Sovereignty Cloud – Secure, iwi-controlled infrastructure with consent-based access.


4. Integrated Apps – Te Pou Hihiri (services), Te Poutama (education), Te Pouranga (transport).


5. Real-Time Dashboards – Live reporting aligned to UN SDGs, He Ara Waiora, and iwi metrics.


6. Case Management & CRM – Workflow orchestration from request to outcome.


7. API Integration – Secure links to government, NGO, and health systems.


8. Procurement Engine – Tracks social spend and links it directly to wellbeing results.
Unique Characteristics:
What Makes AKE Unique

1. Treaty-Led & Culturally Grounded – Built on Wai 262 principles, AKE is designed and governed by iwi, embedding tikanga Māori and He Ara Waiora into every layer of the platform.


2. True Data Sovereignty – Communities own, control, and benefit from their data, with infrastructure and governance models that keep authority local.


3. Integrated Wellbeing & Economic Model – Links health, housing, education, and social procurement with a real-time funding and outcomes engine, turning social spend into measurable community value.


4. Digital Twin Technology for Social Impact – Uses AI to model whānau and community wellbeing in real time, allowing for early interventions and scenario planning.


5. Global-Ready Indigenous Framework – While rooted in Māori governance, the architecture is adaptable for other indigenous and underserved populations worldwide.


6. Direct Economic Empowerment – Redirects procurement and investment into iwi-owned and local enterprises, creating jobs and keeping value within communities.


7. Measurable, Transparent Impact – Real-time dashboards align outcomes with UN SDGs, Treasury wellbeing measures, and iwi priorities, ensuring accountability to both funders and whānau.
Sustainable Change:
Sustainable, Systemic Change – Theory of Change

The AKE solution transforms how social investment is directed, delivered, and measured, shifting from fragmented, Crown-led service provision to integrated, iwi-governed systems.

1. Inputs

Treaty-led governance (Wai 262, data sovereignty)

Digital twin and AI-enabled wellbeing platform

Integrated apps for service access, education, and transport

Procurement engine linking spend to local iwi suppliers

Real-time dashboards aligned with UN SDGs and iwi wellbeing measures


2. Activities

Capture and integrate data from government, NGOs, and community in a consent-based platform

Identify risks and opportunities early using predictive analytics

Direct procurement to local suppliers, creating employment and retaining value in the region

Deliver coordinated services across housing, health, education, and income support

Monitor and report outcomes continuously


3. Immediate Outcomes (1–2 years)

Increased access to essential services through digital platforms

Reduced crisis interventions via early, proactive support

Creation of sustainable local jobs in data, service delivery, and wellbeing navigation

Digital inclusion through universal device and connectivity provision


4. Medium-Term Outcomes (3–5 years)

Measurable uplift in health, housing stability, education attainment, and income for whānau

Strengthened Māori economy through local procurement and enterprise growth

Empowered iwi with full control over service design, delivery, and evaluation

Data-informed decision-making at community level


5. Long-Term Outcomes (5+ years)

Systemic shift to Treaty-led, outcomes-based social investment

Reduced inequalities in health, education, and economic participation (SDGs 1, 3, 4, 8, 10)

Resilient, self-determining communities with the capacity to adapt solutions globally

Scalable indigenous-led service model replicated in other regions and countries


Follow-On Effects
Deployment of AKE will normalise iwi as equal partners in social investment, embed data sovereignty as a standard, and create a feedback loop where economic, digital, and wellbeing gains compound over time. This will reduce dependency on centralised systems, ensure resources remain in community hands, and establish a replicable framework for indigenous-led systemic change.

Through AI-enabled, culturally grounded systems, it redirects investment to local economies, strengthens community resilience, and creates a scalable model for inclusive, sustainable development.

Title: FarmXic AeroGrow™️ Digital Farming Ecosystem
Subtitle: Empowering communities with smart, sustainable farming solutions for food security and inclusive digital growth.
Problem Statement: Over 33 million smallholder farmers in Africa face low yields due to poor access to climate-resilient technology, market information, and finance. At the same time, rural and peri-urban communities remain excluded from the digital economy due to poor connectivity, lack of skills, and minimal access to e-commerce channels. This digital divide perpetuates poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality.
Solution Overview:
FarmXic’s AeroGrow is an IoT-enabled aeroponic planting tower designed to empower households, youth, and smallholder farmers to grow fresh produce year-round using minimal space, water, and energy. The solution integrates precision farming sensors, a cloud-based AI platform, and a mobile application to monitor plant health, nutrient levels, and growth cycles in real time. Users receive tailored recommendations, predictive yield analytics, and access to an e-marketplace to sell surplus produce, bridging the gap between production and market access.

Methodologies and Technologies Used:
	•	Aeroponics & Soilless Farming: Uses nutrient-rich mist, reducing water usage by up to 95% and eliminating soil-borne diseases.
	•	IoT & Sensor Networks: Tracks pH, EC, humidity, and light intensity to optimize crop growth.
	•	AI-Driven Analytics: Provides predictive farming insights and automates irrigation/nutrient delivery.
	•	Digital Marketplace Integration: Connects growers to buyers, enabling inclusive participation in the digital economy.
	•	Data-Driven Capacity Building: Offers digital literacy and agritech training through the mobile app.

Partnerships and Collaboration Models:
FarmXic operates through a co-creation model, collaborating with:
	•	Agritech hardware partners for local manufacturing and cost optimization.
	•	Telecom operators to ensure rural internet connectivity.
	•	NGOs and development agencies for community outreach, training, and gender inclusion programs.
	•	Financial institutions and micro-lenders to provide lease-to-own financing for low-income users.
	•	Off-taker agreements with supermarkets and agro-processors to secure market access for AeroGrow users.

By combining smart agriculture with digital inclusion, AeroGrow transforms small spaces into income-generating, climate-resilient farms while enabling underserved communities to actively participate in the digital economy.

Title: NDZILA AI & OGOOUE PAD – Inclusion numérique abordable et hors ligne pour l’Afrique
Subtitle: Combler la fracture numérique africaine grâce à des tablettes IA abordables et hors ligne dédiées à l’éducation, l’entrepreneuriat et le développement communautaire.
Problem Statement: Dans de nombreuses régions d’Afrique, l’accès à Internet reste coûteux, instable ou inexistant, laissant des millions de personnes exclues de l’éducation numérique, des opportunités entrepreneuriales et des services essentiels. Le coût élevé des appareils et la dépendance à une connexion constante accentuent la fracture économique numérique
Solution Overview:
Notre solution associe NDZILA AI, une plateforme intelligente d’éducation et de développement des compétences, à l’OGOOUE PAD, une tablette robuste et peu coûteuse optimisée pour un usage hors ligne.

Fonctionnement : NDZILA AI est préchargée avec du contenu éducatif multilingue, des modules de formation professionnelle, des ressources entrepreneuriales et des services communautaires. L’OGOOUE PAD fonctionne entièrement hors ligne et ne se synchronise que lorsqu’une connexion à faible bande passante est disponible.

Technologies : IA pour l’apprentissage adaptatif, compression de contenu hors ligne, intégration du chargement solaire, synchronisation store-and-forward.

Partenariats : Collaboration avec des ONG locales, des institutions éducatives et des fournisseurs d’énergie renouvelable pour la distribution et le support.
Solution Provider(s): OGOOUE CORPS TECHNOLOGIES (Chef de projet) – Innovation numérique, solutions IA et fabrication de matériel abordable. Partenariats avec des institutions éducatives et ONG locales au Gabon, ainsi que des fournisseurs d’énergie renouvelable pour l’intégration solaire.
Implementation location(s): Déploiement prévu au Gabon (Mekambo, Libreville, Port-Gentil,Franceville Oyem Makokou) avec potentiel d’extension aux communautés rurales d’Afrique centrale et de l’Ouest
Implementation timeline(s): Pilote prévu du 4ᵉ trimestre 2025 au 2ᵉ trimestre 2026.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 à 6 mois, incluant la localisation du contenu et l’intégration des partenaires.
SDGs addressed: SDG 4 (Quality Education);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);
Desired impact:
Fournir un accès numérique abordable et hors ligne à 1 million d’Africains en 5 ans.

Réduire de plus de 70 % les coûts d’accès numérique pour les communautés ciblées.

Créer des emplois locaux dans l’assemblage, la maintenance et la formation.
Key technologies: Intelligence artificielle (IA), systèmes de gestion de contenu hors ligne, technologie de chargement solaire, protocoles de synchronisation à faible bande passante.
Unique Characteristics: Solution IA “offline-first” adaptée aux zones à faible connectivité, matériel abordable conçu pour les conditions africaines, contenu multilingue préchargé et modèle de partenariat public-privé évolutif.
Sustainable Change: En supprimant les obstacles liés à la connectivité et aux coûts, NDZILA AI & OGOOUE PAD permettent une inclusion durable dans l’économie numérique, favorisant l’autonomie, le développement des compétences et les écosystèmes d’innovation locaux.
Funding Sources: La solution a jusqu’à présent été financée principalement par des ressources propres, des contributions d’ONG locales et des partenariats ponctuels avec des acteurs privés. Dans certaines implémentations pilotes, un soutien en nature (fourniture d’équipements, expertise technique) a été apporté par des organisations partenaires. Aucun financement institutionnel à grande échelle n’a encore été mobilisé, mais des discussions sont en cours avec des investisseurs à impact et des programmes d’innovation technologique.
Testimonials and Endorsements:
Grâce à NDZILA AI sur l’OGOOUE PAD, les enseignants, les élèves, les parents et les habitants de Libreville, Oyem, Makokou, Franceville, Mekambo et d’autres villes du Gabon peuvent accéder à des contenus éducatifs de qualité, même sans connexion Internet." — Enseignant partenaire, Gabon.

"Les modules d’éducation à la santé préchargés sur la tablette permettent aux familles et aux communautés d’accéder facilement à des informations fiables, renforçant la prévention et la sensibilisation dans plusieurs régions du pays." — Agent de santé communautaire, Gabon.

"Les ressources disponibles sur la tablette, notamment en agriculture et en gestion d’entreprise, m’ont aidé à développer mes compétences et à améliorer mes revenus." — Jeune entrepreneur, Gabon.

L’expérience pilote avec NDZILA AI sur l’OGOOUE PAD a montré un fort intérêt de la part des enseignants, élèves, parents et habitants, aussi bien en zones urbaines qu’en zones rurales. La capacité d’utiliser la solution hors connexion répond à un besoin crucial dans de nombreuses régions du Gabon, et les retours confirment que cette accessibilité favorise un apprentissage continu et une meilleure diffusion des connaissances.
Des améliorations envisagées incluent l’ajout de nouveaux contenus sectoriels (santé, agriculture, entrepreneuriat) et l’expansion du réseau de partenaires pour faciliter le déploiement dans d’autres villes du Gabon et, à terme, dans d’autres pays africains.
