AI-Powered Learning Platform
Core technology for delivering personalized training content.
Uses machine learning algorithms to assess each participant’s skills, learning pace, and preferred style, then adapts the curriculum accordingly.
Supports multilingual delivery and accessibility for low-bandwidth environments.

Central hub for courses, assignments, assessments, and resources.
Enables offline learning options for areas with limited internet access.

Title: Business Growth
Subtitle: Business Growth is a 5 to 7 month acceleration program which aims to strengthen the economic power of women responsible for SMEs through E-commerce and International Trade around four (04) main components.
Problem Statement:
In developing countries, women-led businesses are on average less productive than those led by men, due to constraints related to access to skills, financing, technology, inputs, training, networks, as well as availability given their multiple responsibilities as women. Women-led businesses are also less involved in international trade. The percentage of women business owners generating 25% or more of their turnover with international customers is very low in developing regions (4% in sub-Saharan Africa, 5% in Latin America and the Caribbean, and 10% in East/South Asia and the Pacific).
Several obstacles therefore hinder women's entrepreneurship and access to markets, ranging from social norms to family obligations and transportation issues. Women often find themselves unable to physically travel to markets to sell their products or participate in international trade fairs. On the one hand, digital technologies and e-commerce have promoted women entrepreneurs' access to markets by reducing investment requirements, allowing flexible time management, and offering the possibility of overcoming cultural and mobility barriers. On the other hand, the pandemic has created new opportunities, particularly for women entrepreneurs, thanks to the expansion of the e-commerce sector. It is important to support women in the use of technology and connectivity so that they can better benefit from the expansion of e-commerce.
Solution Overview:
Overall objective: Business Growth is implemented over two main phases, each aiming to provide women entrepreneurs with innovative tools to promote their businesses and/or services online, with the aim of expanding into local, regional, and international markets. It is comprised of two (2) main phases:
Phase 1 : E-commerce Tour (1 to 3 months)
 A national training tour in targeted municipalities for women SME managers. Training focuses on:
E-commerce (awareness from the design stage of their product and how to go about it);
Using the local platform www.lons.africa to create an online store in less than 15 minutes;
An introduction to Artificial Intelligence to create content (packaging, product sheets, visuals);
Export rules and the AfCFTA.
Phase 2 : Acceleration, a hybrid support phase lasting 3 to 4 months Women SMEs trained for Phase 1 are selected from across the country.
Four (04) components: (Deepen the concepts seen during phase 1 followed by personalized coaching)
Component I: Promote the commercial and economic integration of African women in international markets through e-commerce and international trade, with the aim of increasing their business potential by strengthening their skills in these sectors.
Component II: Optimize the export plans of women-led SMEs by supporting them in creating effective strategies to increase their international sales through the development of robust export plans.
Component III: Promote women's leadership and develop the skills needed to become effective entrepreneurs, aiming to equip each woman with sharp leadership and solid managerial skills.
Component IV: Strengthen the financial management skills of women's SMEs with digital accounting www.iwo.bj, by supporting them so that they can access fundraising and establish credible partnerships, while facilitating their integration into the formal economy through up-to-date accounting discipline, up-to-date and printable financial statements, separation of the company's cash and that of the household, for example.
Methodology
Phase 1: National Tour called “E-commerce Tour”
The launch of a national tour called "E-Commerce TOUR" in 10 strategic municipalities in Benin, which will reach 300 women, with 30 women per municipality. This training tour will last two (2) days per intervention area and aims to address several key topics, namely:
What is e-commerce and how to do it online?
Understanding and identifying the opportunities and obstacles in e-commerce.
The steps for registering and creating online stores.
How to conduct prospecting, promote products, and set online prices in the face of competition?
How to process online orders and, above all, how to export their products internationally. This involves:
Knowledge of export methods and related costs.
Access to reliable platforms specializing in import/export e-commerce at very affordable prices.
This preparatory tour helps break down mental and ideological barriers to women's access to international markets, understand their challenges, appreciate their experiences in these fields, and train them on e-commerce. It will also allow for advance preparation of the support phase itself based on their needs.
Phase 2: Four-month acceleration phase.
Proceed with the selection of 75 SMEs which will enter the 4-month acceleration program.
This acceleration phase aims to provide tailored support to these 75 women selected after the tour phase. In order to effectively and efficiently achieve the program's objectives, several areas of expertise are made available to support these women. The SMEs emerge from this phase with a new level of maturity.

This combination of technology, training, financing, and women's empowerment makes the program a differentiated model, particularly suited to the realities of Benin and West Africa.
Sustainable Change:
The Business Growth Women EdTech program aims to generate lasting systemic change by acting at multiple levels: individual, community, economic, and institutional. It is based on a theory of change that presumes that if women SME managers are trained, supported, connected to digital tools, and equipped with international trade skills, they will be able to sustainably increase their economic autonomy, generate employment, influence their environment, and integrate into global value chains.
In the short term, the program strengthens the technical, managerial, financial, and digital skills of 300 women, enabling them to access new markets, particularly through e-commerce. Through individualized support and the use of tools such as the platform

In the medium term, 75 accelerated women will develop operational export plans, increase their revenue (target: +30% in 24 months), and create at least 100 direct jobs, thereby contributing to inclusive growth. These SMEs, now visible internationally, are helping to boost local economies by promoting "Made in Benin" products and strengthening regional and international trade ties.
In the long term, the program creates a multiplier effect by strengthening an active network of women entrepreneurs, facilitating peer mentoring and skills transfer. It also contributes to changing social and economic norms by promoting the acceptance and recognition of female leadership in the business world. By aligning with regional initiatives such as the AfCFTA and establishing partnerships with financing institutions, Business Growth 3.0 influences policies supporting women's entrepreneurship and contributes to a more equitable and accessible ecosystem.
Thus, the desired follow-up effects include: a sustainable increase in the export rate of SMEs led by women, better financial inclusion, increased formalization of women's businesses, increased business collaborations between women, and a concrete reduction in gender inequalities in the digital economy. The program therefore acts as a catalyst for systemic change by anchoring new, replicable, and sustainable practices in the Beninese entrepreneurial ecosystem.

Title: IoT-Powered SmartWTI for Sustainable & Inclusive Water Economy
Subtitle: A digital IoT-based solution optimizing water usage, empowering communities, and promoting inclusive and sustainable growth.
Problem Statement: Many communities and small businesses face water scarcity, high waste, and inflated operational costs due to inefficient monitoring. Lack of real-time data prevents proactive management, while marginalized groups often lack affordable tools, deepening economic and environmental inequalities. SmartWTI leverages IoT and AI to optimize water use, reduce waste, and empower inclusive, sustainable growth.
Solution Overview:
How the Solution Works:
SmartWTI deploys a network of IoT sensors across water infrastructure to monitor flow, quality, and pressure in real time. Data is transmitted securely via LoRaWAN, cellular (4G), or WiFi to a cloud analytics platform, where AI algorithms:

Detect leaks and contamination

Predict consumption patterns

Optimize distribution

Users access web/mobile dashboards with actionable insights and automated alerts. Automated valves and pumps adjust flow based on analytics to ensure efficient water management.

Core Technologies:

Edge Computing for local data processing

Machine Learning (LSTM networks) for predictive analytics

Modular Sensor Arrays (quality, quantity, environment)

Hybrid Connectivity with failover (LoRaWAN + cellular)

Solar-powered batteries for long-term operation

Methodologies:

Agile Development: Rapid prototyping for sector-specific needs

Human-Centered Design: Co-creation with farmers, utilities, and communities

Lean Deployment: Plug-and-play installation (<2 hours)

Predictive Maintenance: Algorithm-driven service scheduling

Strategic Partnerships:

Technology: Microsoft (Azure IoT), Libelium, Cisco

Implementation: PepsiCo, UNICEF, Jordanian Ministry of Water

Research: Royal Scientific Society, MIT REAP

Collaboration Models:

Pay-per-Save (revenue-sharing based on water savings)

Franchise deployment by local partners

Tech licensing for utilities

Joint ventures with industry leaders

Impact Metrics:

30–40% reduction in non-revenue water

25% operational cost savings

3× faster leak detection

90% reduction in manual meter reading

SmartWTI combines industrial IoT, AI, and affordable pricing models to serve utilities and smallholder farmers, creating resilient, sustainable, and inclusive water management solutions.

Title: Micson: Inclusive Digital Platform for Creative Economy in Central Asia
Subtitle: Micson is an inclusive digital platform and festival that empowers youth and women in Central Asia by providing digital skills, income opportunities, and access to global markets. The platform supports a wide variety of creative genres — from contemporary digital art, fantasy, and social storytelling to works inspired by Central Asian myths, legends, and cultural heritage. This diversity ensures broad appeal and inclusivity while also preserving traditions in modern digital formats.  The Micson ecosystem combines education, entrepreneurship, and creativity. Through online and offline training programs, participants gain knowledge in digital art, animation, storytelling, as well as practical legal and business skills such as copyright, intellectual property, and entrepreneurship. The platform and mobile application are already developed (with the support of GIZ and the Tamchy Tasma Foundation) and are now at the stage of being populated with content, attracting authors and readers, and launching monetization.  Micson has already proven its relevance and earned community trust. The Saima Comics competition, supported by the Goethe-Institut, Alliance Française, and the European Union, engaged 22 young authors and sent winners to Germany. In 2025, the first Micson Fest in Bishkek, supported by the Creative Industries Park Foundation, brought together over 600 visitors and more than 100 participants. With UNIDO’s support, Micson will scale across Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan, strengthening digital inclusion and creating new opportunities for women and youth in the creative economy.
Problem Statement:
Central Asia faces a unique paradox: it is one of the youngest regions in the world, with more than half of the population under the age of 30, yet opportunities in the digital and creative economy remain very limited. Youth and women are particularly disadvantaged, as they lack access to digital skills training, affordable tools, and international markets. As a result, many talented creators are unable to build sustainable careers and often leave the sector altogether.

While the global creative industry continues to expand and generate value, the sector in Central Asia remains underdeveloped and fragmented. Local artists, illustrators, and animators struggle not only with monetization, but also with essential legal and business knowledge, such as copyright and intellectual property rights. This lack of infrastructure limits their ability to compete and innovate.

At the same time, the region’s rich cultural heritage — which could serve as a powerful foundation for storytelling and creative industries — risks being underutilized in modern digital formats. Without inclusive and forward-looking solutions, Central Asia may lose both its creative potential and important aspects of its cultural identity.
Solution Overview:
How the solution works
Micson is a digital platform and festival that connects authors, readers, and the wider creative industry across Central Asia. It operates through a website and mobile application, where artists can publish comics, fairy tales, illustrated books, and animations in both digital and print formats. Authors gain visibility, readers access affordable creative content, and both communities engage through interactive challenges, competitions, and the annual Micson Fest. The festival further strengthens the ecosystem by showcasing works, hosting workshops, and linking creators with publishers, investors, and international markets.

Methodologies and technologies used
The platform integrates modern digital publishing tools with e-commerce functions and community-building features. Its methodology emphasizes inclusivity: onboarding youth and women, offering training in digital art, animation, copyright, intellectual property, and entrepreneurship. By combining storytelling rooted in cultural heritage with modern digital design, the solution makes local creativity visible and competitive on a global scale. Its mobile-first design ensures accessibility for young audiences, while hybrid workshops and events create strong offline-to-online synergies.

Partnerships and collaboration models
Micson was initiated by the Tamchy Tasma Foundation and supported by GIZ. It has successfully collaborated with the Goethe-Institut, Alliance Française, and the EU Delegation in Kyrgyzstan through the Saima Comics competition, as well as with the Creative Industries Park Foundation during the first Micson Fest. These collaborations demonstrate both institutional support and community trust. Future partnerships will focus on scaling across Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan, with joint training programs, cultural exchanges, and integration into international creative networks.
Solution Provider(s): The lead implementing organization is Tamchy Tasma Public Foundation (Kyrgyzstan), established in 2018 and specializing in cultural heritage preservation, creative industries development, and audiovisual production. The foundation has successfully implemented projects supported by international organizations, including GIZ, the Goethe-Institut, the Alliance Française, and the Delegation of the European Union in Kyrgyzstan.  Its expertise covers documentary filmmaking, animation, comics, and large-scale cultural events. Through these projects, the foundation has built strong partnerships with local and international institutions, combining professional production skills with community engagement.  Key partners include:  GIZ Kyrgyzstan – support in platform development and capacity building.  Goethe-Institut, Alliance Française, and EU Delegation in Kyrgyzstan – co-organizers of the Saima Comics competition.  Creative Industries Park Foundation – partner of the Micson Fest digital art festival.   Together, these partners bring international experience, local expertise, and community networks to ensure scalability, inclusivity, and long-term sustainability of the project.
Implementation location(s): Implemented in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, with training and onboarding activities across Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan.
Implementation timeline(s): 2023 – Concept introduced and recognized at Prosperity Cup.  2024 – Saima Comics held.  2025 – First Micson Fest in Bishkek; new website and mobile app.  2026 – Second Micson Fest in Bishkek; regional trainings in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan. The platform will be expanded with online/offline learning modules, community programs, and promotional campaigns in Central Asia.

Our solution aims to strengthen creative industries in Central Asia through digital tools.

Provide accessible digital education for young creators in comics, animation, and storytelling.
Promote gender equality by supporting women artists and giving them visibility.
Stimulate local creative economy through a marketplace for digital and printed works.

It has not been an easy journey, but every step shows me how strongly people need these opportunities — young artists searching for a platform, women creators seeking recognition, and communities eager to see their heritage valued in modern ways.

This work is about more than preserving traditions. It is about inspiring new generations, opening doors for inclusive digital expression, and proving that voices from Kyrgyzstan and Central Asia can shine on the global stage. I continue despite challenges, because I know this is necessary, and I see how many people are waiting.

With meaningful international support, these seeds can grow into a flourishing ecosystem that empowers local talent, connects cultures, and ensures that creativity becomes not only a form of expression, but also a driver of hope, identity, and sustainable development.
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: Micson is a digital platform and festival that empowers youth and women in Central Asia by providing digital skills, income opportunities, and access to global markets. It supports a variety of creative genres, integrates local cultural heritage, and promotes inclusivity in the creative economy. The platform offers training, digital publishing tools, and a hybrid model combining e-commerce with offline events like festivals and workshops.

Title: Scaling digital industrial symbiosis for new, circular economies - previously unimagined.
Subtitle: A
Problem Statement:
Every year, an estimated $1.6 trillion worth of surplus goods, materials, and industrial by-products goes unused or discarded (World Bank, 2023). While this surplus holds enormous potential for economic recovery, climate mitigation, and social equity, it remains largely out of reach for the businesses and communities that could benefit most.

Micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), informal workers, and social ventures often operate at the margins of supply chains. They lack access to affordable inputs, digital infrastructure, and the visibility required to participate in resource-sharing systems. At the same time, large corporations continue to generate excess inventory, idle assets, and unsold stock that are typically wasted rather than redirected.

This persistent gap is driven by three structural barriers: limited access to digital tools, unequal distribution of material value, and the absence of systems that support redistribution at scale. As a result, valuable resources are wasted, while underserved actors remain locked out of economic opportunity.

Solving this problem requires more than just recycling. It calls for a new kind of digital infrastructure, one that makes surplus discoverable, traceable, and accessible to all.
Solution Overview:
The Surpluss is an award-winning B Corp-certified climate technology platform that transforms surplus materials, assets, and capacity into economic, environmental, and social value. Operating as a digital sustainability exchange, The Surpluss enables companies to list, match, and repurpose underutilized resources—ranging from excess inventory and scrap materials to unused warehouse space and skilled labor—across industries and geographies.

We work with thousands of SMEs and corporates to accelerate resource efficiency, reduce waste, and unlock circular business models. Our platform integrates geospatial intelligence, AI-powered material matching, and sustainability reporting tools to help businesses capture hidden value from what they already own. Whether it’s pairing excess textiles with recyclers, finding secondary markets for construction by-products, or matching unused space with NGOs, The Surpluss enables smart, traceable exchanges.

What makes us unique is our modular approach: companies can trade, donate, or exchange surplus via resale, CSR, or internal redeployment, each action tracked and quantified. We also support governments and conglomerates in creating “circular clusters” through our unique approach to the localized circular economy.

-Methodologies:
1.Digitization of Surplus
Companies list surplus assets on the platform via bulk uploads, API integrations, or mobile capture. Items are geotagged, categorized using a proprietary taxonomy, and matched with demand across the network.
2. LLM Powered Matching Engine
A recommendation algorithm suggests high-probability reuse matches based on user profiles, location, industry, and capacity—reducing transaction friction and eliminating the need for SMEs to "search" for relevant resources.
3.Low-Tech Access Layer
4. The system supports mobile-first, multilingual interfaces with offline functionality to accommodate regions with low digital penetration. NGOs and local partners act as digital intermediaries where necessary.
5. Verification and Tracking
Each transaction is traceable with a digital audit trail, enabling ESG reporting, impact measurement, and compliance tracking. Blockchain integration is currently being piloted for authenticity and fraud prevention.

-Tech used: 
AI and machine learning for matchmaking, demand prediction, and anomaly detection, big data (in process), QR/DPPs for material traceability, more in process.
The underlying methodology draws from complex adaptive systems theory, industrial symbiosis frameworks, and human-centered design, prioritizing systems interoperability, minimal onboarding friction, and circular equity.

-Partnerships and Collaboration Model
The Surpluss is a circular economy intelligence platform that enables large companies to digitize their underutilized assets and redistribute them to the right recipients—whether for donation, resale, or reuse—across a trusted network of SMEs, NGOs, and informal actors.

The platform acts as a multi-sided infrastructure:
-On one side, corporate and public sector partners list surplus inventory, equipment, and even knowledge hours.
-On the other, SMEs, social enterprises, and vetted third-party organizations can discover, match, and request access to these resources.
-Rather than operating as a marketplace that profits from transactions, The Surpluss serves as an enablement layer. It empowers partner institutions such as Dubai Holding, Mothercare, BASF, 3M, Maybank and others—to deploy the platform across their own ecosystems and act as orchestrators of local circular economies (in the case of Maybank their SME customers, in the case of others vertically integrated within their own value chain)
-The platform is intentionally designed to operate with or without our direct presence, allowing localized actors to replicate the model using our infrastructure or white-label toolkits.

With operations across 3 continents, a pipeline of 50,000 business users by the end of the year.
Solution Provider(s): While we do have key partners (such as logistics providers, economic zone/business park operators) they do not pertain to contributing to our digital operations. However, we are happy to furnish examples of our projects.
Implementation timeline(s): Depends on project, but usually 3-4 months for partner planning, GTM, "partner dashboard" specifications, etc.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 months - 1 year depending on partner preferences but we recommend 1 year
SDGs addressed: SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production);SDG 13 (Climate Action);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);
Desired impact:
-Accelerate the mainstream adoption of localized industrial symbiosis by enabling SMEs to trade surplus materials, space, and assets through trusted institutional networks.
-Equip SMEs with the data, traceability, and operational tools required to transition toward circularity and regulatory readiness (e.g. EPR).
-Democratize access to industrial symbiosis by embedding it into everyday operations, not just industrial parks or eco-clusters.

-IS has the potential to:
1. reduce 15–20%  in raw material input costs,
2.Significant drops in landfill volumes, and
3. 5–12% reductions in CO₂ emissions per participating company. 
-->If adopted by just 200,000 SMEs globally, localized surplus exchange could lead to:
-Estimated 18–25 million metric tons of CO₂e savings per year,
-A circular reallocation of over $100 billion in underutilized assets,
-And substantial resilience-building in local economies through material self-sufficiency and reduced import dependency.

To date, we've helped reallocate 4.8 million AED in avoided procurement costs, unlocking working capital for SMEs and reducing their dependency on new materials and helped redustribute 500k+ items/materials from landfill.
Key technologies:
The Surpluss blends traditional platform logic with emerging technologies to support scale, adaptability, and inclusion. Its modular backend is designed to serve both formal and informal economies, with components including:

-LLM Integration for Classification and Matching
Large language models (LLMs) are used to improve surplus classification, translate donor-uploaded descriptions into standardized tags (e.g. via SMIC), and support contextual brokering—for example, recommending reuse pathways, resale potential, or donation eligibility across sectors.
-Rules-Based Matching Engine
A configurable engine allows partners to define custom logic (e.g. prioritize donations to female-led SMEs, or exclude certain geographies). This enables targeted redistribution based on ESG goals, compliance, or urgency.
-Geospatial Intelligence
Mapping APIs and regionally layered data help surface surplus-distribution opportunities across clusters, economic zones, and logistics corridors.
-Material Identity Framework (SMIC)
A proprietary standard to classify surplus materials using sector, composition, and reuse potential. This supports auditability, inventory integration, and emissions reporting (with a US patent)
-Multi-lingual and Low-Literacy Access Layer
LLMs also support natural language queries and simplified interfaces, enabling access by users who may not be digitally fluent or who speak non-dominant languages.
-Impact Intelligence Module
Every transaction is linked to ESG and SDG-relevant metrics such as CO₂e reduction, value recovered, and number of SMEs reached. Auto-generated narratives and dashboards are tailored for donor reporting, impact storytelling, and compliance for partners for visibility.
Unique Characteristics:
-From Marketplace to Intelligence Layer
Unlike competitor platforms like Rheaply or Excess Materials Exchange, The Surpluss is not built to move individual items. It's designed to help partners (banks, holding companies, governments) map, activate, and strategically deploy surplus as part of a resource intelligence strategy.

-SME Inclusion by Design
Most circular platforms serve well-resourced corporates. We focus on distributing access down to SMEs, NGOs, and informal actors via institutional partners, enabling inclusive economic participation at scale.

-Zero-Commission Infrastructure
While others monetize transactions, The Surpluss takes no cut. Our platform is infrastructure, not a middleman. Revenue comes from licensing, reporting, and API access, making it more budget friendly for smaller companies with an ROI period.

-Circular Asset Recognition
We don't just help companies dispose of surplus, we help them account for it. Surplus becomes a tracked, reportable asset that can be monetized, donated, or reused with ESG and cost-saving benefits that cuts across extra space (warehouse), time (knowledge hours), by products and assets.

-Built for Flexibility
The same infrastructure can power donation drives, resale channels, disaster response, or internal reuse programs each with its own rules, workflows, and verification logic.
Sustainable Change:
-We reclassify surplus as infrastructure, not inventory
The Surpluss changes the economic identity of surplus. Most platforms treat excess as a disposal problem. We treat it as latent infrastructure—a dynamic, underpriced asset class that can be deployed for resilience, ESG arbitrage, or circular liquidity. Through identifier codes, embedded emissions values, and audit-ready traceability, we turn static waste into a strategic lever that unlocks new value on company balance sheets, ESG portfolios, and risk-adjusted supply models. Ultimately, this helps reshape transitions to the circular economy with built in intelligence that has practical uses for resource-constrained SMEs.

-We build localized, self-sustaining circular ecosystems
Our platform isn’t a marketplace—it’s a blueprint. We enable institutions (banks, governments, holding groups) to activate localized surplus economies without building their own infrastructure. Every deployment can be customized with regional logic, informal participation, and trust-based redistribution models. The result is not just transactions, but embedded circularity.. ie where surplus flows become predictable, regenerating loops across sectors and cities.
Funding Sources: Bootstrapped + award/competition winnings, equity free. Currently looking for funding within next 6 months to scale up.
Testimonials and Endorsements: Please check our website (www.thesurpluss.com)
Further comments/feedback: Thank you for your consideration! We are an underrepresented team of (mostly) women from emerging economy backgrounds and we are truly passionate about making an impact and expanding into emerging economy contexts through partnerships to help plug the digital gap, particularly for SMEs to transition to a more resource efficient circular economy.
Primary thematic focus area: Stable and Resilient Digital Supply Chains
Summary: The Surpluss is a B Corp-certified platform enabling the circular economy by connecting businesses with excess resources to SMEs and informal actors, promoting sustainability and economic growth. The solution is innovative in its approach to digital industrial symbiosis, using AI, geospatial intelligence, and an LLM-powered matching engine. However, its scalability and long-term sustainability may be impacted by its current reliance on bootstrapping and the need for external funding.

Name of your organization: E-waste Producer Responsibility Organisation of Nigeria (EPRON)
Title: Recirculate to Digitize
Subtitle: Innovative Circular Economy Model to foster Digital Inclusion in Nigeria
Problem Statement:
Nigeria faces a dual challenge of growing digital exclusion and escalating electronic waste. While internet penetration in the country has reached roughly 48% as of 2023, this headline number masks a deep urban–rural divide. In rural areas, internet usage remains between 23% and 36%, compared to about 64% in urban centers (Daily Trust, New Telegraph). Device affordability is a significant barrier: the high cost of desktops, laptops, and smartphones, combined with the expense of connectivity, excludes many low-income households from participating in the digital economy. This inequality is compounded by low digital literacy, especially among women, where only 34% of rural women are literate compared to 51% of rural men, and awareness of mobile internet lags at 45% for women against 62% for men (Wikipedia – Digital divide in Nigeria). 

At the same time, Nigeria contributes to the global surge in electronic waste. Worldwide, over 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste were generated in 2022, yet only around 22.3% was formally recycled (Global E-waste Monitor 2024). The rest is often discarded unsafely, leading to toxic environmental impacts. In Nigeria, a large proportion of end-of-life electronics still holds reuse potential if properly refurbished, representing an untapped opportunity to bridge the device gap while reducing e-waste. There is an urgent need to address digital inequality and environmental degradation simultaneously by leveraging circular economy practices, specifically through the recovery, refurbishment, and redistribution of usable electronic devices, coupled with skills development.
Solution Overview:
EPRON’s proposed Corporate WEEE Collect program tackles these dual challenges with a single, scalable solution: transforming corporate electronic waste into a pathway for digital inclusion. The initiative will establish a structured channel for collecting decommissioned IT assets—such as desktops, laptops, and accessories—from corporate organizations, offering them an environmentally responsible disposal route that aligns with their corporate social responsibility goals and ensures certified secure data destruction. 

Once collected, devices will be transferred to our refurbishment partner, Digicycle, where they will undergo a rigorous restoration process involving diagnostics, repairs, parts replacement, and quality testing. By extending the life of these devices, we reduce the flow of electronics into landfills and create affordable, high-quality technology for those who would otherwise be excluded from the digital world. 

Distribution will focus on two key pathways: directly to low-income individuals at subsidized rates, and to underserved schools where we will establish fully equipped computer labs. These labs will provide consistent access to technology for students and, where possible, will be made available to community members outside school hours. Each lab installation will be paired with a structured digital literacy training program, covering foundational ICT skills, safe internet use, online learning navigation, and pathways to employment. This ensures that beneficiaries gain not just access to hardware, but the skills to use it meaningfully. 

Our methodology is rooted in the circular economy, maximizing the lifespan of existing devices, reducing environmental harm, and lowering barriers to technology adoption. The program leverages blended learning methods for training, with both hands-on sessions and locally stored digital resources for offline use in low-connectivity areas. Impact will be tracked through measurable indicators: number of devices collected and refurbished, number of labs installed, beneficiaries trained, improvements in digital literacy scores, and reductions in e-waste volumes sent to informal disposal. 

The project is built on a multi-stakeholder collaboration model. Corporate partners supply devices, Digicycle manages refurbishment, training centre for ICT skills acquisition, schools and community organizations host and maintain computer labs. This collaborative approach ensures sustainability, community ownership, and policy alignment. It empowers underserved communities to participate fully in the digital age while mitigating the environmental impacts of e-waste. 

Needs Assessment & Distribution: Community surveys identify target beneficiaries; public schools, rural youth, women entrepreneurs, people with disabilities.
Solution Provider(s): Digicycle (Technology sector), E-terra Technologies (Recycling) Hinckley recycling (Recycling), Tech 365 (Education), Lagos State Ministry of Education (Government)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 Months
SDGs addressed: SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);SDG 13 (Climate Action);SDG 4 (Quality Education);
Desired impact:
The project seeks to transform Nigeria’s growing stream of decommissioned corporate electronics into a catalyst for digital inclusion, environmental sustainability, and economic opportunity. By channeling end-of-life IT assets into a structured refurbishment and redistribution system, the initiative addresses two urgent challenges: the digital exclusion of underserved communities and the environmental hazards of unmanaged e-waste. 

Objectives are: 

i) Increase access to affordable, reliable digital devices for underserved communities and schools. 

ii) Attaining circularity by slowing material loops through the extension of product lifespan of electrical and electronics equipment  

iii) Reduce the volume of e-waste entering informal disposal streams by extending the life of corporate electronics. 

iv) Improve digital literacy among students and community members to enable meaningful participation in the digital economy. 

v) Support environmental goals by reducing greenhouse gas emissions associated with the production of new electronic devices and informal disposal practices prevalent in Nigeria. 

vi) Foster local economic activity by engaging refurbishers, trainers, and support staff. 

vii) Tracking of products, to the end of life, ensuring that they are collected back at end of life for material loop to be closed.  

Key Achievements: 

i)1,200 devices collected from at least 10 corporate donors. 

ii) 1,000 devices refurbished and made operational (85% refurbishment rate). 

iii) 20 school computer labs installed, each serving an average of 525 students annually. 

iv) 300 devices distributed directly to individuals and community learning hubs. 

v) 7 tonnes of e-waste diverted from landfills and informal dumpsites. 

vi) 20+ local jobs supported, including refurbishers, trainers, lab technicians, and logistics staff.
Key technologies: GIS & Mapping, PC-Doctor, Linux Lite, Blancco Drive Eraser, KillDisk, Google workspace, software installation
Unique Characteristics:
i) Dual-Impact Model: Tackling E-Waste and Digital Exclusion Together: EPRON’s solution is unique because it integrates both: reducing hazardous e-waste while simultaneously bridging the digital divide by transforming discarded assets into affordable digital tools. 

ii) Local Circular Economy Approach: Refurbishment is handled by local partner Digicircle, creating green jobs and building technical capacity within Nigeria. This keeps value creation within the country rather than exporting devices abroad for refurbishment, which is the common model.

iii) Affordability with Sense of Ownership: Instead of free device handouts, refurbished devices are offered at subsidized but affordable rates, fostering ownership, responsibility, and longer-term use. 

iv) Scalability and Replicability: The model is designed to be scalable across Nigeria and adaptable to other African countries, since it leverages existing corporate e-waste flows and local refurbishment capacity. 

v) The initiative embeds structured digital literacy programs, covering basic ICT, online learning, safe internet use, and digital economy participation ensuring users can effectively leverage the technology.
Sustainable Change:
Our solution creates sustainable, systemic change by embedding circular economy principles into Nigeria’s digital inclusion strategy. Instead of treating e-waste as a problem to be discarded, we transform it into a resource that expands access to technology for underserved communities. By establishing a structured pipeline where corporate organizations donate their depreciated IT assets, we unlock a continuous, reliable supply of hardware that can be refurbished locally. This not only reduces environmental harm but also builds an ecosystem that consistently supplies affordable digital devices. 

Sustainability is reinforced through our choice to work with local refurbishing partner Digicycle, which ensures that skills, jobs, and value remain within the Nigerian economy. By pairing refurbished devices with digital literacy training and the establishment of school computer labs, the solution addresses not just access but also the capacity to use technology meaningfully. This dual focus helps beneficiaries transition from passive consumers of technology to active participants in the digital economy, with measurable impact on education, employability, and entrepreneurship.
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: Recirculate to Digitize addresses Nigeria's digital divide and e-waste problem by repurposing corporate electronics into affordable devices for underserved communities. The solution integrates e-waste management, digital literacy, and market access for smallholder farmers, with a dual focus on environmental sustainability and digital inclusion. The project shows strong potential but lacks a clear funding strategy for long-term sustainability and scaling.

Name of your organization: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH
Title: AI-Powered Labour Market Intelligence for Inclusive and Equitable Digital Futures
Subtitle: From Iraq to the world: Up-to date, granular and disaggregated insights to match skills with jobs in the Digital Economy for the Youth and transform policy.
Problem Statement: Across many economies in transition, youth (particularly young women) face the dual challenge of high unemployment and limited access to quality digital jobs. In Iraq, over 35% of young people are unemployed, and 60% lack the digital skills required for today’s economy. Policymakers, educators, and employers often operate in the dark due to fragmented, outdated labour market data that often ignores informal recruitment channels where most SMEs and startups hire. This information gap perpetuates skills mismatches, slows digital transformation, and risks leaving entire communities behind. Without timely, inclusive data, that is easy(easier) to gather, reforms and policies are at risk of missing their mark, and the digital divide will deepen.
Solution Overview:
How the Solution Works:
The initiative leverages emerging technologies and alternative data sources to address gaps in labour market information. By transforming fragmented data into policy-ready intelligence, it enables stakeholders to bridge the gap between skills, jobs, and inclusive economic growth. The solution is designed to both deliver actionable insights and build local capacity so that methods can be sustained and replicated over time.

Methodologies:

Data2Policy Navigator Approach – provides a framework to translate data into evidence-based policymaking.

Data Ecosystem Mapping (Open Data Institute) – identifies and organizes available data sources, ensuring gaps and opportunities are visible.

CrowdVOICE – an approach developed by ProsperIA and inspired by a larger project deployed in Mexico with the White Ribbon Alliance, financed by BMZ.

Technologies:

Large Language Models (LLMs) for classification and natural language processing.

Kedro-based Python pipelines to enable scalable and reproducible data processing.

API integrations for continuous, real-time updates from multiple sources.

Multilingual AI chatbots (Arabic, Kurdish, English) to expand accessibility; easily scalable to additional languages.

Partnerships and Collaboration Models:

Public Sector: Office of the Prime Minister, Development Fund of Iraq

Private Sector: SMEs (KAPITA Iraq), ProsperIA Social

International Partners: German Cooperation, Open Data Institute (ODI)
Solution Provider(s): Office of the Prime Minister of Iraq (Lead and Beneficiary), Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development of Germany (BMZ) (Funding and strategic support), Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) (Policy integration-capacity building-and implementation), ProsperIA (Lead technical Implementer), KAPITA (Private sector research and ecosystem building), Open Data Institute (Ecosystem mapping and governance)
Geographic focus: Implemented in Iraq and Scalable to different Regions and Contexts
Implementation location(s): Pilot in Iraq: Baghdad, Erbil, Basra, Karbala representing urban hubs, emerging markets, and underserved areas.
Implementation timeline(s): Pilot: May 2024 – September 2025 (ecosystem mapping, technology deployment, national job market analysis, and capacity building for local institutions, both private and public).
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 7–12 months (from stakeholder engagement to functional, live data platform, including local training programs)
SDGs addressed: SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals);
Desired impact:
Desired Impact of the Solution

Solution Objectives:  1) Equip governments with timely, granular, and disaggregated labour market data to support evidence-based policymaking. 2) Align national training systems with employer demand by identifying both hard and soft skills. 3) Build lasting local capacity for data-driven labour market analysis through training and institutional partnerships. 4) Expand women’s and youth’s access to higher-value roles in the digital economy.

Key Achievements and Impacts (to date) -- A) 2,036 verified job offers analyzed from 35,000 digital economy postings in Iraq in less than 90 days, generating policy-ready intelligence. B) Top in-demand skills identified: Soft skills: creativity (26.8%), communication (23.3%), attention to detail (19.6%); Hard skills: graphic design (37.3%), technical support (13.3%), content creation (10.1%). C) Revealed sex-based disparities in job allocation, providing evidence to address barriers for women’s participation in technical fields. D) Capacity-building workshops delivered to ministry analysts and SME representatives, ensuring data insights can be interpreted and acted upon locally (rollout to expand in September 2025). E) Policy integration achieved: Insights have already been embedded into German bilateral cooperation with the Iraqi government to strengthen youth access to digital jobs.

Sustainability and scalability ensured through partnerships with the Office of the Prime Minister, SMEs (e.g., KAPITA Iraq), and international partners (GIZ).

Impact Pathway: The solution strengthens the labour market ecosystem by connecting skills supply with employer demand, reducing mismatches, and supporting inclusive economic growth. It builds institutional capacity for evidence-based policymaking while creating pathways for women and youth to access high-value digital opportunities.
Key technologies:
AI & LLMs (classification, skill mapping, bias detection) 
Kedro-based Python data pipelines 
Real-time API integrations 
Multilingual AI chatbots and dashboards
Unique Characteristics: This solution combines cultural sensitivity, innovation, and sustainability in ways that set it apart from conventional labour market tools. It recognizes patterns of underrepresentation without reinforcing stereotypes—for example, multilingual AI chatbots (Arabic, Kurdish, English) ensure women and youth can share experiences and access insights without barriers. Unlike large-scale surveys that can take months and cost millions, the solution delivers results in under 90 days and at a fraction of the cost, analyzing 35,000 job postings to identify over 2,000 verified digital opportunities. This provides governments with real-time intelligence from SME and informal channels often invisible to national statistics. Capacity building is embedded, enabling ministries and SMEs to apply the methodology independently and sustainably. Already integrated into German–Iraqi cooperation strategies, the model complements national statistics, reduces costs, and strengthens workforce planning. Its modular design makes it globally adaptable, enabling SME competitiveness, youth employment, and inclusive economic growth.
Sustainable Change:
Iraq's Digital Future: Theory of Change

Young people in Iraq—especially women and those outside major economic hubs—face three interlinked barriers to entering the digital economy:

* Invisible opportunities – many SME and local market jobs never appear on formal job boards.
* Mismatched skills – training curricula often do not reflect real employer demand.
* Structural access gaps – connectivity, awareness, mobility, and social norms limit participation.

Our solution tackles these barriers in three ways:

1) Reaching underserved voices and markets: We capture hiring trends from SME and informal recruitment channels across regions such as Basra, Karbala, and rural Kurdistan. Surveys are multilingual (Arabic, Sorani Kurdish, English), mobile-first, and voice-enabled to include those with limited literacy or connectivity. Culturally sensitive prompts ensure women feel comfortable participating.

2) Turning data into equitable action: Disaggregated by sex and geography, insights reveal skill demand in smaller towns alongside national averages. This data can inform policy reforms and targeted programs—for example, localized digital skills bootcamps and mentorship schemes for young women in technical fields. Already, insights are being integrated into the German bilateral cooperation with the Iraqi government, providing an entry point for systemic adoption.

3) Building institutional capacity for replication in other policy/economic areas: We train government analysts and SME  teams to independently extract and interpret data, supported by a “replication kit” with methodology, AI pipeline templates, and facilitation guides. This ensures the approach can be scaled in different levels and replicated without external dependency.

Desired systemic outcomes:

1) Government officials integrate timely labour market intelligence into national statistics systems, complementing surveys.
2) Training systems adjust curricula to reflect employer demand, lowering skill mismatches.
3) Women and youth gain measurable access to higher-value digital roles, especially in underserved regions.
4) A sustainable ecosystem emerges where evidence-based policymaking is embedded locally, supporting inclusive economic growth.
Funding Sources:
Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development of Germany (BMZ) via the Bilateral Program Promoting employment in the digital economy in Iraq (ProDIGI) - Hosting the Digital Transformation Centre in Iraq

European Union – Next Generation via the Data Lab from BMZ and its Global Program “Learning from experience – Data for evidence-informed policy”
Testimonials and Endorsements:
"The centre (BMZ's Digital Transformation Center) is offering support to government institutions in creating infrastructure and supporting data preparation. The centre’s goal is to offer data as a service. Mostafa Sabah, director of software solutions and data management, NDC Iraq 
“We heard valuable insights from diverse voices, especially private sector representatives, on how data management could benefit their work.” (Mostafa Sabah, director of software solutions and data management, NDC)
Further comments/feedback:
The questionnaire was clear and well-structured. One suggestion for future rounds would be to include a dedicated section on “lessons learned and early systemic impacts.” This would allow applicants who have already tested and refined their solutions to show how evidence and experience translate into scalable change.

For example, this initiative has already moved from concept to impact in Iraq. It has convened government, private sector, and civil society actors around an AI-powered labour market intelligence engine that respects cultural norms and promotes inclusive participation of women and youth. The methodology and first results are openly published through the Data2Policy Navigator (final update due October 2025), making them available for adaptation in other contexts.

Early learnings have already influenced bilateral cooperation between Germany and Iraq, guiding concrete programs to expand youth access to the digital economy. Capacity-building workshops are equipping ministry analysts and SMEs to replicate the methods independently, ensuring sustainability.

This type of learning—what worked, what was adapted, and what was integrated into policy—illustrates why capturing lessons is so valuable. With UNIDO’s reach, such proven, evidence-based models can be accelerated and scaled to ensure youth and women everywhere have equal visibility and opportunity in digital labour markets.
Primary thematic focus area: Innovation Acceleration & Knowledge Sharing
Summary: The AI-Powered Labour Market Intelligence initiative pilots in Iraq to provide timely, granular, and inclusive labour market insights that connect skills with jobs in the digital economy. By leveraging AI, alternative data sources, and partnerships with government, SMEs, and international agencies, it identifies in-demand skills, reveals gender and regional disparities, and equips policymakers, training providers, and employers with evidence for targeted reforms. Distinct from conventional surveys, the approach analyzes informal recruitment channels and delivers results within 90 days at lower cost. Already embedded in German–Iraqi cooperation frameworks, the model is designed for scalability and replication across other transition economies.

Title: Civic Voices
Subtitle: Civic Voices is a digital civic engagement platform that helps Kenyans add their voice in the budget and policy-making process.
Problem Statement: The key challenge is that many Kenyans are unable to take part in public participation in a meaningful way. Access to information and participation spaces is unequal, leaving out low-income groups, rural communities, the elderly, women, and youth. The high cost of travel, time lost from work, and limited channels for sharing participation details make it even harder for ordinary citizens to engage. At the same time, Kenya faces deep economic inequality, where a small minority controls most of the wealth, while the poor majority have little influence over how public resources are shared. Because of these barriers, public decisions often fail to reflect the needs of marginalized groups, leading to greater poverty, misuse of resources, and growing mistrust between citizens and government.
Solution Overview: Civic Voices is a mobile-based platform that bridges the gap between citizens and government by making public participation more accessible, affordable, and inclusive. It allows citizens to easily access government information, give feedback, and engage in consultations, while helping governments share data, gather input, and reduce the high costs of physical meetings. Built on user-friendly, mobile-first technology and an open data approach, the platform promotes transparency, accountability, and collective citizen voice. Civic Voices works through partnerships with government institutions (Nairobi County), civil society, donors (USAID), and community networks to ensure that women, youth, and marginalized groups are included, ultimately strengthening democracy and public trust.
Solution Provider(s): Nairobi County - Piloting Organization - https://nairobi.go.ke/.  - USAID - Funding Organization (YALI TF3)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 12 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities);SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives

1. Enhance citizen participation by providing inclusive digital tools for engaging in legislative and policy-making processes.

2. Amplify marginalized voices (women, youth, persons with disabilities, and ethnic minorities) to ensure equitable representation in governance.

3. Increase government transparency and accountability by making policies, budgets, and official responses easily accessible.

4. Foster sustainable development by enabling communities to advocate for policies that align with social equity and environmental responsibility.

Key Achievements & Impacts

1. In partnership with Nairobi County, Civic Voices increased public participation in policy discussions by 1,500%, from 75 to 10,000 participants in eight months, and an online reach of over 200,000 people. With this kind of impact, Nairobi County invited us to rollout county-wide post-pilot.

2. As a result, all Nairobi County policies and budgets are now published exclusively on our platform, creating a single, transparent hub for citizen engagement.

3. Enabled historically excluded groups to contribute feedback on critical issues such as education access, gender equity, climate action, and community development.

4. Strengthened accountability by allowing citizens to track policymaker responses, encouraging responsive governance.

5. Supported inclusive policy outcomes, with measurable evidence from community-driven recommendations incorporated into local government strategies.
Key technologies:
Civic Voices is built on mobile-first technology, ensuring accessibility for the majority of Kenyans who rely on smartphones for internet access. The platform uses:

1. Mobile App: Provides an easy-to-use interface for citizens to access information, share feedback, and participate in consultations from anywhere.

2. Cloud-based Infrastructure: Ensures secure storage, scalability, and real-time access to government documents, budgets, and citizen input.

3. Survey and Feedback Tools: Digital questionnaires and polls to collect community opinions and feed them directly into government decision-making.

4. Notifications & Alerts System: Keeps citizens informed of upcoming participation opportunities, deadlines, and new policies.

5. Data Analytics Dashboards: Helps governments analyze citizen feedback, identify trends, and make evidence-based decisions.
Unique Characteristics: Civic Voices is unique because it shifts public participation from costly, centralized physical meetings to an inclusive, mobile-first platform that reaches people wherever they are. Unlike traditional approaches, it combines open data access, real-time citizen feedback, and government accountability tools in one space. Its innovation lies not only in technology but also in the collaborative model, working with government, civil society, and community networks to ensure marginalized voices are heard. By lowering participation costs, widening access to information, and fostering grassroots organizing, Civic Voices creates a scalable, transparent, and citizen-centered system for governance. This combination of inclusivity, affordability, and partnership-driven design sets it apart from existing public participation methods.
Sustainable Change:
Civic Voices contributes to long-term systemic change by transforming how citizens and governments interact. By expanding access to information and participation, the platform builds an informed, engaged citizenry that can hold leaders accountable. In turn, governments benefit from inclusive, evidence-based decision-making that reflects the needs of all citizens, not just the wealthy or well-connected.

Theory of Change

- If citizens are given easy digital access to public information and channels to contribute their views,

- Then participation becomes more inclusive, reducing barriers for women, youth, rural, and low-income communities,

- Which leads to fairer allocation of public resources, reduced corruption, and stronger accountability,

- Resulting in greater trust between citizens and government, fewer resource-based conflicts, and a more resilient democracy.

Follow-on Effects

- A culture of transparency and accountability embedded in governance.

- Increased citizen ownership of policies and development initiatives.

- Stronger grassroots movements amplifying marginalized voices.

- Long-term poverty reduction as resources are allocated more fairly.

- Replicable digital model for other counties and African countries to adopt, scaling systemic change across regions.

Title: “Enhancing Agricultural Yields and Improving Farmers’ Income through Agri-tech”
Subtitle: Essymart Agtech provides affordable, sustainable agri-inputs and innovative solutions to farmers, boosting productivity while supporting food security, climate resilience and rural livelihood
Problem Statement: Essymart tackles critical challenges faced by smallholder farmers and rural communities. Farmers often lack access to quality and affordable agricultural inputs, forcing them to rely on costly or counterfeit products that reduce yields and income. Climate change worsens this situation by degrading soil fertility, increasing pest outbreaks, and threatening food security. Many farmers also struggle with post-harvest losses due to poor processing and storage facilities, which limits their ability to earn fair returns. Additionally, rural communities face barriers to knowledge, technologies, and sustainable farming practices, keeping them trapped in cycles of low productivity and poverty.
Solution Overview:
Essymart addresses these challenges by providing affordable, high-quality agri-inputs, climate-smart solutions like organic fertilizers, pesticides and improved market linkages. This empowers farmers to increase productivity, reduce costs, improve resilience, and build sustainable livelihoods while strengthening local food systems.

Essymart leverages innovative, sustainable methodologies and technologies to support farmers.  The enterprise promotes climate-smart agriculture by providing eco-friendly agri-inputs and training farmers in sustainable practices. Digital platforms enhance access to inputs, knowledge, and market linkages, reducing inefficiencies in rural supply chains. Essymart also integrates small-scale processing and storage technologies to minimize post-harvest losses. By combining biotechnology, digital tools, and farmer-centered approaches, Essymart drives productivity, resilience, and sustainability in African agriculture while supporting rural livelihoods.

Essymart builds partnerships and collaborations that strengthen its impact and scale. It works with local farmer cooperatives and community groups to reach smallholders collectively, ensuring affordable access to inputs and knowledge. Strategic collaborations with research institutions and universities enable continuous innovation in areas like organic fertilizers, and climate-smart practices. Essymart partners with NGOs and development organizations to extend training, capacity building, and financial literacy programs for rural farmers. It also collaborates with government agencies to align with national agricultural policies and sustainability goals. Through private-sector partnerships, Essymart develops inclusive market linkages, processing, and distribution networks. This multi-stakeholder collaboration model fosters shared value, where each partner contributes expertise, resources, and networks, while Essymart ensures last-mile delivery, adoption, and measurable community impact. By integrating science, business, and grassroots engagement, Essymart’s partnership approach drives long-term agricultural resilience, food security, and economic empowerment for smallholder farmers.
Solution Provider(s): Namayingo Agro producers Sacco- Provides Essymart access to farmers and provide them with agricultural loans- sector: Finance Budhaya Farmers cooperative- provides Essymart with access to farmers- sector, agriculture and finance, Export Trading Company- supply Essymart with agri-inputs,
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);
Desired impact:
- Over 5,000 smallholder farmers impacted
150+ monthly online transactions
$76,000 in total revenue
20+ last-mile agents
25% cost saving for farmers
Partnered with 10 major input suppliers, 5 cooperatives, 50 farmers groups 
$45,000 in funding raised
Key technologies: E-commerce, USSD, SMS
Unique Characteristics:
- Integrated Tech-Based Ecosystem for Farmers: Essymart offers a fully integrated platform combining e-commerce, fintech, agricultural advisory, USSD, SMS, and mobile money, all tailored to smallholder farmers in rural Uganda. This enables seamless access to quality inputs, expert guidance, financing, and market linkages all in one solution.
- Last-Mile Delivery Leveraging Local Agripreneurs: To overcome logistics challenges, Essymart deploys Village Agripreneurs—local agents who help farmers place orders and receive deliveries directly on the farm. This approach ensures accessibility even where connectivity and transport are limited.
- Inclusive Multi-Channel Access: Essymart recognizes that not all farmers have internet access, so it supports multiple user interfaces: web app, USSD (e.g., dialing a code to place orders), bulk SMS, voice calls, and mobile money. This inclusive design ensures that every farmer from tech-savvy to phone-only users can benefit.
- Data-Driven, Location-Specific Advisory: Beyond supply, Essymart offers personalized agricultural advice—covering weather, market prices, farming practices, and regenerative techniques—tailored to each farmer's location. This empowers farmers to make more informed, context-specific decisions.
- Financial Inclusion & Credit for Input Purchase: Essymart addresses cash flow constraints by enabling farmers to pay on credit using mobile money. This support is especially impactful for smallholder farmers who may lack the capital to purchase inputs upfront.
- Tangible Impact on Costs, Yield, and Income- Essymart has demonstrated measurable results: Farmers save 10–20% on input costs (seeds, fertilizer, pesticides, and logistics), Achieved up to a 40% increase in production, 70% uplift in income from produce sales, Delivered up to $1,000 additional income per farmer per year and a 60% boost to food security
- Clear Social Mission & Recognition:  Essymart is a for-profit social enterprise part of Uganda’s agritech transformation, with deep roots in rural community development. It has been recognized with awards like Best Social Enterprise at the Africa Tech Summit (2023) and featured in programs such as HiPipo’s 40Days40FinTechs.
Sustainable Change:
- Strengthening Food Systems (Systemic Change in Agriculture): Challenge in the system: Smallholder farmers (who produce ~80% of food in Uganda) face poor input access, fake products, lack of finance, and low bargaining power. Essymart’s systemic role: By integrating e-commerce + fintech + advisory + logistics, Essymart closes multiple gaps in the agricultural value chain—making farming more reliable, productive, and market-oriented. This shifts smallholder farming from subsistence to sustainable agribusiness.
- Improving Farmer Resilience & Productivity: Provides authentic, affordable inputs → prevents farmers from being exploited with fake or overpriced seeds/fertilizers. Gives location-based agronomic advice → increases yields by up to 40%.
Facilitates input financing via mobile money credit → helps farmers plant on time, breaking cycles of low productivity. Farmers are no longer stuck in survival mode but can plan for growth and invest in their futures.
- Inclusive Last-Mile Access (Equity & Inclusion): Uses USSD, SMS, and local Agripreneurs → ensures even the most remote, low-literacy farmers can access modern services. Focus on women and youth farmers → tackles gender and generational inequality in agriculture.  This builds system-wide inclusion, not just serving the “connected elite.”
- Sustainable Livelihoods & Poverty Reduction: Farmers save 10–20% on inputs and gain 70%+ increases in income.
Reported up to $1,000 extra income per farmer per year → significant in rural Uganda.
Income stability → better education, health, and resilience to shocks. This creates a poverty escape pathway for thousands of families.
- Promoting Regenerative & Climate-Smart Agriculture: Advises farmers on soil health, organic practices, and climate-resilient crops. Helps reduce harmful farming practices by guiding input use responsibly. Over time, this contributes to healthier soils, sustainable yields, and climate adaptation.
- Community Empowerment Through Agripreneurs: Engages Village Agripreneurs as delivery agents and local champions.
This creates rural jobs, strengthens community trust, and decentralizes the system. Farmers are not just “beneficiaries” but active participants in building the system. 
- Scaling Impact Beyond Individual Farmers:  With tech + data, Essymart can aggregate farmer demand and supply → giving farmers market power. Partners with other stakeholders (fintechs, NGOs, governments) → creating an ecosystem-level impact, not just isolated interventions. This shifts the whole system from fragmented, inefficient chains into coordinated, transparent, and farmer-friendly networks.
Funding Sources: Essymart has received funding of $12,000 grant from Alliance for Green Revolution Africa, $5,000 grant from Tony Elumelu Foundation, $2,000 grant from Roddenberry Foundation, $5,000 grant from All-Inrecruiting and Talent Boutique, $16,000 loan from OVO and $5,000 loan from Capital Solutions
