Title: Aya Essentials: Inclusive AI Assistant for Community Clinics
Subtitle: An AI-powered assistant helping clinics in emerging markets improve patient access, reduce missed appointments, and bridge the digital healthcare divide.
Problem Statement: Community clinics in emerging markets face staff shortages, missed appointments, and a lack of affordable digital tools. Patients, especially low-income and rural groups, struggle with access, language, and information gaps, widening health inequities and digital exclusion.
Solution Overview:
Aya Essentials is an AI-powered assistant designed to augment clinic operations in the Philippines. It automates repetitive communication to reduce staff workload and prevent revenue loss from patient no-shows. Developed by RightLens AI with a "human-in-the-loop" principle, it empowers healthcare staff without replacing them.

How it Works: The process is a continuous loop. A patient inquires via web chat, and Aya answers FAQs & collects booking details. This information is then passed to the clinic staff for final confirmation. Aya then sends automated SMS reminders to the patient (preventing or reducing patient no-shows), and every interaction enriches the clinic's operational database.

Technologies & Methodologies: We utilize accessible cloud tools tailored for low-resource settings, including Voiceflow for conversational design, Make.com for automation, Airtable as a database, and Semaphore for SMS. Our core methodology is Human-Centered Design.

Partnership Model: We use a collaborative pilot program, partnering with clinics to co-create the solution, ensuring it meets their real-world needs.
Solution Provider(s): RightLens AI, a technology startup based in Laguna, Philippines, focused on developing accessible AI solutions for MSMEs in emerging markets.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 months. This includes one month for co-creation and customization with the partner clinic, followed by two months of implementation, staff training, and impact monitoring.
SDGs addressed: SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);
Desired impact:
Our primary objective is to enhance the operational capacity and financial stability of community clinics in emerging markets. Key anticipated impacts within a 3-month pilot include:
- Reduce patient no-show rates by up to 30%, recovering significant lost revenue for the clinic.
- Save 10+ hours of administrative staff time per week by automating FAQs and booking requests.
- Improve patient access to care by providing a 24/7 digital channel for inquiries and appointments.
Key technologies: Our solution utilizes an integrated stack of accessible no-code/low-code cloud technologies, allowing for rapid and affordable deployment. The core components are AI-powered conversational design platforms (Voiceflow), process automation tools (Make.com), and cloud-based databases (Airtable), connected to local telecommunication infrastructure for SMS delivery.
Unique Characteristics:
Our solution's uniqueness lies in its "accessible innovation" mode.

- Hyper-local Co-creation: We partner directly with local clinics (and/or NGOs) to design the solution, ensuring it fits the specific cultural and operational context of the Philippines.

- Radical Affordability: By using a no-code/low-code stack, we can develop, deploy, and maintain the solution at a fraction of the cost of traditional software development, making it viable for MSMEs in low-resource settings.

- Human-in-the-Loop by Design: Unlike fully automated systems that can alienate users, our model is intentionally designed to augment and empower existing clinic staff, ensuring a trusted human remains the ultimate decision-maker in the patient care journey.
Sustainable Change:
Our theory of change is that by demonstrating a successful, affordable, and easily replicable model for digital augmentation in one clinic, we can create a blueprint for systemic change across the local healthcare ecosystem.

The desired follow-on effects are:
- Increased Adoption: Other clinics will see the clear ROI and adopt similar accessible technologies, improving the efficiency of the entire sector.

- Upskilling of Non-Technical Staff: Clinic staff will become proficient in using and managing digital tools, creating a more digitally literate healthcare workforce.

- Creation of a Scalable Model: We aim to prove that a human-centered, no-code approach can sustainably bridge the digital divide for MSMEs, creating a model that can be scaled to other sectors (e.g., education, social services) and geographies.
Funding Sources: The development of Aya Essentials to its current MVP stage has been self-funded (bootstrapped) by the founder. We are actively seeking pilot partners and grant opportunities to support implementation and scaling.
Testimonials and Endorsements: Not applicable at this pilot-ready stage. We look forward to gathering testimonials from our initial pilot partners.
Further comments/feedback:
Thank you for this opportunity. The most inclusive and sustainable digital solutions for emerging markets will come from the ground up. 

RightLens AI is committed to a model of co-creation, and we are confident that by partnering with local clinics, we can build a solution that is not only technologically effective but also deeply integrated into the community it serves. We are ready to begin.
Primary thematic focus area: MSME Empowerment & Local Digital Innovation
Summary: Aya Essentials is an AI-powered assistant designed to improve the operational capacity of community clinics in emerging markets. It reduces patient no-shows, automates administrative tasks, and provides a 24/7 digital channel for inquiries and appointments, empowering healthcare staff without replacing them.

Title: Digital Infrastructure Program
Subtitle: Providing digital learning tools and opportunities to 350,000+ students and teachers in 539 schools across 12 countries by delivering computer labs and digital skills training in developing countries.
Problem Statement: Across the Asia–Pacific, millions of young people are excluded from the opportunities of a digital world because of deeply entrenched infrastructure deficits. In countries such as Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and Solomon Islands, internet penetration remains among the lowest globally, with connectivity often unreliable, prohibitively expensive, and concentrated in urban centres. Vast rural populations are left entirely disconnected, reinforcing geographic, economic, and social isolation. Schools across these regions operate without the basic foundations of digital learning: electricity supply is inconsistent, internet access is scarce, and computers are either unavailable or unaffordable. In Papua New Guinea alone, 88% of students have never used a computer, while less than one-third of the population has access to the internet. These barriers not only restrict access to quality education but also perpetuate cycles of poverty by excluding communities from digital economies, global knowledge networks, and essential government and health services. The Digital Infrastructure Program, delivered successfully across 12 countries, has installed 539 computer labs into schools and trained hundreds of teachers in IT.
Solution Overview: The Digital Infrastructure Program is LiteHaus International’s flagship education initiative designed to address the severe lack of digital resources in schools across eleven countries – Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, the Philippines, Cambodia, Samoa, Fiji, Tonga, Kiribati, Timor-Leste, Nauru, and Ukraine. At its inception in Papua New Guinea in 2017, fewer than one per cent of the country’s 3,500 schools had functioning computer laboratories. The program was therefore established to bridge this divide by creating communal digital learning facilities rather than focusing solely on individual device distribution. The program works by installing fully equipped digital classrooms, each comprising fifteen refurbished desktop computers with Windows and LibreOffice installed, a projector or LCD screen, surge protection, and lifetime access to Niunet – an offline e-library containing millions of educational resources. This infrastructure is complemented by LiteHaus International’s “Teaching Digital Skills” and “Digital Skills Training Manual,” which provide structured 11–12 week curriculums for teachers with limited ICT backgrounds. Each school receives ongoing support, teacher training, mentorship, and equipment replacement after three years to ensure sustainability and relevance. Since its establishment, the program has achieved substantial impact. 539 digital classrooms have been completed across Asia-Pacific, with over 340,000 students empowered with access to digital learning. The initiative has enhanced student engagement, improved teacher confidence, and expanded equitable participation in education, particularly in underserved rural areas. Key outcomes include the institutionalisation of ICT within the PNG education system, reduced digital illiteracy across all countries, and a foundation for long-term digital competency among future generations. The program has been recognised on three occasions by International Telecommunications Union for outstanding contributions to fostering digital equity globally, including twice at the WSIS Awards in Geneva and once at the SDG Digital Gamechanger Awards in New York.
Solution Provider(s): We provide the solution. We have funding partners and some logistics partners, but the Digital Infrastructure Program is wholly 'owned' and led by us.
Implementation location(s): Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, the Philippines, Cambodia, Samoa, Fiji, Tonga, Kiribati, Timor-Leste, Nauru, and Ukraine
Implementation timeline(s): The Digital Infrastructure Program has been running continuously since September 2017.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 months. We have a proven track record expanding the Digital Infrastructure Program across 11 countries.
SDGs addressed: SDG 4 (Quality Education);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);
Desired impact:
The Digital Infrastructure Program is LiteHaus International’s flagship initiative to transform education across Asia-Pacific by embedding digital learning into the daily experience of students and teachers. Its framework is built around five interconnected outcome domains: Usage, Instruction, Ability, Inspiration, and Equity. These domains ensure that investments in infrastructure deliver meaningful, measurable change rather than symbolic value.

The first domain, Usage, focuses on ensuring that digital classrooms are not idle but integrated into school timetables and lesson plans. Students engage with technology routinely, while teachers facilitate structured access so that computer labs operate at high frequency. In this way, digital usage becomes habitual, supporting learning, creativity, and equitable participation.

The second domain, Instruction, develops teacher capacity. Recognising that most teachers have limited digital training, the program provides structured resources through the Digital Skills Training Program and Teaching Digital Skills Unit. This ensures teachers deliver measurable outcomes in digital literacy while also embedding technology into broader pedagogy, including lesson delivery, research, and assessments. Over time, this builds confidence, enhances professional pride, and creates school-wide cultures of digital teaching.

The third domain, Ability, focuses on students acquiring foundational ICT competencies such as typing, word processing, and data handling, as well as fluency in digital exploration. These skills not only prepare students for employment and further study but also enhance wider academic performance in literacy, numeracy, and science.

The fourth domain, Inspiration, positions technology as a catalyst for ambition. Students discover new possibilities for their futures, while teachers find renewed motivation in their roles. Communities, in turn, see schools becoming hubs of innovation and pride.

Finally, the fifth domain, Equity, ensures fair access for girls and students with disabilities. By actively monitoring who uses the tools and how, the program challenges exclusion and promotes inclusion. This equity-driven approach guarantees that digital empowerment drives broader progress in gender equality and disability inclusion.

Together, these domains ensure that digital infrastructure is not just installed, but fully utilised, sustained, and transformative, creating digitally enabled centres of excellence across Asia-Pacific.
Key technologies:
The Digital Infrastructure Program does not seek to expand access to frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, or the Internet of Things. Instead, it addresses the urgent reality that millions of students in Papua New Guinea and across the Asia-Pacific region still lack access to even the most fundamental digital tools. Our solution delivers refurbished desktop computers, offline e-learning servers, and structured digital literacy curricula to underserved schools, ensuring that basic access is not a privilege but a right. By creating digital classrooms and equipping teachers with the resources to integrate technology into everyday pedagogy, the program lays the essential foundation upon which future digital innovation can occur.

For this application, our work fits squarely within “Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development” by building core digital skills among women, youth, and marginalised groups. By bridging the basic access gap, we enable inclusive participation in tomorrow’s digital economy. School students today will be working well into the 2060s and 2070s - they need the skills to succeed in the economy of the twenty-first century which are already digital.
Unique Characteristics: The Digital Infrastructure Program is unique in its ability to deliver scalable, low-cost digital education to the last mile. Unlike models that rely on expensive infrastructure or continuous internet access, our solution provides fully equipped computer labs and an offline e-learning server containing millions of resources, ensuring that students in even the most remote schools can access transformative digital learning. At just USD $3,000 per lab, including devices, curriculum resources, and installation, our approach is remarkably cost-effective and sustainable. This affordability has enabled us to scale rapidly, with hundreds of labs already delivered across Papua New Guinea and beyond. Our offline-first design overcomes connectivity barriers that exclude marginalised communities from the digital world, while our partnerships with schools, provincial education authorities, and community stakeholders embed long-term ownership. This model combines innovation, inclusivity, and sustainability, making it one of the most effective approaches to bridging the digital divide at scale.
Sustainable Change: The Digital Infrastructure Program contributes to sustainable, systemic change by embedding digital learning within education systems across Asia-Pacific. Guided by a clear theory of change, the program ensures that access to infrastructure is paired with teacher training, structured curricula, and equitable usage plans. This combination transforms technology from a symbolic resource into a core part of teaching and learning. The desired follow-on effects include students graduating with foundational digital competencies, teachers developing long-term confidence in digital pedagogy, and schools positioning themselves as digitally enabled centres of excellence. Over time, these changes foster improved academic outcomes, stronger community engagement, and a culture of digital inclusion that supports gender equality and disability inclusion. At a systems level, the program strengthens provincial education departments, drives replication, and creates momentum for further investment in ICT in education, ensuring enduring digital capability beyond each installation.
Funding Sources: Since its inception in 2017, the Digital Infrastructure Program has been funded primarily through private and corporate philanthropy. Individual donors have provided consistent grassroots support, while partnerships with leading corporations and philanthropic foundations have enabled scale and sustainability. Companies such as Deloitte, EY PNG, ExxonMobil PNG, and the Sir Brian Bell Foundation have contributed both financial resources and in-kind support, recognising the program’s transformative potential. This blended model of private giving and corporate partnerships has ensured that thousands of refurbished devices, digital classrooms, and teacher training resources could be delivered, making digital education accessible to hundreds of thousands of students.

I have also grown in confidence, learning alongside my students and seeing how technology opens new ways of teaching and learning."

The offline e-library has become a lifeline for both students and teachers. We can now teach lessons with updated content, and our students have opportunities equal to those in other countries."

The smiles on my students’ faces when they complete digital tasks remind me why I became a teacher – to inspire and prepare them for the future."

Summary: The Digital Infrastructure Program provides scalable and low-cost digital learning tools to schools in underserved areas across Asia-Pacific. The initiative bridges the digital divide by installing computer labs and delivering digital skills training to students and teachers. The main challenge lies in ensuring long-term sustainability and expanding the model beyond the current donor funding base.

Title: HydroFresh: Sustainable Hydroponics for Armenia
Subtitle: Innovative hydroponic systems providing year-round fresh produce with minimal water and land use with complete remote and automated maintenance.
Problem Statement: Armenia, and not only, faces challenges in food security, limited arable land, water scarcity, and agricultural waste. Traditional farming methods are resource-intensive and vulnerable to climate change, creating inefficiencies and environmental impact.
Solution Overview: HydroFresh develops hydroponic systems that grow fresh vegetables without soil, using up to 90% less water and 70% less land than traditional farming. Our systems are modular, scalable, and designed for households, businesses, and farms. We combine IoT sensors for monitoring nutrients, water, and growth conditions with sustainable materials for long-lasting infrastructure. We collaborate with local engineers, agronomists, and educational institutions to optimize system design, conduct training, and promote circular reuse of byproducts.

Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6–9 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production);SDG 13 (Climate Action);
Desired impact:
Reduce water use in agriculture by up to 90%

Produce fresh vegetables year-round locally

Empower communities and businesses with sustainable farming solutions

Promote circular reuse of agricultural byproducts
Key technologies: IoT sensors for nutrient and water monitoring, automated irrigation systems, modular hydroponic infrastructure, cloud-based AI data monitoring, and sustainable material design.
Unique Characteristics:
Soilless, water-efficient farming system

Modular and scalable design suitable for homes, businesses, and farms

Circular economy approach: reuse of water, nutrients, and system components

Combines hardware, software, and training for end-to-end solutions
Sustainable Change: HydroFresh enables communities and businesses to produce food locally, reducing reliance on imports and decreasing environmental footprint. By promoting circular design and sustainable agriculture practices, we create a replicable model for resource-efficient farming that strengthens resilience, reduces waste, and inspires systemic adoption of sustainable technologies in Armenia and beyond.
Primary thematic focus area: MSME Empowerment & Local Digital Innovation
Summary: HydroFresh is an innovative hydroponic system that allows for year-round vegetable production using up to 90% less water and 70% less land than traditional farming. The solution is modular, scalable, and integrates IoT sensors for monitoring growth conditions, with a focus on sustainability and circular reuse of agricultural byproducts.

Title: DestinBeni
Subtitle: Data-driven platform promoting access to finance for improved climate adaptation and resilience through the use of alternative credit scoring
Problem Statement:
Accessing climate finance is a challenge among farmers and agri-SMEs

Republic of the Congo is already experiencing the impacts of climate change with more frequent droughts, rising temperatures, and reduced agricultural output. Due to the overwhelming dependence on rain-fed agriculture, the reduction in rainfall has significantly reduced productivity in food production.

The agriculture sector, which accounts for 4% of Congo's GDP, despite approximately 40% of the population being involved in subsistence agricultural production. While agriculture is a significant employer, particularly in rural areas, its productivity is low, and the sector struggles to meet domestic food needs, leading to heavy reliance on food imports. However, limited access to climate finance is hindering farmers and MSMEs from adopting climate-adaptive solutions.

Women, who are more likely to be financially excluded, are particularly affected by climate change.

On a global scale, World Bank reports more than 1 billion women still do not use or have access to the financial system. International Finance Corporation (IFC) estimates a $300 billion gap in financing exists for formal, women-owned small businesses and more than 70 % of women-owned small and medium enterprises have inadequate or no access to financial services.

The lack of access to finance coupled with climate change aggravates poverty, with small-scale farmers and women being hit hardest. The common barriers contributing to the challenge of accessing finance by farmers and MSMEs include

Poor credit score and/or lack of financial track record.
Ineffective channels for delivering climate finance directly to farmers.
The high transaction costs associated with lending to farmers and agricultural SMEs, due to their location far from financial institutions and the inadequate physical infrastructure, present a substantial barrier to access to credit. To reach this market segment, financiers would need to make substantial investments in expanding their branch networks, recruiting and training staff, and building loan processing systems. These transaction costs can reduce profit margins and discourage financiers from lending to farmers.
 Lack of Capacity to Manage Agricultural Risks: The agriculture sector poses specific and multifaceted risks that both farmers and financiers must manage, including risks related to seasonal cash flows, production, marketing, and price fluctuations. Smallholder farmers and agricultural SMEs often struggle to manage these risks due to their dependence on seasonal production cycles, lack of knowledge, and capacity to diversify activities. This lack of risk management and diversification limits their capacity to invest in productive activities and repay loans, while also presenting risks for financiers who face irregular cash flows and loan repayment.
Solution Overview:
DestinBeni is a digital finance platform that assists smallholder farmers and Agricultural MSMEs (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises) in gaining access to climate finance while keeping proper records through inventory control, asset management, crop yields, and basic financial reporting. The application operates as a record-keeping system where farmers can keep proper financial and farm operation records for their business transactions while directly receiving and making payments using mobile money. This enables farmers to have digital copies of their transactions, thus making it easy to build credit history. Farmers using the application can also extract financial statements and performance reports.

With machine learning the platform use the records as alternative data to determine the creditworthiness of users. Active social microlending institutions and finance providers are added to the application to share the climate financing opportunities they provide. Farmers can directly apply for financing to increase climate resilience and mitigation capacity. The financiers can review and approve financing requests and disburse funds directly to the farmers through their mobile money while keeping track of their financial performance on the application.

Part of the solution delivery is the organization of farmers' community outreach programs for training and teaching communities about climate resilience, basic financial literacy, and agriculture risks. This is to improve their knowledge of financial management, climate change, and its impact on agriculture. Improved knowledge plays a role in making decisions as they practice agriculture and become climate resilient. The community outreach programs are organized and delivered by our local extension officers. The extension officers also help farmers to understand financing opportunities and act as facilitators and communications for farmers. Extension officers also serve as mobile money agents in order to provide the physical presence and `infrastructure` necessary for farmers to deposit and withdraw into their mobile money accounts.

It is worth noting that users of our digital platform receive weather forecasts as it helps farmers to plan and make decisions too.
Solution Provider(s): EST GLOBAL INC  , Global Alliance for Artificial Intelligence, Avvena
Duration to pilot in a new geography: The estimated duration to pilot your solution in a new geography is 5 years
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);
Desired impact:
Our solution aims to serve smallholder farmers and agri - (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises) MSMEs in Congo who are currently underserved in accessing climate finance due to limited access to financial services, lack of financial literacy, and inadequate collateral. These farmers and MSMEs are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, which has led to reduced agricultural productivity.

The target population is made up of smallholder farmers and MSMEs who are heavily reliant on rain-fed agriculture for their livelihoods. 

We address the needs of this underserved population by providing a digital finance platform that assists farmers and MSMEs in gaining access to climate finance. The platform uses machine learning to determine the creditworthiness of users based on their records such as crop yields, type of crops, market price, cooperative or farmers group membership, and mobile money financial history, allowing them to apply for financing to increase capacity for climate resilience and mitigation. Active social microlending institutions and finance providers are added to the application to share the climate financing opportunities they provide.

We also organize community outreach programs to train and educate farmers on climate resilience, financial literacy, and agriculture risks. These programs are delivered by local extension officers who act as facilitators and communications for farmers, helping them understand financing opportunities and other important information. The extension officers also serve as mobile money agents. Through these efforts, we are directly improving the lives of farmers by making it easier to access mobile money services and empowering them with knowledge and resources to build resilience against climate change and other risks.

Overall, the solution aims to directly and meaningfully improve the lives of smallholder farmers and MSMEs in Congo by increasing their access to finance, improving their financial literacy, and building their capacity for climate resilience and mitigation. By doing so, DestinBeni contributes to reducing poverty, improving food security, and promoting sustainable economic development.
Key technologies:
At the heart of our solution lies a combination of web technology, USSD technology, machine learning, and SMS capabilities. These cutting-edge technologies work in tandem to deliver a seamless and comprehensive user experience.

Our platform utilizes web technology as the primary means for users to access and interact with the platform. Through web-based interfaces, users can effortlessly save records, transfer money, and access a wealth of valuable information crucial to their farming activities.

To ensure inclusivity and reach farmers without internet connectivity, we leverage USSD technology. This technology enables users with basic 2G mobile phones to access our platform and avail of its functionalities without internet connectivity. By dialing specific codes on their mobile devices, farmers can conveniently manage their accounts, access critical services, and easily stay connected.

To revolutionize creditworthiness assessment, we employ machine learning algorithms. This advanced technology empowers our platform to analyze vast amounts of user data, extracting valuable insights and determining creditworthiness with remarkable accuracy. By leveraging machine learning, we provide users with fair and efficient evaluations, unlocking access to climate finance opportunities.

Complementing our core technologies is SMS technology, which plays a vital role in communication. We utilize SMS capabilities to send important information, updates, and notifications to users. This ensures that users stay informed, empowered, and connected even in areas with limited internet access.

By harnessing the power of web technology, USSD technology, machine learning, and SMS capabilities, our solution combines accessibility, data-driven insights, and effective communication to revolutionize how farmers access financial services and make informed decisions.
Unique Characteristics:
Our solution (DestinBeni) leverages the power of alternative data and machine learning to determine the creditworthiness of individuals seeking climate finance. Our solution is designed to empower even smallholder farmers with limited internet connectivity and technology, allowing them to manage their accounts using USSD technology or with the help of our extension officers

By integrating with mobile money, DestinBeni enables financial inclusion for those without bank accounts or track records, providing a pathway for individuals to access essential financial services.

Integrating extension officers as part of our solution(digital platform) is an innovative approach that addresses the digital divide and provides localized assistance. These officers serve as knowledgeable resources, offering personalized support, collecting feedback, and building trust with farmers. Additionally, by acting as mobile money agents, they facilitate financial inclusion, enabling farmers to access financial services conveniently through the platform. This comprehensive solution enhances the overall user experience and empowers farmers both technically and financially.

 Empowering farmers with timely weather information is paramount to their success. In collaboration with the Meteorological Department of the Government Ministry of Green Economy, weather forecasts are shared with `our` farmers through our extension officers and via SMS. By effectively incorporating weather data into their decision-making process, we pave the way for enhanced agricultural yields and mitigate the risks of poor harvests. Improved productivity not only secures livelihoods but also bolsters creditworthiness, amplifying opportunities for growth and prosperity. 

 DestinBeni: Redefining credit assessment, enabling climate financial inclusion, and empowering farmers for a brighter future without leaving anyone behind.
Sustainable Change: Our impact-driven theory of change is designed to empower farmers and agricultural SMEs by providing them with a comprehensive digital finance platform solution that enables them to access climate finance while keeping proper financial farm operations records. By educating them about climate change, agricultural risks, and financial literacy, we equip farmers with the knowledge and skills to make informed decisions about their agricultural practices and become more resilient to the impacts of climate change. Our approach is to train  3000  farmers, each supporting at least 3 dependents, benefiting from improved record-keeping, creditworthiness, and agricultural productivity. Our ultimate goal is to reduce the negative impacts of climate change on farmers, increase their climate resilience, and enhance food security and agricultural productivity in the long run.
Primary thematic focus area: MSME Empowerment & Local Digital Innovation
Summary: DestinBeni is a digital platform leveraging alternative credit scoring and machine learning to provide underserved smallholder farmers and agri-SMEs in the Republic of the Congo with access to climate finance. The platform supports farmers with record-keeping, mobile money transactions, climate resilience, and financial literacy, aiming to enhance their climate adaptation capacity and foster inclusive economic growth.

Title: PikaBox: Empowering Chefs, Consumers, and Farmers through Digital Inclusion
Subtitle: Transforming the culinary economy through digital innovation that connects farmers, chefs, and food lovers while tackling unemployment, nutrition, and food waste.
Problem Statement: In Kenya and many parts of Africa, small chefs, home cooks, and food vendors face limited access to digital markets, stable income, and formal recognition. Consumers lack affordable, healthy, and traceable food options. Meanwhile, food waste and unemployment persist in local food ecosystems.
Solution Overview:
PikaBox is an inclusive food-tech platform that brings together farmers, chefs, home cooks, and consumers into one connected ecosystem. It makes it easy for anyone to plan, prepare, and enjoy meals while creating new opportunities for small businesses and individuals who are often left out of the digital economy.

Here’s how it works:

Recipes to Meal Kits: A user can browse recipes, order pre-portioned ingredients, and have them delivered to their door — supporting farmers and supermarkets who supply fresh produce.

Chef on Demand: Users can hire a chef to cook at home or in the chef’s kitchen, making it easy to host events or enjoy healthy meals while giving chefs, many of them underemployed, access to reliable income.

Home-Cooked Marketplace: Talented home cooks can sell their meals through PikaBox, turning kitchens into micro-businesses, reducing food waste, and offering customers affordable, authentic dishes.

Community Engagement: “PikaSocial” allows food lovers to connect, share, and join challenges that promote healthier lifestyles. Surplus meals can also be directed to charities, ensuring no food goes to waste.

Partnerships are at the heart of PikaBox. We have already begun working with Chandarana Foodplus Supermarkets and local farmer groups for supply, and with NGOs that channel surplus food to vulnerable communities.

PikaBox creates jobs for chefs and home cooks, new markets for farmers and vendors, healthier food choices for families, and stronger, more resilient supply chains. It is more than a food delivery app — it is a pathway to inclusive growth and community empowerment.
Solution Provider(s): PikaBox Limited (Food Technology, Kenya): Lead implementer, platform development and operations.  Chandarana Foodplus Supermarkets (Retail, Kenya): Grocery and meal kit supply partner.  Independent Chefs & PikaChef Network (Hospitality, Kenya): Service providers and culinary trainers.  Local Farmer Cooperatives (Agriculture, Kenya): Fresh produce sourcing and traceability.  NGOs & Food Charities (Nonprofit, Kenya): Redistribution of surplus meals to vulnerable communities.
Implementation location(s): A mini-pilot has been conducted in Nairobi with a controlled group ahead of a full commercial pilot. The PikaBox application is already live and available on both the Android Play Store and Apple App Store.
Implementation timeline(s): A mini-pilot was conducted in Nairobi from October 2024 to February 2025 with a controlled group of users. A broader commercial pilot is scheduled to roll out from Q4 2025 onwards.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: It would take approximately 3–6 months to pilot PikaBox in a new geography, covering vendor onboarding, chef recruitment, logistics setup, and user acquisition.
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 2 (Zero Hunger);SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives:
PikaBox is building the digital backbone of Africa’s culinary economy. Our objective is to:

Unlock livelihoods for chefs, home cooks, and small vendors by giving them access to structured digital markets.

Transform food access by making healthy, affordable, and traceable meals as easy to order as a ride-hailing service.

Build resilience in food supply chains, linking farmers and supermarkets directly to end-consumers.

Key Impacts & Achievements:

Job Creation & Income Generation: By 2027, PikaBox will directly enable income for 10,000+ chefs, home cooks, riders, and small-scale vendors — many of them women and youth entering the digital economy for the first time.

Market Access for MSMEs: Integration of farmer groups and supermarkets into the platform ensures thousands of small producers gain digital visibility and steady demand.

Scalable User Growth: PikaBox projects 50,000 active paying users with an average revenue per user of USD 20/month, unlocking an annual gross revenue potential of over USD 12 million by 2027.

Food Waste Reduction: The home-cooked meals marketplace and NGO partnerships channel surplus food into secondary markets or charities, addressing a problem where up to 40% of prepared food is lost or wasted.

Health & Nutrition Impact: Through personalized meal plans and community challenges, PikaBox empowers families to make healthier food choices, reducing the rising burden of diet-related illnesses.
Key technologies:
PikaBox integrates scalable, accessible technologies to build an inclusive digital food ecosystem:

Mobile & Web Platforms: Android, iOS, and web applications supporting recipes, meal kits, chef booking, and home-cooked meal marketplaces.

E-Commerce Infrastructure: Secure payments (M-Pesa, cards, wallets), vendor dashboards for order and inventory management, and automated settlement cycles.

Digital Logistics & Tracking: Rider management, route optimization, and real-time delivery tracking to ensure transparency and reliability.

Identity & Vetting Tools: Digital KYC, certification uploads, and compliance checks for chefs and vendors to build trust and guarantee food safety.

Community & Engagement Layer: “PikaSocial” — an interactive food community platform enabling challenges, reviews, and user-generated content.

Supporting Technologies:

AI: Used for personalized meal planning and recommendation engines (e.g., tailoring meal plans to dietary needs such as weight loss, vegan diets, or family-based nutrition).

IoT: Integrated where relevant in the supply chain (e.g., cold chain monitoring, smart storage at vendor level, and rider delivery tracking for perishable goods).

Data Analytics: Aggregated platform data supports vendor performance insights, consumer trends, and supply chain optimization.
Unique Characteristics:
Inclusive Business Model

Unlike conventional food apps that only partner with restaurants, PikaBox empowers chefs, home cooks, and small-scale vendors to participate in the digital economy.

This opens income streams for women, youth, and informal workers traditionally excluded from formal food markets.

Farm-to-Fork Traceability

Ingredients for meal kits are sourced through vetted farmer groups and supermarket partners, ensuring freshness, transparency, and consumer trust.

This provides a unique value proposition for both everyday consumers and premium buyers seeking quality and traceability.

Hybrid Marketplace + Social Platform

PikaBox combines commerce with community: a marketplace for meals and ingredients plus PikaSocial, a food-centric social network that builds engagement through recipes, challenges, and peer-to-peer interaction.

This creates both transactional and relational value for users.

Partnership Model for Scale

Strategic partnerships with established players like Chandarana Foodplus Supermarkets, farmer cooperatives, and NGOs provide supply chain resilience and market credibility.

This ecosystem approach enables rapid scale and systemic impact.

Charity & Circularity Built-In

Surplus meals are redirected through NGOs to food-insecure communities, reducing waste and contributing to urban food resilience — a built-in circular economy mechanism.

Accessible Technology

The platform leverages mobile-first design, lightweight e-commerce, and digital logistics, ensuring accessibility for MSMEs and informal workers who may have limited digital literacy.
Sustainable Change:
Across Africa, millions of chefs, home cooks, and small vendors work in the informal economy with little job security, no access to digital markets, and limited pathways to scale. At the same time, urban households face rising food costs, poor nutrition, and massive food waste, while farmers struggle to access markets. These challenges are structural, not incidental — and require systemic solutions.

PikaBox addresses these gaps by digitizing the entire farm-to-fork journey, creating a platform where informal actors and MSMEs are not only included but empowered to thrive.

Breaking the cycle of informality:
PikaBox formalizes opportunities for chefs and home cooks through digital vetting, rating systems, and structured income streams. What was once invisible or informal becomes part of a recognized, trusted digital economy.

Tackling unemployment and underemployment:
By 2027, PikaBox will have created 10,000+ direct income opportunities for chefs, home cooks, riders, and small vendors — many of them women and youth who otherwise face joblessness. This is not gig work at the margins, but a new form of dignified digital livelihood.

Confronting food insecurity and waste:
Through meal kits, curated recipes, and home-cooked meal resale, households gain affordable and healthier food options, while surplus meals are rerouted to charities instead of landfills — directly reducing food waste in cities where up to 40% of prepared food is lost.

Strengthening fragile supply chains:
By linking farmer groups, supermarkets, and households through digital ordering, logistics, and traceability, PikaBox makes food supply chains more stable, transparent, and shock-resistant in the face of urbanization, climate pressures, and price volatility.

Shifting culture and community norms:
With PikaSocial, communities engage in meal challenges, shared nutrition goals, and peer-to-peer support — fostering a culture of healthier living and collective responsibility for food.

Systemic Change Vision:
PikaBox is not just a platform; it is a blueprint for inclusive digital economies. The follow-on effect is a structural shift where:

Informal food workers become part of the formal, digital economy.

MSMEs gain steady digital access to markets.

Food systems become less wasteful, more transparent, and more resilient.

Households gain healthier, affordable, and traceable meals.

This is how PikaBox transforms fragmented, inequitable food systems into inclusive engines of economic growth, job creation, and social resilience.
Funding Sources: The development and initial pilot of PikaBox have been entirely self-funded through contributions from the company’s directors.
Testimonials and Endorsements:
Chandarana Foodplus Supermarkets (Retail Partner):
“Partnering with PikaBox has allowed us to extend our reach into digital food services and connect with new consumer segments. It strengthens our supply chains while aligning with our vision for healthier, traceable food delivery.”

App Users (Google Play & App Store Reviews):
“The meal kits are a game-changer — affordable, fresh, and easy to use.”

“I love that I can get local chefs and discover authentic meals from my neighborhood.”


Sources:

Chandarana Foodplus Supermarkets (official partner communication).

User reviews on Google Play Store and Apple App Store.
Further comments/feedback:
PikaBox represents more than a food delivery service; it is a blueprint for inclusive digital participation in the food economy. As a young solution, it has already demonstrated its ability to:

Digitize informal actors such as home cooks and small vendors, giving them visibility and income in formal markets.

Build resilient supply chains by linking supermarkets, farmer cooperatives, and households into a traceable digital platform.

Reduce urban food waste by enabling redistribution to charities and resale of surplus meals.

Foster a community of food culture and healthier living through PikaSocial.

We see PikaBox as a replicable model that can be adapted across geographies, helping to solve interconnected challenges of employment, food insecurity, and digital exclusion.
Primary thematic focus area: MSME Empowerment & Local Digital Innovation
Summary: PikaBox is a digital platform designed to empower chefs, home cooks, farmers, and consumers by connecting them in a digital ecosystem. The platform addresses key challenges such as food waste, unemployment, and limited access to digital markets, especially for underrepresented groups. Its hybrid marketplace and social platform, along with its focus on traceability and supply chain resilience, provide a unique value proposition. However, its long-term scalability may depend on securing funding and expanding partnerships beyond its initial self-funded model.

Title: WazobiaDigi
Subtitle: Empowering women, youth, and MSMEs with digital and entrepreneurial skills in local Nigerian languages.
Problem Statement: Despite Nigeria’s rapidly growing digital economy, millions remain excluded due to low digital literacy, language barriers, and limited access to inclusive training especially among women, youth, and micro-entrepreneurs. According to the National Bureau of Statistics (2023), over 60% of Nigerian MSMEs operate informally, lacking the digital skills needed to compete in the modern economy. Additionally, the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report (2022) notes that only 24% of women in Nigeria use mobile internet, compared to 39% of men, highlighting a significant gender gap in digital access. Many digital training programs are delivered in English, excluding a large portion of the population who speak primarily Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, or Pidgin. This exclusion deepens inequalities and limits opportunities for economic participation and innovation.
Solution Overview:
WazobiaDigi is a multilingual mobile learning platform designed to empower underserved Nigerian populations particularly women, youth, and MSMEs with essential digital and entrepreneurial skills. The platform delivers localized, culturally relevant training in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, and Pidgin English, using low-bandwidth mobile technology accessible via smartphones and basic devices.

How the Solution Works:

1. Mobile Platform Access:
 Users register via a mobile app or USSD/SMS gateway and access short, modular training courses in their preferred local language. Topics include:

- Digital literacy (basic phone use, mobile internet, digital safety)
- Entrepreneurial skills (business planning, recordkeeping, pricing)
- E-commerce and social media marketing
- Mobile money and digital payment systems


2. Gamified Learning and Certification:
 Users earn points and badges for completing modules. Upon completion, they receive digital certificates that can support loan applications or job opportunities.

3. Offline Accessibility and Radio Blends:
 Select content is made downloadable or accessible offline, and community radio partnerships extend learning reach through scheduled broadcasts and Q&A sessions.

4. Micro-Mentorship and Peer Learning:
 Local facilitators or “digital champions” help onboard learners, while peer groups are created via WhatsApp or Telegram for ongoing support and motivation.



 Methodologies and Technologies Used:
1. Human-Centered Design (HCD): The platform is co-designed with input from local women, youth, and informal entrepreneurs to ensure usability and relevance.

2. Mobile-First Architecture: Built using lightweight frameworks for low-end Android devices and offline-first access.

3. AI-Based Personalization: Adaptive content delivery tailored to users’ progress, language preferences, and business interests.

4.Data Analytics Dashboard: Real-time reporting on user engagement, completion rates, location, and gender-disaggregated metrics for impact tracking.


In Summary:
WazobiaDigi blends digital innovation, language inclusion, and economic empowerment to break down barriers to participation in Nigeria’s digital economy. By equipping underserved individuals with practical skills and linking them to financial services through trusted partnerships, the solution creates a scalable and sustainable pathway for inclusive growth.
Solution Provider(s): WazobiaDigi’s success relies on strong, cross-sector partnerships that ensure sustainability, access, and financial empowerment:  Microfinance Institutions (e.g., LAPO, Accion Microfinance) – Offer small business loans to certified users – Co-create financial literacy modules  Commercial Banks (e.g., GTBank, Access Bank) – Integrate digiPartner wallets or payment tools – Sponsor program reach and host business clinics  Telecom Providers – Zero-rate access to the platform – Offer discounted data bundles  Community-Based Organizations – Recruit learners – Host digital onboarding sessions – Provide grassroots support  State Agencies/SMEDAN – Align program with national MSME support frameworks and policies  Technology Partners – Provide platform infrastructure – Deliver cybersecurity tools – Support translation and localization
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 2-3 Years
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 4 (Quality Education);SDG 5 (Gender Equality);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives:

1. To empower women, youth, and MSMEs with practical digital and entrepreneurial skills using local language mobile training.

2. To promote inclusive economic participation by bridging the digital literacy gap across underserved Nigerian communities.

3. To support financial inclusion by connecting trained users with microfinance institutions and digital financial tools.

4. To enable scalable digital upskilling through partnerships with telecoms, banks, and grassroots organizations.


Key Achievements and Expected Impact (Quantifiable):

1. 25,000+ individuals (at least 60% women and youth) trained in digital literacy and business skills within 18 months.

2. 5,000+ MSMEs supported with mobile-friendly business tools, e-commerce onboarding, and financial literacy modules.

3. 3,000+ users linked to microloans, digital wallets, or savings products through partner MFIs and banks.

4. 40% increase in digital tool adoption (e.g., mobile money, WhatsApp Business) among rural MSMEs in pilot communities.

5. Creation of 150+ jobs through community mobilizers, trainers, and peer mentors.

6. Significant reduction in language-related learning barriers, with 100% of training content available in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, and Pidgin.
Key technologies:
WazobiaDigi leverages a blend of accessible, inclusive, and scalable technologies to empower women and MSMEs in the digital economy:

1. Mobile-First Platform: Designed for low-bandwidth environments, accessible via smartphones and feature phones.

2. AI-Powered Learning & Matching: AI recommendation engine to personalize learning pathways, match users to financing options, and recommend relevant digital tools.

3. Digital Wallets & FinTech Integration:  Secure mobile wallets linked with partner banks and microfinance institutions to enable savings, payments, and access to small business loans.

4. Data Analytics Dashboard: Tracks user progress, financial literacy outcomes, and business growth for impact monitoring.

5. Multilingual Support & Localization Tools : Technology-enabled translation and voice features to reach users in diverse Nigerian languages.

6. Cybersecurity & Privacy Safeguards:  Encryption and identity protection to ensure safe transactions and data trust.

7. Telecom Integration:  Zero-rated/low-data access in partnership with telecom providers to reduce connectivity barriers.

These technologies ensure that WazobiaDigi is inclusive, scalable, and sustainable, bridging the digital and financial gap for underserved women and small businesses.
Unique Characteristics:
What Makes WazobiaDigi Unique :

1. Multilingual and Culturally Rooted: Unlike most digital training platforms, WazobiaDigi delivers content in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, and Pidgin English, breaking language barriers that exclude millions from digital upskilling.

2. Mobile-First, Low-Bandwidth Design: Optimized for basic smartphones and rural internet conditions, the platform works offline and via USSD/SMS, making it accessible in low-connectivity areas.

3. Integrated MSME Enablement Tools: Beyond learning, users can access business tools like invoice templates, mobile money integrations, and e-commerce onboarding directly from the app.

4. Inclusive Financing Linkages: Through partnerships with microfinance institutions, commercial banks, and fintechs, users can transition from training to real economic participation, accelerating access to microloans, savings products, and mobile wallets.

5. Community-Based Mentorship Model: Local “digital champions” and peer learning groups promote uptake, retention, and trust, especially in underserved rural and peri-urban areas.

6. Data-Driven Personalization: The platform adapts content based on user profiles (e.g., gender, business type, literacy level) to deliver personalized learning journeys and support inclusive growth.

7. Partnership-Enabled Scalability: The program is designed to scale through multi-sector partnerships with telecoms, MFIs, NGOs, and government agencies, allowing for regional and national expansion.
Sustainable Change:
At its core, WazobiaDigi is more than a digital tool, it is a vehicle for breaking cycles of exclusion that keep women and small businesses from thriving in the digital economy. Our approach combines technology with capacity-building and partnerships to drive long-term change.

Theory of Change:

1. If underserved women and MSMEs gain access to affordable digital skills, financial literacy, and market tools,

2. And if these services are delivered in local languages, through low-bandwidth, mobile-first technology, and supported by trusted community networks,

3. Then they will be able to increase their financial independence, grow their businesses, and actively participate in the formal economy.


Desired Follow-On Effects:

1. Economic Empowerment: Women-led MSMEs can access credit, grow revenues, and create jobs, reducing poverty at the household and community levels.

2. Systemic Financial Inclusion: Partnerships with banks, MFIs, and telecoms normalize the integration of women and grassroots entrepreneurs into the financial system.

3. Digital Equity: By removing language, literacy, and connectivity barriers, the platform sets a precedent for inclusive technology design in Nigeria and beyond.

4. Community Multipliers: Trained women become peer mentors, passing on digital and financial knowledge within their communities.

5. Policy Alignment: Collaboration with agencies like SMEDAN ensures that learnings feed into national strategies for MSME development and women’s economic participation.

Over time, WazobiaDigi aims to shift mindsets, policies, and market structures, so that inclusion is no longer a project but the standard.
Funding Sources: Not Applicable
Testimonials and Endorsements: Not Applicable
Further comments/feedback: Not Applicable
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: WazobiaDigi is a mobile-first, multilingual platform designed to empower women, youth, and MSMEs in Nigeria by providing essential digital and entrepreneurial skills. The initiative addresses the digital divide by offering localized, culturally relevant training in Nigerian languages. While the project has strong potential for social impact, more clarity on scalability and funding sustainability is needed for long-term success.

Title: SimulDigital – Écosystèmes numériques pour la formation et l’autonomisation / SimulDigital – Digital ecosystems for training and empowerment
Subtitle: Une plateforme intégrée avec une application mobile “all-in-one” connectée à une application web de suivi/ évaluation, pour former, outiller, accéder au marché et au financement, pour les jeunes artisans et producteurs africains./ An integrated platform with an “all-in-one” mobile application connected to a monitoring/evaluation web application, to train, equip, access markets and financing, for young African artisans and producers.
Problem Statement:
En Afrique, des millions de jeunes et de petits producteurs manquent d’accès à des infrastructures de formation, à des enseignants qualifiés et à des outils modernes pour développer leurs compétences dans tous les domaines, l’entrepreneuriat, la formation métier, la gestion technique et financière, la commercialisation, le financement. Ils manquent également d’outils simples pour gérer leurs activités, prendre des décisions éclairées, accéder au marché, monter des plans d’affaires et accéder au financement. Les inégalités numériques et géographiques aggravent l’exclusion et freinent la transition vers une économie durable et circulaire./

In Africa, millions of young people and small producers lack access to training infrastructure, qualified teachers, and modern tools to develop their skills in all areas: entrepreneurship, vocational training, technical and financial management, marketing, and financing. They also lack simple tools to manage their activities, make informed decisions, access markets, develop business plans, and secure financing. Digital and geographical inequalities worsen exclusion and slow down the transition toward a sustainable and circular economy.
Solution Overview:
Description :
La plateforme digitale SimulDigital combine :
Des jeux éducatifs et des simulations en langues locales (apprentissage par le jeu et la décision),
Une application mobile incluant les jeux d’apprentissage, un outil de gestion de petite entreprise, de coopérative et d’exploitation agricole, un outil de montage de plan d’affaires, un outil de commercialisation (achat/ vente), une messagerie  et des forums thématiques d’échange avec les experts et une médiathèque,
Une plateforme web de pilotage et de diffusion des données de suivi/ évaluation pour les acteurs clés (experts, facilitateurs, acheteurs, financeurs).

Le bénéficiaire télécharge l’application à partir de Playstore en choisissant sa langue. Après activation de son compte en ligne, Il est invité à télécharger les jeux d’apprentissage disponibles (immédiatement ou jeu par jeu en fonction des capacités de son smartphone). Il peut alors utiliser tous les contenus de l’application hors ligne. A chaque connexion, les données de suivi/ évaluation sont automatiquement synchronisées avec la base de données dédiée au projet.
Les administrateurs de l ‘application web ont la possibilité de paramétrer l’envoi de notifications auxquelles sont associés de nouveaux documents de la médiathèque et des capsules de jeux pour assurer une formation en continue. Ils peuvent aussi adresser de cette façon aux bénéficiaires, ou à des cohortes, des vocaux en langues locales pour leur communiquer une information, une nouvelle pratique, …

Méthodologie et technologies :
. Logiciel SimulFactory (no-code) pour produire localement des contenus éducatifs,
. Utilisation d’un modèle IA spécialisé permettant la production des spécifications du scénario d’un jeu et des médias associés, à partir de l’énoncé des constituants du périmètre d’activité,
. Scénarisation avec logiciel en ligne no-code SimulFactory, basé sur la modélisation graphique des situations de vie et d’activités professionnelles, quelque soit leur complexité, et des échanges entre les personnages. 
. Ateliers de co-création et de validation par prototypage itératif avec les experts du domaine.
. Objectif de former des équipes locales pour une production autonome complète des jeux en langues locales.

Partenariats et modèles de collaboration :

Title: ACISP - The Algerian Citizen and Social Open-Innovation Programme
Subtitle: The Architects of Change
Problem Statement: In Algeria’s mid-sized cities and rural communes, youth, women, and MSMEs remain largely excluded from the digital economy. Key barriers include: (1) scarce, job-ready digital and entrepreneurial skills; (2) low MSME uptake of e-commerce, digital payments, data/marketing, and basic cybersecurity due to cost, know-how, and trust gaps; (3) fragmented, urban-centric support that disconnects training from market entry, finance, and procurement; (4) geographic and linguistic inequities in last-mile access and locally relevant content; (5) weak evidence-to-policy feedback loops that prevent successful pilots from scaling; and (6) insufficient cohesion across territorial strata (commune–wilaya–national) coupled with limited citizen participation and co-creation, which hampers coordination, ownership, and scale. These constraints drive underemployment, low productivity, and limited market reach for local firms and talent.
Solution Overview:
Framework — “Neuronal Social Infrastructure”
ACISP operates as a neuronal social infrastructure: territories are the “brain,” citizens and MSMEs are the “neurons,” and our caravans, forums, mentors, and data flows are the “synapses.” The caravan creates local connections; the 12-month incubation converts experience into reusable memory (toolkits, datasets, playbooks) via a shared capitalisation platform—speeding up learning and scale across communes, wilayas, and national level. 

1) How the solution works (end-to-end)
Phase 1 — Territorial Caravan (16 cities / 4 wilayas).
On-the-ground activations (pop-up fab labs, workshops, hackathons), with youth (6–18) initiation tracks and a gamified ideathon to surface local problems/solutions, diagnose needs, and pre-select projects for wilaya events. 
Phase 2 — Wilaya Events.
Public forums showcase youth projects, convene partners and a careers forum, then run a one-month student “feasibility–MVP” challenge so each selected team arrives at national level with a first MVP and a project map. 
Phase 3 — National Launch Event.
Bootcamp + mixed student–founder teams; final selection of 15–20 incubated projects; official start of ACISP incubation. 
Phase 4 — ACISP Incubation & Open Innovation (12 months).
Hybrid accompaniment (quarterly seminars, mid-term bootcamp) and a capitalisation platform that captures methods, deliverables and data for replication. 
Phase 5 — National Forum (Closing).
Final pitches and showcases, institutional panels, Startup label delivery, and on-ramp to post-programme instruments (funding, accelerators, calls). 
Scale & targets (pilot 2025–26).
16 cities (4 wilayas), 1,500+ participants, 60 local projects exhibited, 15–20 incubated, 100+ documented outputs, 30+ partners. 

2) Methodologies and technologies used
Research–Action & MRV across phases.
Caravan: sensitive cartographies, light interviews, digital-maturity scoring, narrative capture → local barrier typologies and needs. 
Wilaya: panels, self-positioning, cross-observation → territorial dashboards and inter-wilaya comparison grids. 
Incubation: longitudinal tracking, progression grids, project/territory scoring, reflective narratives → standardised project sheets, trajectory models, context-fit methods. 
National forum: narrative synthesis, impact visualisation, and policy recommendations for replication. 
Incubation curriculum (12 months).
From pre-integration and acculturation to structuring (BMC, MVP, storytelling), then test & iterate (field tests, impact grid, budget), and consolidation & launch (legal status, identity, online presence, ecosystem integration). 
Technologies & learning stacks (low-cost, mobile-first).
Pop-up fab labs and kits for hands-on prototyping: programming, electronics/robotics, audiovisual, Arduino/Raspberry Pi-type projects and maker tools. 
Adult MSME tracks: monthly modules for digital marketing, AI tools, online productivity, business digitisation; presence-building and basic CRM/ops practices. 
LMS + toolkit repository for resources, deliverables deposit, and shared templates to harmonise practice and accelerate replication. 
Cohesion & participation by design.
Shared governance tools (common digital platform, harmonised grids, multi-level dashboards) ensure commune–wilaya–national alignment and citizen co-creation throughout. 

3) Partnerships and collaboration models
Multi-level distributed governance.
Local (city): a local cell (referents–facilitators) manages field ops, mobilisation, and documentation.
Wilaya: coordination committee validates projects and prepares regional events.
National: ACISP steering + strategic committees handle supervision and alignment with ministries. 
Stakeholder roles & benefits (win–win logic).
Ministries: strategic backing, data access → policy-relevant local evidence and measurable impact.
Sponsors & companies: funding/logistics, stands, buyer access → RSE visibility & user insights.
Mentors & experts: coaching, bootcamps, panels → recogn
Solution Provider(s): Young Creators — digital FabLab & social incubator leading the programme (social innovation; education & incubation), , Keybox — pedagogy partner for ages 6–18 and provider of the national learning platform and educational kits (EdTech; learning design), Ministry of Knowledge Economy, Startups and Micro-Enterprises (Algeria) — institutional partner with High Patronage requested and participation in key milestones (government; public administration), , Municipal & Wilaya Authorities — local governments supporting mobilisation, rural transport and hosting (local public administration), , Universities & Schools - Numidia Institute of technologie, polytechnique alger — academic hosts and co-animators; student teams support feasibility/MVP challenges (higher education & research), , Local Associations & Community Hosts — civil society partners providing spaces, outreach and co-animation (civil society; community development).
Implementation location(s): 2023-2025 - Algeria, Tlemcen - (Nedroma and Djebella) - Children (6–18) — “Pop-up Fab Labs & Creative Tech” Purpose: Early digital literacy, creativity, and problem-solving; build confidence and identity with tech. Formats: Pop-up fab labs (electronics/robotics/coding/media), workshops, discovery tracks, and a gamified ideathon to surface local challenges from a child’s perspective. Outputs: Mini-projects (games, sensors, short videos), end-of-day demos, and a public showcase at wilaya events. Safeguarding & inclusion: Mixed-level groups, accessible materials, local-language facilitation; girls’ participation targets. Where piloted: Aïn Teïne Numérique (children-only experiment; no incubated ventures originate from this stream). Diaspora supported equipment and continuity. Adults (18+: youth, women, MSMEs) — “Digitisation & Incubation” Purpose: Practical digitisation of local MSMEs and venture creation for underserved talent. Formats: On-site MSME clinics (e-commerce, payments, basic cybersecurity, marketing/data) with a 90-day digitisation plan; entrepreneur track feeding a 12-month incubation (BMC→MVP→go-to-market→formalisation→online presence). Implementation timeline(s): Implementation timeline(s) Jun–Aug 2024 — Nedroma.io (Nedroma, Tlemcen province, Algeria). 12 participatory workshops + 1 immersive residency; 45 direct learners; structured 3-module pathway (territory exploration → prototyping → collective storytelling). Summer 2024 — “Aïn Teïne Numérique” (Aïn Teïne, rural Algeria). Children-focused pop-up fab-lab experiment during school holidays (1-week to 1-month formats), targeting rural/underserved audiences. Pilot Year 2025 — ACISP multi-wilaya rollout (Alger, Tlemcen, Ilizi, Aïn Temouchent, Annaba). Programme pilot defined for 2025 with three indicative pilot wilayas. Planned field launch of the Caravan: December 2025, with ministerial High Patronage requested (official letter dated 19 April 2025). Sequence thereafter: national launch event (selection of 15–20 projects) → 12-month ACISP incubation → national closing forum.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Fast breakdown Weeks 1–3 — Territorial mapping & setup Rapid territorial diagrams/diagnostics (needs, assets, barriers), baseline KPIs. Stakeholder mapping, partner mobilisation & MoUs (national, wilaya, commune), venue scouting. Local host onboarding; risk, safeguarding, and logistics plan. Weeks 4–6 — Mobilisation & localisation Communications rollout; recruitment (children 6–18 & adults/MSMEs). Facilitator training; procurement of pop-up fab-lab kits; agenda adapted to local context. Finalise MSME clinic menu (e-commerce, payments, marketing/data, basic cyber). Weeks 7–8 — Field activation (Caravan, 3–5 days) Pop-up Fab Labs (kids/teens), gamified ideathon, and MSME digitisation clinics. Desired impact:
Solution Objectives
Inclusive skills & pipelines. Deliver job-ready digital and entrepreneurial skills (youth 6–18; adults/MSMEs) via a territorial Caravan, then channel selected teams into a 12-month incubation to move from idea → MVP → launch. 
Economic empowerment. Convert training into venture creation and MSME digitisation, producing MVPs, market entry and formalisation (legal status, online presence). 
Cohesion & governance. Strengthen commune–wilaya–national coordination with a shared platform, harmonised grids and dashboards; ensure citizen participation and partner alignment.

Scale & replication. Build a nationally replicable model from pilots to 16 cities across 4 wilayas, then prepare export to similar contexts. 
Key achievements / impacts (quantified where available)
Pilot outcomes (Nedroma.io, 2024). 12 participatory workshops + 1 immersive residency; 45 direct learners. Post-pilot: 86% reported higher local agency, 72% moved from no career projection to a first project intention, 33% (15 people) initiated or joined a collective project. 
Programme 2025–26 targets (pilot year). 16 cities / 4 wilayas, 1,500+ participants, 60 projects exhibited, 15–20 projects incubated over 12 months, 100+ documented outputs (MVPs, pitches, action plans), 200h+ mentoring, 4 wilaya events, 2 national events, 30+ partners engaged, 3–4M social-media views. 
Incubation deliverables & market readiness. Standard path to MVP, impact grid, budget, legal status, brand/online presence, and Startup label at the national forum—plus on-ramps to finance/accelerators. 
Territorial & institutional cohesion. Multi-level governance (local cells, wilaya coordination, national steering & strategic committees) + shared tooling (platform, reporting, scoring) to reduce fragmentation and improve execution. 
Employment generation (pathway). Jobs are created through new ventures and MSME digitisation; employment effects are measured longitudinally within the MRV framework. Early pilot data (Nedroma.io) shows a strong pipeline of new initiatives (33% initiating/joining projects), which the 12-month incubation converts into operating enterprises and local jobs.

Unique Characteristics:
Unique / Differentiated Characteristics of ACISP
1) Model & Governance
“Neuronal social infrastructure” frame: territories operate like a brain—citizens/MSMEs as neurons, caravans/incubation as synapses, the capitalisation platform as memory—optimising signal flow between commune, wilaya, and national levels.
Distributed, multi-level governance (commune → wilaya → national): harmonised scorecards, shared dashboards, and one playbook keep all strata aligned while preserving bottom-up ownership.
Evidence-to-policy loop by design: research-action + MRV turn field results into policy-ready standards that de-risk replication for public authorities.
2) Delivery & Pedagogy
Dual pipeline (Children 6–18 ↔ Adults/MSMEs): pop-up fab labs for early skills and imagination + MSME digitisation clinics for immediate economic value—bridged by a gamified ideathon and a student “feasibility → MVP” sprint.
Itinerant Caravan → Wilaya Forums → National Launch → 12-month Incubation: a staged, repeatable funnel that converts local needs into MVPs, then into operating ventures linked to buyers/finance.
90-day MSME Digitisation Plan: every participating firm leaves the field phase with a concrete adoption roadmap (e-commerce, payments, basic cyber, marketing/data).
3) Technology & Data
Low-cost, low-bandwidth stack: Arduino/ESP32, entry-level robotics/3D where available, mobile-first web, simple CRM/ops tools—maintainable locally and resilient to connectivity constraints.
Open-knowledge capitalisation: LMS + toolkit repository (templates, playbooks, case libraries) that speeds up learning curves across territories.
Territorial dashboards: standard KPIs and narrative data capture (stories + metrics) to compare outcomes across communes/wilayas and steer decisions.
4) Partnerships & Financing
Coalition-of-capacity: local anchors (youth centres/associations), universities, ministries, private sponsors, and diaspora—each with clear roles (venues, mentors, buyer access, logistics, crowdfunding).
Blended financing architecture: cash sponsorship tiers + in-kind tech/logistics, municipal support, diaspora crowdfunding, fee-for-service MSME packages, and performance-based public funds—reducing single-donor dependency.
Market linkage built-in: supplier directories, demo-days with buyers, and procurement pathways ensure projects meet real demand.
5) Replicability & Scale
Two deployment scenarios per wilaya (itinerant vs. centralised hub) + a 3-month pilot kit (ops, budget, KPIs, risk & safeguarding) to start fast in new geographies.
Startup-Studio logic & cooperative backbone: shared services and a cross-territorial consortium allow simultaneous multi-city rollout with consistent quality.
Why it’s innovative: ACISP fuses civic participation, MSME enablement, and incubation into one field-to-policy pipeline that is affordable, data-driven, and engineered for replication—so impact compounds as the network (the “brain”) grows.
Sustainable Change:
Core mechanism
ACISP builds a neuronal social infrastructure: caravans and forums create dense local “synapses” (citizen–MSME–institution links); the 12-month incubation and a national capitalisation platform convert field learning into reusable memory (playbooks, datasets, standards). Impacts (18–36+ months). Job creation via new ventures and MSME growth; increased MSME revenues and market reach; reduced territorial fragmentation (routine commune–wilaya–national coordination); adoption of ACISP playbooks in public programmes; replication from pilots to 16 cities, then other wilayas/countries.
Follow-on effects (designed flywheels)
Capability flywheel. Trained facilitators + open toolkits → faster next deployments → lower costs → more territories onboarded.
Market flywheel. MSME digitisation → better visibility & sales → anchor buyers engage → more firms join clinics.
Policy flywheel. Comparable data across territories → evidence-based decisions → budget lines & procurement windows → stable demand for incubated solutions.
Community flywheel. Children’s demos inspire families; diaspora mentors/crowdfunding reinforce local ownership.

Cooperative backbone. Shared services across ventures (design, tech, media) compress costs and speed multi-city rollout.

Risk & mitigation (summary)
