Title: Ethyx – DPI-Native ESG Credit Infrastructure for Inclusive MSME Finance
Subtitle: Turning MSME invoices into verifiable, programmable assets with embedded ESG and subsidy data to unlock inclusive, climate-aligned finance at scale.
Problem Statement: Over 60% of MSMEs, especially women-led and rural enterprises, lack access to affordable credit due to missing digital histories, small ticket sizes, and high perceived risk. Traditional lending rails cannot embed ESG, subsidy, or climate-linked incentives at the transaction level, leaving climate-relevant MSMEs excluded from formal finance.
Solution Overview: Ethyx is India’s first DPI-native fintech protocol that transforms ordinary invoices into finance-ready, auditable instruments by embedding IoT-derived ESG metrics, quality data, and subsidy eligibility tags directly at the transaction level. Integrated with GST, OCEN, and UPI, the platform enables lenders, NBFCs, cooperatives, and government programs to deliver targeted, climate-aligned finance in minutes. AI-driven scoring reduces default risk, ensures verifiable sustainability reporting, and unlocks micro-ticket lending that traditional systems cannot serve efficiently. Our model blends public digital infrastructure with impact-linked capital flows, ensuring scale without additional compliance burden. We collaborate with financial institutions, cooperatives, and climate funds to deploy ESG-tagged credit tranches in underserved geographies.
Solution Provider(s): Ekarth Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Ethyx) – Fintech innovation for ESG credit infrastructure; partner networks include NBFCs, cooperatives, climate funds, and government-linked digital platforms.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3–6 months, depending on integration with local digital and financial infrastructure.
SDGs addressed: SDG 5 (Gender Equality);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);SDG 13 (Climate Action);
Desired impact: Ethyx seeks to pilot its DPI-native ESG credit infrastructure with MSMEs and SHGs in priority sectors, demonstrating how traceable, climate-aligned credit can be delivered efficiently. Over 3 years, the aim is to validate reductions in loan processing time, lower cost of capital for small borrowers, and enable transaction-level ESG performance tracking — creating a model that can be scaled responsibly.
Key technologies: AI/ML for preliminary impact scoring and credit risk signals, IoT for optional data verification, blockchain-ready audit trails for ESG tagging, and API integration with GST, OCEN, and UPI to align with India’s digital public infrastructure.
Unique Characteristics: One of the first ESG credit rails designed to work natively with DPI, embedding sustainability metrics and subsidy logic directly into invoice/payment data. Targets the gap in micro-ticket MSME lending where verifiable ESG compliance is rarely feasible without additional reporting burden.
Sustainable Change: By embedding ESG, subsidy, and quality data at the transaction layer, Ethyx demonstrates how MSME finance can move from trust-deficit to traceability-first. Even at pilot stage, this approach has the potential to build long-term credit histories, attract blended capital flows, and align financial incentives with sustainability outcomes — in a way that can be adapted to other geographies.
Funding Sources: The Ethyx solution has been founder-funded to date, with early-stage development supported through in-house resources. We are now seeking catalytic grant and blended-finance support to pilot the infrastructure in partnership with MSMEs, SHGs, and financial institutions
Testimonials and Endorsements: As the solution is at a pre-deployment stage, formal beneficiary testimonials are not yet available. However, early discussions with sector experts, incubators, and policy stakeholders (including DPIIT-linked initiatives) have indicated strong interest in piloting the model.
Further comments/feedback: The questionnaire comprehensively addresses solution, impact, and scalability considerations. Given that some innovations are at pilot readiness rather than full implementation, it may be helpful to include more tailored questions for pre-deployment solutions to capture their innovation potential and partnership readiness.
Primary thematic focus area: MSME Empowerment & Local Digital Innovation
Summary: Ethyx is an innovative platform that transforms MSME invoices into verifiable, climate-aligned assets by embedding ESG and subsidy data directly into transactions. The solution aims to unlock affordable credit for underserved MSMEs, particularly in rural and women-led enterprises. While the platform’s integration with India’s digital public infrastructure (DPI) and its potential for scaling ESG-linked finance is promising, its long-term success will depend on securing funding and proving its effectiveness during the pilot stage.

Title: Machi-Logue
Subtitle: AI Facilitator for local consensus building
Problem Statement:
Many communities in the Asia-Pacific region face complex decision-making in areas such as disaster prevention, environmental conservation, and human resource development. The challenge here is not simply the diversity of opinions, but rather the critical lack of opportunities for constructive dialogue.
・Lack of inclusion in disaster prevention plans
Local disaster prevention plans are often developed by experts and government officials, and do not sufficiently reflect the perspectives of people who require assistance in times of disaster, such as the elderly, people with disabilities, and foreign residents. A mechanism for dialogue that allows their urgent voices to be heard is necessary.
・Conflicting interests in environmental conservation
There are often conflicts between local residents, tourism operators, fishermen, and environmental protection groups over the conservation of mangrove forests in coastal areas, the construction of dams on rivers, and the rules for using national parks, which often leads to delays in planning.
・Mismatch between regional needs and TVET
There is a mismatch between the human resources required by local industries and those trained by vocational training schools (TVET institutions).There is no platform for dialogue where industry, educational institutions, and young people can share their vision for the region's future and collaborate to design educational programs. 
To address these challenges, it is essential to establish mechanisms that enable diverse stakeholders to engage in dialogue in a psychologically safe environment, deepen mutual understanding, and collectively create solutions.
Solution Overview:
“Machi-Logue” is a new type of digital citizen café that fully incorporates the dialogue promotion techniques of “Environmental Cafés,” a two-way dialogue method developed by the National Institute for Environmental Studies. Here, citizens engage in deep and constructive dialogue about local issues in a relaxed atmosphere.

1,Invitation to the digital café and topic presentation: Users access a user-friendly platform (digital café).First, municipal officials and experts act as “topic providers” and explain background information and data related to the theme in short videos and illustrations in an easy-to-understand manner. 

2, Sharing dialogue rules and forming small groups: Before starting the dialogue, participants agree to the “Machi-Logue Café Rules” (e.g., “Let's try to accept opinions that differ from our own with an open mind,” “Let's discuss ideas, not personalities”).Participants then divide into small discussion groups. Each group consists of several citizen participants and multiple AI personas representing diverse resident perspectives. 

3, AI facilitators ensure high-quality dialogue: Dialogue in each group is facilitated by AI facilitators, who act like experienced facilitators at an “environmental café.”
A, Bridging opinions: “Ms. A (AI), who is raising children, said she wants to park for a short time, while Mr. B (AI), who owns a store, said it would be a problem for his store. Both opinions are serious. Are there any ideas that would allow both to be accommodated?” The AI facilitator bridges the opposing opinions.
B, Visualization of key points: As discussions become complex, opinions are organized in real time and visualized on a whiteboard, such as “The current key points seem to be ‘safety’ and ‘convenience.’”
C, Promotion of full participation: Participants who are reluctant to speak up or AI personas are gently prompted with questions like “From the perspective of high school student C (AI), how do you see this issue?” to ensure everyone participates in the dialogue.

4, Sharing with the whole group and next steps: After small group discussions, the AI facilitator summarizes the unique ideas and points of agreement from each group and shares them with all participants. This allows participants to see how their discussions contributed to the overall solution.

[Application scenario: Expansion in the Asia-Pacific region] 
We will expand “Machi-Logue” as a consensus-building platform for solving specific issues faced by communities in the Asia-Pacific region.

Disaster prevention: Creating evacuation plans that leave no one behind
Example of use (typhoon-prone areas in the Philippines): Based on local hazard maps, residents will participate in establishing safer evacuation routes and rules for operating evacuation shelters.AI personas such as “elderly people using wheelchairs,” “foreign residents who only speak Japanese,” and “parents with young children” participate in the dialogue. This enables the incorporation of diverse perspectives that were previously overlooked, facilitating the co-creation of inclusive regional disaster prevention plans.

Environmental Conservation Field: “Envisioning a Future in Harmony with Nature”
Application Example (Coastal Communities in Indonesia): This is used to resolve conflicts between development plans and mangrove forest conservation. On the platform, AI personas representing fishermen who rely on traditional fishing for their livelihoods, resort operators seeking to develop tourism, scientists studying mangrove ecosystems, and local residents engage in dialogue with citizens.With the help of AI facilitators, creative solutions that balance environmental conservation and economic development, such as “eco-tourism,” will be explored.
Solution Provider(s): We will collaborate with local governments as demonstration experiment partners. We will cooperate with local NPOs and civic groups as community engagement partners. We will collaborate with university laboratories as academic partners. We will establish a system to continuously improve the quality of dialogue on the platform by welcoming dialogue facilitation experts as dialogue process advisors.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: The pilot implementation in the new city is expected to take approximately 12 months.
SDGs addressed: SDG 14 (Life Below Water);SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives: 
1. Enhancing regional resilience and sustainability (SDG 11.B, 13.1, 8.6): Support communities in the Asia-Pacific region to develop and implement effective, participatory plans to address challenges such as disaster prevention, climate change adaptation, and youth employment. 
2. Realize inclusive decision-making (SDG 16.7): Ensure responsive, inclusive, participatory, and representative decision-making at all levels by structurally incorporating the voices of people who are socially marginalized. 
3. Promote co-governance: Build trust between citizens and government as partners in shaping the future of their communities, rather than as adversaries.  

Key Achievements or Impacts: 
1. Qualitative Achievements A culture of dialogue that respects different opinions and promotes constructive discussion will take root in local communities. Citizens' trust in the policy-making process will be restored, and it will become easier to obtain cooperation for the policies that are decided.  
2. Quantitative Achievements (Pilot Targets) We aim to increase the number of participants by three times compared to traditional resident meetings, particularly among young people and parents, due to the ease of online participation. We aim to reduce the time required to reach consensus on a single issue by an average of 25% through constructive discussions that clarify issues early on. We aim for 85% of participants to respond that they felt their opinions were respected and that the discussion was meaningful.
Key technologies:
1. Generative AI / Large Language Models (LLMs): Generates AI personalities that serve as “topic providers” with diverse backgrounds.

2. AI Facilitation Technology: The technical core of this solution. It learns the skills of skilled human facilitators (asking questions, summarizing, organizing points, and considering emotions) to maximize the quality of dialogue in small groups.This is not merely moderation, but rather serves as a catalyst to inspire mutual understanding among participants.

3. Data analysis and visualization technology: Analyzes the content of conversations in real time and visualizes discussion points on a whiteboard-like interface to aid participants' understanding.
Unique Characteristics:
1. A relentless focus on the quality of dialogue
While other citizen participation tools focus primarily on collecting opinions, this solution leverages the insights gained from “environmental cafés” to design the process and quality of dialogue itself, which is its most unique feature.

2. AI-powered scalable facilitation
Training a large number of high-quality facilitators requires significant time and cost, but AI facilitators can support hundreds of small group conversations simultaneously while maintaining consistent quality. This scalability represents a breakthrough for social implementation.

3. Balancing Structural Inclusivity and Psychological Safety
The AI personality ensures structural diversity of opinions, while the AI facilitator and dialogue rules create a psychologically safe space where everyone can speak freely. This innovative approach is a key differentiator.
Sustainable Change:
Short-term results
Our “Theory of Change” begins with creating countless high-quality “dialogue spaces” in local communities. By participating in AI-facilitated digital citizen cafes, citizens not only express their opinions but also listen to the opinions of others and work together to find solutions, thereby gaining “successful dialogue experiences.”

Long-term outcomes
These successful experiences enhance citizens' political efficacy (the sense that their actions can change society) and foster a sense of ownership over local issues. In the long term, communities where such a culture of dialogue takes root will see administrative bodies and citizens become trusted partners, enabling them to tackle complex and challenging issues through co-governance with perseverance.

This is not merely the introduction of digital tools. It is an attempt at sustainable, systematic social transformation, updating the “operating system” of democracy from a confrontational model to one based on dialogue and co-creation.
Primary thematic focus area: Innovation Acceleration & Knowledge Sharing
Summary: Machi-Logue is a digital citizen café that uses AI facilitators to improve dialogue and consensus-building on critical issues such as disaster prevention, environmental conservation, and human resource development. The platform fosters inclusive, participatory decision-making and bridges diverse stakeholder perspectives in Asia-Pacific communities, addressing gaps in representation and communication.

Title: Scaling Kitso2.0: Future Skills Development for South African Educators

Solution Overview:
• How it works: Kitso2.0 delivers bite-sized, chat-based lessons on WhatsApp with AI-guided pathways, automated nudges, quizzes, and micro-credentials. Content is localized and mapped to national educator development frameworks, with SACE accreditation to count toward CPD.

Title: Inclusive Digital Innovation Hubs: Expanding Opportunities for Underrepresented Startup Communities in the Philippines through Regional Hubs and Digital Support Platforms
Subtitle: Bridging Gaps in Access, Skills, Streamlining Processes, and providing opportunities for Startup Women, Indigenous Peoples, and Grassroots Innovators
Problem Statement:
The Philippines is steadily progressing toward becoming a strong startup ecosystem in the Asia-Pacific region (StartupBlink, 2025). Over the past decade, enabling policies such as the 2015 Roadmap for Digital Startups and, in 2019, the Innovative Startup Act and Philippine Innovation Act, have strengthened support for local startups in the country. However, the ecosystem remains heavily concentrated in major urban centers like Metro Manila, Cebu, and Davao. The number of active startups grew from roughly 100 in 2015 to approximately 700 in 2023, with significant presence in fintech, media and entertainment, and e-commerce, and emerging sectors in agri-technology, edtech, cleantech, and health technology (Teves, 2023).

This urban concentration overlooks numerous early-stage startups particularly those based in rural communities or led by women, youth, indigenous entrepreneurs, and grassroots innovators. Most of these enterprises are grounded in local culture, heritage, agripreneurship, and grassroots innovation, yet they face persistent barriers, such as limited access to mentorship, funding, and incubation programs, as well as, limited opportunities for networking and market linkage and a shortage of local skilled talent trained to meet the special needs of startup development.

Collaboration within the ecosystem also remains fragmented, with industry, academe, government, and communities often working in isolation rather than in synergy. Complex, costly, and time-consuming processes for business registration, compliance, and intellectual property protection discourage formalization and scaling. The absence of a centralized, accessible platform for startup support means many innovators miss opportunities for funding, mentorship, and strategic partnerships.

As a result, women, indigenous peoples, grassroots innovators, and culture and heritage-based enterprises remain underrepresented in startup participation and leadership. Innovation remains concentrated in a limited number of cities and industries, with regional economies yet to be developed and the enormous potential of community-led, culturally rooted innovations yet to be tapped. This uneven and inequitable landscape limits the country’s ability to harness its full diversity of ideas, talents, and resources to address both local and national challenges, and prevents the Philippines from realizing its full innovation potential.
Solution Overview:
The proposed solution is the establishment of Regional/Provincial Innovation Hubs integrated with a Digital Startup Support Platform that provides:
1.	Regional/Provincial Inclusive Innovation Hubs
o	Co-located within universities, LGUs, or co-working spaces in underserved regions/provinces these hubs will serve as community-based centers for ideation stage for potential grassroots innovators.
o	They will offer mentoring, incubation programs, networking opportunities, and digital skills training tailored to the needs of marginalized and region-based innovators.
o	Founders can access both in-person and virtual services, ensuring consistent support regardless of geographic barriers.

2.	Unified Startup Resource Platform
o	A mobile app-based, cloud-based portal will map all available startup resources including funding opportunities, training programs, events, and government services using filters for region, sector, and founder profile to make information accessible and relevant.
o	The platform will also enable AI-driven matchmaking, connecting founders with mentors, investors, potential collaborators, and talent pools.

3.	StartupEase Compliance Toolkit
o	A multilingual, plain-language online toolkit will guide entrepreneurs through business registration, tax compliance, and IP protection processes.
o	Integrated with e-government portals (DTI, SEC, BIR, IPOPHL), it will provide step-by-step instructions, auto-filled forms, and status tracking to reduce the time and cost of compliance.

4.	Regional Sectoral Clusters
o	The program will promote sector-specific clusters aligned with local strengths and market opportunities such as agri-tech in Mindanao, heritage-based creative enterprises for indigenous communities, and eco-tourism ventures in rural provinces.
o	This approach fosters specialization, resource sharing, and collective branding to increase competitiveness.

The success of this solution relies on a strong pentahelix collaboration model that integrates government, academe, industry, and International Development Partners and Donors and media:

This collaborative approach assures that the solution is locally grounded but nationally connected, having a sustainable ecosystem that empowers under-represented innovators while enhancing the overall Philippine startup ecosystem.
Solution Provider(s): •	Lead Implementer: Department of Science and Technology XI •	Core Partners: Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), Philippine Commission on Women (PCW), Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), private accelerators/incubators, and Local Government Units.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 1-2 years
SDGs addressed: SDG 5 (Gender Equality);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);
Desired impact:
•	A more diverse and inclusive startup ecosystem, with greater participation of women, indigenous peoples, and grassroots communities.

•	Decentralized innovation growth across the Philippines, with at least 50% of new startup engagements coming from outside major cities.

•	Streamlined and accessible startup registration and compliance processes.

•	A single-window platform for all startup resources, making the ecosystem easier to navigate for first-time founders.
Key technologies:
•	Cloud-based resource mapping platform with geolocation features.
•	AI-driven recommendation engine to match founders with funding, mentors, or training.
•	Learning Management System (LMS) for startup training in multiple languages.
•	API integration with government e-services (DTI, SEC, IPOPHL, BIR).
Unique Characteristics:
•	Equity-first approach targeting marginalized and underrepresented founders.

•	Decentralized + digital model combining physical hubs for community-building with a national digital platform for reach and scale.

•	Localized sectoral focus that aligns with regional economic strengths and cultural heritage.

•	Multilingual and culturally sensitive design, ensuring accessibility for indigenous communities.
Sustainable Change:
By integrating inclusion and accessibility into the infrastructure of the Philippine startup ecosystem, this solution ensures that digital innovation opportunities reach all regions and social groups. The combination of physical hubs, digital tools, and policy integration will:
•	Build long-term capacity among grassroot innovators.
•	Create continuous market and funding access through digital connectivity.
•	Influence policy reforms for simpler startup registration and compliance.
•	Establish regional innovation ecosystems that continue to operate and expand beyond the project timeline, contributing to a more balanced and resilient national economy.
Funding Sources: Government Funding
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: The proposed solution involves setting up inclusive regional innovation hubs and a digital startup support platform to provide underserved startup communities in the Philippines, particularly women, indigenous peoples, and grassroots innovators, with digital skills, entrepreneurial training, and market access.

Title: Closing the Financing Gap in Africa’s Agri Supply Chains
Subtitle: Unlocking agri-SME growth through digital credit solutions that bridge cash flow gaps, strengthen supply chains, and promote inclusive economic development.
Problem Statement:
Agri-SMEs are the backbone of Sub-Saharan Africa’s agricultural economies, yet they face a $65 billion annual financing gap. Traditional banks require collateral and long approval processes, excluding most SMEs from formal credit. At the same time, microfinance institutions typically provide only small, high-cost loans that are insufficient for business growth.

As a result, agri-SMEs struggle with severe cash flow constraints, limiting their ability to purchase inputs, scale operations, or bridge delayed invoice payments. This financing gap weakens agricultural supply chains, reduces trade capacity, restricts job creation, and undermines food security. Without innovative financing models, the sector remains trapped in a cycle of underinvestment and systemic vulnerability, holding back its potential to drive inclusive economic growth across the region.
Solution Overview:
How the Solution Works
Avenews provides short-term, flexible credit tailored to the needs of agri-SMEs across Sub-Saharan Africa, starting with Kenya. Through our digital platform, businesses access liquidity precisely when needed — whether to purchase inputs, secure stock, or bridge invoice payment delays. Our products, including the Agri Credit Line (ACL), Agri Business Financing (ABF), and Agri Supply Financing (ASF), are designed to supplement cash flow, allowing enterprises to grow trade volumes, respond to market demand, and build financial resilience.

Methodologies and Technologies Used
Our solution leverages machine learning models that analyze transaction history, supply chain records, and alternative data to create dynamic risk profiles and enable rapid, responsible lending. APIs integrate seamlessly with agri-value chain partners, financial institutions, and digital marketplaces, embedding finance directly into trade flows. The platform is mobile-first and integrates with mobile money systems widely used across Sub-Saharan Africa, ensuring accessible and frictionless disbursements and repayments. Automation reduces costs and shortens approval times, while digital repayment features give SMEs the flexibility to manage multiple repayment schedules.

Partnerships and Collaboration Models
Collaboration is central to our model. We partner with agri-SMEs, cooperatives, and corporate buyers to embed financing into everyday transactions. Strategic collaborations with financial institutions and impact investors provide capital depth and sustainability. We also engage with farmer organizations, fintech providers, and development agencies to extend outreach, particularly for women and youth-led enterprises. By aligning private and public stakeholders, Avenews fosters an inclusive ecosystem where finance flows seamlessly and strengthens resilience across Sub-Saharan Africa’s agricultural supply chain.

SDGs addressed: SDG 5 (Gender Equality);SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);
Desired impact:
Desired Impact of the Solution

Solution Objectives

Expand access to affordable, flexible credit for agri-SMEs across Sub-Saharan Africa, beginning in Kenya.

Strengthen resilience of agricultural supply chains by ensuring SMEs can purchase inputs, meet market demand, and bridge invoice gaps.

Drive inclusive growth by prioritizing women and youth-led enterprises, rural SMEs, and underserved value chain actors.

Enable long-term economic transformation by embedding financial services into digital trade ecosystems.

Key Achievements & Impacts (to date and projected)

Financial Inclusion: Over 500 agri-SMEs in Kenya provided with access to short-term credit, unlocking liquidity where traditional banking is limited.

Increased Trade Volumes: Businesses financed by Avenews report an average 30–40% increase in trade capacity during peak demand cycles.

Job Creation & Community Impact: By enabling SMEs to scale, Avenews indirectly supports rural employment — with each SME supported estimated to sustain or create 10–15 local jobs.

Gender Inclusion: Targeting women-led agribusinesses, with a goal of 40% of financed SMEs being women-owned by 2026.

Supply Chain Resilience: Faster access to credit reduces disruptions, ensuring continuous flow of goods across agricultural markets.

Digital Transformation: By leveraging mobile money, APIs, and machine learning credit scoring, Avenews accelerates digital adoption among SMEs and promotes financial literacy.

Scalability: Projected to reach 5,000+ agri-SMEs across Kenya and neighboring Sub-Saharan African countries by 2027, driving regional impact.
Key technologies:
Avenews leverages a digital-first technology stack to deliver inclusive and scalable agricultural finance solutions across Sub-Saharan Africa:

Machine Learning (AI) – Used for dynamic credit scoring and risk assessment. Our models analyze transaction history, supply chain performance, and alternative datasets (e.g., market trends, repayment behaviors) to generate accurate risk profiles, enabling faster and more inclusive lending decisions.

APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) – Facilitate seamless integration with agri-value chain partners, financial institutions, and digital marketplaces. APIs also allow interoperability with third-party fintech platforms, ensuring embedded finance within trade flows.

Mobile Money Integration – Core to accessibility in Sub-Saharan Africa. Disbursements and repayments are processed via mobile money platforms (e.g., M-Pesa), ensuring SMEs in rural and peri-urban areas can transact securely and instantly without reliance on traditional banking infrastructure.

Cloud-Based Platform – Ensures scalability, security, and efficiency, allowing SMEs and partners to access services anytime, anywhere, with minimal infrastructure requirements.

Data Analytics Dashboards – Provide SMEs and partners with real-time insights into loan status, repayment schedules, and performance metrics, fostering transparency and informed decision-making.
Unique Characteristics:
Unique and Differentiated Characteristics

Faster and More Relevant than Banks – Traditional banks require heavy collateral and lengthy approvals, leaving agri-SMEs underserved. Avenews uses machine learning–driven risk assessment and alternative data, approving loans in days instead of weeks and without rigid collateral requirements.

Smarter than MFIs – Microfinance institutions often offer very small, high-cost loans that don’t meet SME growth needs. Avenews provides larger, more flexible facilities aligned with trade cycles, enabling SMEs to actually scale operations instead of just surviving.

More Specialized than Generic Fintechs – Most fintech lenders focus on urban retail and consumer finance. Avenews is purpose-built for agriculture, embedding financing directly into supply chains through APIs and partnerships with buyers, suppliers, and cooperatives. This makes our risk exposure tied to actual trade transactions, not just individual creditworthiness.

Truly Inclusive via Mobile Money – While many financial players still rely on traditional banking rails, Avenews is integrated with mobile money systems, ensuring last-mile accessibility for rural SMEs that are excluded from the formal banking sector.

Tailored Credit Products – Unlike one-size-fits-all products offered by banks or fintechs, Avenews’ Agri Credit Line, Agri Business Financing, and Agri Supply Financing are short-term, transaction-linked, and structured around the real cash flow cycles of SMEs.

Dual Impact Edge – Unlike pure commercial lenders, Avenews combines profitability with impact. We deliberately target women and youth-led SMEs, building both supply chain efficiency and inclusive growth at the same time.

Scalability Across Sub-Saharan Africa – While banks and MFIs remain country-locked due to infrastructure and regulatory barriers, Avenews’ API-driven, cloud-based platform can rapidly scale across markets with minimal adaptation, making it regionally competitive.
Sustainable Change:
Problem Context
Agri-SMEs are the backbone of Sub-Saharan Africa’s food systems but remain chronically underfinanced. Traditional lenders exclude them due to collateral requirements, high risk perception, and lack of tailored products. This financing gap constrains productivity, limits trade, and stifles rural job creation.

Our Theory of Change

Inputs (Solution Deployment)

Use machine learning, APIs, and mobile money to embed finance into supply chain transactions.

Partner with banks, cooperatives, and corporate buyers to reduce risk and increase reach.

Immediate Outcomes

Improved trade volumes (30–40% on average) allow businesses to meet demand and expand markets.

SMEs strengthen their credit histories and graduate into broader financial ecosystems, reducing dependence on informal lenders.

Financial inclusion becomes institutionalized as SMEs demonstrate creditworthiness through data-driven lending models.

Agricultural value chains become more resilient, competitive, and attractive for further investment.

Inclusive growth contributes to poverty reduction, food security, and gender equity across Sub-Saharan Africa.

By embedding finance in digital ecosystems, Avenews catalyzes a sustainable shift away from dependency on donor-driven interventions toward self-sustaining, market-led development.

Demonstration effect that encourages traditional banks and investors to extend services to agri-SMEs.

Stronger ecosystems where farmers, SMEs, and buyers are linked through finance-enabled supply chains, driving long-term resilience and prosperity.

Title: Scaling Inclusive Digital Governance for Resilient and Smart Communities: A Unified Systems Approach in Cauayan City
Subtitle: The City Government Unit (CGU) of Cauayan, known as the “Innovative City of the Nation,” is committed to advancing inclusive and sustainable local governance through digital transformation. This proposal is anchored on the strategic imperative of strengthening last-mile delivery of social welfare services, institutionalizing disaster risk reduction and management readiness, and accelerating the digital transformation of official records and processes. Furthermore, it aims to establish an integrated, multi-functional digital dashboard that will enable real-time, inter-agency access to critical data, thereby enhancing coordination, decision-making, and policy responsiveness. By modernizing governance systems, the CGU aims to ensure efficiency, transparency, and accessibility of services across all sectors of society.
Problem Statement: Despite Cauayan City’s pioneering efforts in developing multiple digital governance systems, full implementation at the barangay level remains constrained by insufficient resources. Most barangays lack the necessary tablets, laptops, and weather-proof devices to access platforms for real-time disaster reporting, service delivery, and data management. Fragmented system integration and limited coverage of smart queuing services also hinder operational efficiency and citizen satisfaction. Without adequate funding and support, the city’s digital innovations risk remaining underutilized, leaving gaps in grassroots service delivery, disaster readiness, and inter-agency coordination.
Solution Overview:
The proposed solution consolidates Cauayan City’s existing digital governance systems into an integrated and barangay-accessible platform. By equipping all 65 barangays with tablets, laptops, and weather-proof devices, local officials will be able to directly access government databases, submit real-time disaster reports, and manage community-level services. A centralized, multi-functional digital dashboard will interconnect systems such as the Serbisyong Una Ka Dito (SUKD), CARES, GIS platforms, and Smart Queuing systems, enabling inter-agency data sharing, monitoring, and coordinated response. This integrated approach ensures that citizens experience faster, more reliable services while government offices gain greater efficiency and transparency in operations.

Methodologies and Technologies Used

Systems Integration: Consolidation of existing digital platforms into a unified, interoperable dashboard supported by secure cloud-based infrastructure.

Digital Resilience: Deployment of weather-proof devices and solar-powered backup systems to ensure uninterrupted operations during disasters.

Smart Service Delivery: Expansion of Smart Queuing Systems in frontline offices to reduce congestion and improve citizen experience.

Desired impact:
To institutionalize a resilient, inclusive, and technology-driven governance system in Cauayan City by scaling up digital innovations to all 65 barangays, thereby enhancing service delivery, disaster preparedness, and inter-agency coordination in line with national priorities, the Sustainable Development Goals, and UNIDO’s Inclusive and Sustainable Industrial Development (ISID) framework. Thus, it aims the following: 

•	To equip all 65 barangays with tablets, laptops, and weather-proof digital devices within the first two years of project implementation, ensuring reliable access to government platforms and real-time reporting during disasters.

•	To expand and integrate smart queuing systems across at least 80% of the city’s frontline services within three years, reducing service congestion and improving citizen satisfaction.

•	To operationalize an inter-agency digital dashboard within the first 18 months, enabling real-time data sharing, monitoring, and decision-making across departments and partner institutions.

•	To digitize and archive at least 90% of city government records and service-related documents by the end of the project period, strengthening efficiency, accountability, and institutional memory.

•	To mainstream gender-responsive and socially inclusive features in all digital systems within the first two years, ensuring equitable access for women, youth, vulnerable groups, and persons with disabilities.




•	To build technical capacity among local government staff and barangay-level implementers through regular training and skills development programs, with at least 500 personnel (barangay officials and barangay workers) trained by project completion.
Key technologies:
Unified Digital Dashboard – A centralized platform that integrates multiple existing systems (SUKD, CARES, GIS, LGHRIS, CCSL922, Smart Queuing, etc.), allowing real-time inter-agency data sharing, monitoring, and decision-making.

Geographic Information System (GIS) and QUANTUM GIS – Advanced mapping and spatial data management tools used for disaster risk reduction, territorial planning, and service delivery optimization.

Smart Queuing System – Automated queuing technology deployed in frontline offices to streamline citizen transactions, reduce waiting times, and improve service efficiency.

Weather-Proof Digital Devices with Solar Back-Up – Ruggedized tablets, laptops, and protective casings designed for continuous operations during typhoons or power interruptions, ensuring resilience in disaster scenarios.

Knowledge Management and Archiving Systems (CARES, LGHRIS, LCCPS) – Platforms that digitalize and secure government records, personnel data, and service-related documents, reducing reliance on paper-based processes.

Real-Time Citizen Engagement Tools (CCSL922, iReport, SUNSHINE System) – Mobile and online reporting applications enabling citizens to directly report emergencies, access services, and provide feedback.

Gender-Responsive and Inclusive Systems – Specialized platforms such as the Barangay GAD Plan Monitoring Tool, Unified VAWC Case Management (iReport), and accessibility features to ensure equitable service delivery.

Cloud-Based Data Storage and Cybersecurity Protocols – Secure digital infrastructure for safeguarding sensitive government data, ensuring data privacy compliance, and protecting against cyber threats.
Unique Characteristics:
Grassroots-Centered Digitalization – Unlike many e-governance models that remain centralized, this solution ensures that all 65 barangays—the true frontline of governance—are directly equipped with digital devices and platforms, enabling last-mile delivery of services and disaster response.

Disaster-Resilient ICT Systems – The inclusion of weather-proof, solar-powered devices ensures uninterrupted access to government systems even during typhoons or power outages, a feature rarely prioritized in local government ICT initiatives.

Unified Multi-System Integration – The project consolidates a wide range of existing platforms (service delivery, HRIS, GIS, queuing systems, VAWC case management, archiving, and citizen engagement tools) into a single, interoperable digital dashboard, eliminating silos and enabling holistic decision-making.

Inclusive by Design – Gender and social inclusion are embedded at the system level, with dedicated platforms for monitoring GAD plans, managing VAWC cases, and ensuring accessibility for women, youth, and persons with disabilities.

Real-Time Citizen Engagement – Tools such as CCSL922 and iReport enable direct two-way communication between citizens and government, fostering accountability, transparency, and participatory governance.

Replicable Smart City Model – Cauayan’s approach is not limited to local use; it is designed as a scalable and replicable governance model for other cities and municipalities in the Philippines and the Asia-Pacific region, aligning with UNIDO’s ISID framework.

Balanced Approach: Technology + Capacity Building – The solution does not only focus on technology procurement but equally emphasizes training, awareness campaigns, and institutionalization, ensuring sustainability and long-term adoption.
Sustainable Change:
The solution creates sustainable, systemic change by embedding digital governance directly into the structure and operations of all 65 barangays, ensuring that technology becomes a permanent enabler of service delivery rather than a short-term intervention. By institutionalizing digital platforms through ordinances, integration into the city’s Annual Investment Plan, and alignment with national ICT and resilience strategies, the project guarantees continuity beyond donor funding.

The approach also transforms governance from being reactive and paper-based to proactive, data-driven, and citizen-centered. With real-time reporting, inter-agency dashboards, and disaster-resilient ICT systems, decision-making processes are improved, resources are allocated more efficiently, and service delivery becomes more transparent and inclusive.

Capacity-building and inclusive design further ensure long-term sustainability, as local staff and communities acquire the skills, ownership, and confidence to maintain and expand the systems. This combination of technology, institutional integration, and human capacity development generates systemic change—one that strengthens resilience, empowers citizens, reduces inequalities, and creates a replicable model of sustainable digital governance aligned with UNIDO’s Inclusive and Sustainable Industrial Development (ISID) framework.
Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: The Cauayan City project aims to digitize and integrate local governance through the deployment of technology-driven systems, improving service delivery, disaster management, and governance transparency. The project is well-aligned with national and international development goals and focuses on inclusion, resilience, and sustainability. However, additional details on funding sources and the scalability of the model to other regions would strengthen the proposal.

Title: Award-winning learn-through-play solution for early childhood development
Subtitle: Equitable, internationally accredited curriculum for Early Childhood Development (ECD) centres in game form, with an innovative Edtech app and assessment centre.
Problem Statement:
The economic upliftment of poor South Africans is severely hampered by a lack of quality education.  Various studies have shown that most South African students cannot read, write and compute at grade-appropriate levels, with large proportions being functionally illiterate and innumerate. One of the reasons for this is a widespread lack of school readiness in poor communities. 

About 40% of the approximately 7.6 million children between the ages of 1 and 6 live in disadvantaged communities where they have little to no access to quality early learning programmes (ELP's). The recent Thrive by Five Index reported that 57% of children attending ELPs are not on track for cognitive and/or physical development and face barriers to realising their full potential. For early learning specifically, 55% of children were not able to do the learning tasks expected of children their age and 28% are falling far behind the expected standard. Early learning interventions are desperately needed to get our children school ready by the age of 6.
Solution Overview:
ATB provides equitable and high quality early learning opportunities. Their service offering is made up of the following products and services: 

1.	An Early Learning Curriculum (currently only in South Africa) incorporating Department of Education and National Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS), internationally certified  by Education Alliance, Finland, offering:
-	Play-based learning
-	Online version
-	Printed manuals
-	Workbooks
-	Theme posters
-	Assessment portfolio files

2.	The BambaLearn App that complements the curriculum
-	Learner tablet app 
-	Featuring games and exercises developing numeracy & literacy
-	Encourages critical thinking

3.	Bambanani Early Leaning Assessment Centre – online assessment to provide teachers and principals with insights into which children meet critical foundational early learning milestones in support of school readiness
-	Monitoring Learner & Teacher Progression 
-	Tracking sheets
-	Termly reports
-	Screening Tools
-	Remote Portal

4.	ECD training for principals and teachers 
-	Project trainer supporting 10 ECD centres 
-	Teaching assessments 
-	Ongoing support 

The BambaLearn App is available on the Appstore and Google Play on a ‘Freemium’ basis. The free version offers 25 free games, encouraging users to upgrade to the premium version, which offers over 4000 games, tailor made per age group, with new games added every week with a new theme for each age group. 

The technology underlying the above offering is as follows:

-	AWS (hosting),
-	PHP (backend),
-	Unity (frontend)

-      	iOS App

Title: Digital Bridges: Empowering Namibia’s Women, Youth, and MSMEs for Inclusive Digital Transformation.
Subtitle: A capacity-building initiative providing digital skills, tools, and platforms to marginalized women, youth, and MSMEs in Namibia. Bridging the digital divide and fostering inclusive innovation.
Problem Statement: Namibia’s digital divide is not just a connectivity gap, it is a barrier to opportunity, income, and dignity for thousands of women, youth, and marginalized MSMEs. In underserved communities, limited access to digital tools, relevant skills, and inclusive support systems forces entrepreneurs to operate in isolation and excludes them from rapidly growing digital markets. As global economies move online, these groups risk being permanently left behind, deepening social and economic inequality and suppressing Namibia’s overall innovation potential and competitiveness.
Solution Overview:
Solution:

Digital Bridges is a three-phase capacity-building and digital integration programme designed to bring Namibia’s underserved and early stage entrepreneurs into the digital economy. The project begins with community‐based digital literacy bootcamps delivered in local languages through a mobile innovation hub that travels to rural and urban regions. Once foundational skills are built, participants transition into practical, hands-on training for using digital tools to run and grow their businesses (e-commerce, digital payments, AI-powered market research, bookkeeping apps, etc.). The final phase connects participants to digital markets and policy dialogue by launching a B2B online marketplace and convening the Digital Entrepreneurs Summit where MSMEs showcase innovations and co-develop inclusive digital policies with public and UN partners.

Methodologies and Technologies:

Human‐centered design and adult learning methodologies to ensure culturally relevant and accessible content.

Blended learning approach (in-person + self-paced digital content).

Digital tools and platforms:

• Mobile innovation hub (offline/online learning access)
• Digital resource platform (video tutorials, templates, peer forums)
• Digital B2B marketplace
• Low-bandwidth, multilingual apps adapted for rural contexts (available)

Partnerships and Collaboration Models:

Local Collaboration: Ministry of Industrialization & Trade, Namibia Investment Promotion Board, community radio stations, and local banks to support outreach, policy co-creation and access to finance.

International Partners: UNIDO, UN Trade & Development, African Development Bank and innovation-focused NGOs for technical expertise, global best practices and matchmaking opportunities.

Private Sector Partnerships: Telecom Namibia and technology providers to ensure infrastructure support and affordable access to digital solutions.

The project is designed as a collaborative ecosystem that connects government, private sector, UN agencies and communities to ensure ownership, sustainability and scale.
Solution Provider(s): The Great Facilitator (social enterprise focused on entrepreneurship training and MSME capacity building in Namibia, nonprofit/private sector hybrid), Namibia Investment Promotion and Development Board (government agency supporting MSME development and investment promotion in Namibia, public sector), Telecom Namibia (national telecommunications company providing digital connectivity and infrastructure, private sector), Community Skills Development Centres – COSDECs (public training institutions supporting vocational and entrepreneurship skills development, public sector), Namibia university of Science and Technology ( Technology based institution), NedBank Namibia, First National Bank, Bank Windhoek, Standard Bank( Resource partners)
Implementation location(s): Windhoek, Namibia (pilot trainings delivered at Wanaheda Community Centre and Katutura Multi-Purpose Youth Centre), US Embassy Namibia ( American Spaces), CoCreation Hub Namibia.
Implementation timeline(s): Pilot phase implemented from June 2023 to November 2024.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 6–8 months, including 2 months for stakeholder engagement and mobilisation, 3 months for training delivery, and 1–3 months for follow-up and monitoring.
SDGs addressed: SDG 1 (No Poverty);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities);
Desired impact:
Solution Objectives:

1. Equip women, youth, and MSMEs in communities with practical digital skills to grow and manage their businesses effectively.

2. Increase adoption of digital tools and platforms to enhance productivity, market access, and income generation.

3. Foster a networked community of digital entrepreneurs for peer learning, collaboration, and knowledge sharing.

4. Promote inclusive economic participation by bridging the digital divide in rural and marginalized areas.

Key Achievements / Impacts:

1. Digital literacy: Train at least 300 women, youth, and MSMEs in foundational digital skills within the first pilot year.

2. Business growth: Enable participants to adopt digital tools, leading to an average 20–30% increase in sales or client reach within 6 months post-training.

3. Employment generation: Support participants in creating new job opportunities in their communities (target: 50+ new jobs across pilot regions).

4. Market access: Facilitate connections for 50+ MSMEs to local and national digital marketplaces.

5. Community building: Establish a sustainable peer-support network to ensure ongoing knowledge sharing and problem-solving.

These objectives and impacts directly contribute to inclusive digital transformation, economic empowerment, and sustainable MSME growth in Namibia.
Key technologies:
Key Technologies to be Used:

1. Mobile Learning Platforms – Simple, low-bandwidth platforms (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram, Google Classroom) to deliver training content and micro-lessons to participants in rural and marginalized areas.

2. Digital Business Tools – Off-the-shelf applications for MSMEs, including:

2.1. WhatsApp Business for customer engagement and communication

2.2. Canva for digital marketing and branding

2.3. Wave Accounting for basic bookkeeping and financial management

3. E-Commerce and Market Access Platforms – Existing online marketplaces or B2B platforms to help MSMEs list and sell their products digitally.

4. Data Monitoring & Reporting Tools – Google Sheets, Airtable, or similar tools for tracking training progress, adoption, and impact metrics.

5. Optional AI Tools – Basic AI-powered solutions for market research, content creation, or customer insights, scaled appropriately for participants’ skill levels.

The solution focuses on practical, accessible, and scalable digital tools rather than developing complex proprietary systems, ensuring immediate usability and measurable impact.
Unique Characteristics:
1. Community-Centric Delivery Model – Leverages The Great Facilitator’s existing local networks and trust within marginalized communities, ensuring high engagement and adoption.

2. Practical, Low-Tech Approach – Focuses on accessible tools like WhatsApp Business, Canva, and mobile accounting apps, allowing participants with low literacy or limited tech experience to immediately apply digital skills.

3. Blended Learning & Peer Support – Combines in-person workshops with micro-learning via mobile messaging, supplemented by ongoing peer-support circles, creating a sustainable learning ecosystem.

4. Inclusive Digital Empowerment – Specifically targets women, youth, and MSMEs in underserved areas, addressing both economic and digital inequalities.

5. Partnership Driven Model – Collaborates with local government, telecom providers, and community centres to provide affordable connectivity, technical support, and outreach, enabling scale without heavy infrastructure investment.

6. Scalable and Replicable – Designed for easy adaptation to new geographies, using off-the-shelf tools and low-cost implementation, making it replicable across other regions in Namibia and sub-Saharan Africa.

The innovation lies in merging digital skills training with practical tool application and community networks, creating measurable business growth and inclusive digital participation without requiring high-end technology or infrastructure.
Sustainable Change:
Theory of Change:

1. Inputs & Activities – Deliver accessible digital skills training, provide practical tools (WhatsApp Business, Canva, mobile accounting apps), and create peer-support networks in underserved communities.

2. Immediate Outputs – Women, youth, and MSMEs gain digital literacy, adopt simple digital tools, and establish networks for ongoing knowledge exchange.


3. Short-Term Outcomes :

3.1. Increased business efficiency and productivity.

3.2. Expanded market access through digital platforms.

3.3. Enhanced confidence and entrepreneurial skills among participants.


4. Medium-Term Outcomes :

4.1. MSMEs experience measurable growth in revenue and customer base.

4.2. Creation of new jobs in local communities.

4.3. Stronger community-level digital ecosystems supporting collaboration and innovation.


5. Long-Term Impacts / Systemic Change:

5.1. Reduction of economic and digital inequalities, particularly for marginalized communities.

5.2. Sustained inclusive digital transformation at local and regional levels.

5.3. A scalable and replicable model that informs government policy and private sector approaches to MSME empowerment and digital inclusion.

By equipping underserved communities with digital skills and practical tools while fostering networks of peer support, we as The Great Facilitator are happy to provide the solution that transforms how MSMEs operate, connect them to markets, and create lasting community-level economic empowerment, driving systemic change beyond the initial training phase.
Funding Sources:
The solution has been primarily funded through a combination of:

The Great Facilitator internal funds – Seed funding from the organization’s operational budget to pilot training programs.

Local grants and sponsorships – Support from Namibian government agencies and community development funds for capacity-building initiatives.

Private sector partnerships – In-kind contributions from telecom companies (connectivity, devices) and local businesses (training venues, materials).

International donor support (pilot phase) – Small-scale funding from NGOs and international development organizations supporting youth and women entrepreneurship programs.

This blended funding model demonstrates the capacity to mobilize resources from multiple sectors while maintaining financial sustainability and leveraging partnerships.

Primary thematic focus area: Inclusive Digital Innovation Skills & Entrepreneurial Talent Development
Summary: Digital Bridges is a capacity-building initiative in Namibia that equips women, youth, and MSMEs with digital skills, tools, and market access opportunities. Delivered through mobile innovation hubs, blended learning, and practical toolkits (WhatsApp Business, Canva, bookkeeping apps), the program aims to close the digital divide and foster inclusive economic growth. The solution includes a B2B marketplace and annual Digital Entrepreneurs Summit to connect participants to wider markets and policy dialogues. With strong partnerships across government, private sector, and international organizations, the project is piloting in Windhoek and aims to scale nationally and regionally.

Title: Tech4All: Community-Based Digital Hubs for Youth and MSME Empowerment in Rural Nigeria
Subtitle: Empowering underserved communities in Nigeria through community-based digital hubs for youth skills development, MSME support, and inclusive innovation.
Problem Statement: Many rural and underserved communities in Nigeria face limited access to digital infrastructure, skills training, and economic opportunities. Youth and women often lack the digital literacy, tools, and support needed to participate in the digital economy. MSMEs, which form the backbone of local economies, struggle to adopt digital technologies, access markets, or scale sustainably. This digital divide perpetuates poverty, unemployment, and inequality—hindering inclusive growth and innovation.
Solution Overview:
Tech4All is a community-driven initiative designed to bridge Nigeria’s digital divide by establishing digital innovation hubs in underserved rural and peri-urban areas. These hubs provide youth, women, and MSMEs with access to digital skills training, entrepreneurship support, and tools for sustainable participation in the digital economy.

How the Solution Works:
Community-Based Digital Hubs:

Establish physical hubs in accessible community spaces (e.g., schools, civic centers) equipped with internet access, solar power, and ICT tools.

Each hub serves as a local anchor point for digital learning, mentorship, and business support.

Digital Skills Training:

Offer structured, tiered training in digital literacy, coding, e-commerce, digital marketing, and basic AI.

Courses delivered through blended learning models (online/offline), including mobile and offline-first solutions for remote areas.

MSME Digital Empowerment:

Facilitate hands-on clinics for local businesses on using digital platforms, mobile money, inventory tools, and social media marketing.

Provide one-on-one coaching to help MSMEs adopt digital tools and connect with markets.

Startup Incubation & Innovation Support:

Run innovation challenges, hackathons, and startup bootcamps targeting local social problems.

Offer mentorship, access to funding, and pathways to scale through partnerships with UNIDO, local incubators, and tech platforms.

Methodologies and Technologies Used:
Human-Centered Design (HCD): Co-create solutions with community input.

Blended Learning & Offline-First Platforms: Local language content, low-data e-learning modules, and offline training kits.

Mobile & Solar Technology: Solar-powered mobile units in off-grid areas.

Data Tracking: Basic AI/ML tools for monitoring learner progress and MSME digital readiness.

Open-source tools: Leverage open platforms for affordability and scalability.

Partnerships and Collaboration Models:
Local Governments & Community Leaders: Site identification, mobilization, and sustainability.

Technical Partners: Collaboration with edtech firms, software providers, and telecoms (e.g., MTN Foundation, Google for Startups Africa).

Academic Institutions: Content development and certification with Nigerian universities and polytechnics.

UN Agencies & Donors: Strategic support, visibility, and alignment with SDGs and the Global Digital Compact.

Private Sector: Corporate volunteerism, equipment donations, and potential startup funding pipelines.

This integrated model empowers underserved populations, drives local innovation, and builds a sustainable, inclusive digital economy in Nigeria.

Title: Eazy Chain: Smart Logistics Platform for Inclusive Trade in West Africa
Subtitle: Eazy Chain is a digital logistics platform connecting African SMEs to affordable air and ocean freight, warehousing, and last-mile delivery solutions across West Africa.
Problem Statement: Millions of African SMEs face high logistics costs, lack of visibility, and limited access to reliable freight and warehousing services. These challenges hinder trade, scalability, and regional market integration.
Solution Overview: Eazy Chain is a digital freight platform that centralizes logistics services (air and ocean freight, warehousing, customs clearance) for African SMEs. It uses Flutter, Firebase, and payment APIs (Stripe, UnionPay, Fedapay) to deliver a seamless and accessible experience. The platform operates in partnership with Africa Global Logistics to ensure reliable and scalable services.
Solution Provider(s): Africa Global Logistics, Auda-nepad
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 months
SDGs addressed: SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth);SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure);
Desired impact:
Eazy Chain aims to simplify trade for African SMEs by reducing logistics costs and delays.
It has onboarded 1,200 users and supports 500 active customers with $32,000 MRR.
The platform has generated +10 jobs and fosters regional trade integration.
Future goals include expanding to 3 countries and reducing carbon impact through route optimization.
Key technologies: Eazy Chain leverages AI for route optimization and real-time tracking, Firebase for backend infrastructure, and Flutter for cross-platform mobile app development. It also integrates payment APIs (Fedapay, Stripe, UnionPay) to support seamless transactions across Africa, Europe, and Asia.
Unique Characteristics: Eazy Chain offers a unique combination of digital freight booking, real-time container tracking, and integrated payment solutions tailored for African trade. Its innovation lies in combining a multimodal logistics platform with wind-powered feeder vessels and partnerships with key players like AGL and MSC. The financing model includes revenue-based repayment and strategic equity partnerships, ensuring scalability and inclusivity.
Sustainable Change: Eazy Chain contributes to sustainable, systemic change by reducing logistics costs and emissions through wind-assisted maritime transport and digitized freight operations. By improving port-to-port connectivity, it empowers SMEs, enhances trade fluidity, and reduces dependency on road transport. The solution creates lasting impact by fostering green supply chains, formalizing informal logistics actors, and unlocking cross-border trade for underserved markets. Over time, this leads to greater economic inclusion, job creation, and climate resilience across West Africa.
Funding Sources:
$ 50000 SAFE from Baobab Network
$ 25000 Grant from Auda Nepad
$ 25000 Grant from FARI Ecowas
Primary thematic focus area: Stable and Resilient Digital Supply Chains
Summary: Eazy Chain is a digital logistics platform simplifying freight, warehousing, and customs for African SMEs. Operating in Togo since early 2025, it already serves 1,200 users and 500 active customers, generating $32,000 monthly recurring revenue and creating over 10 jobs. The solution integrates AI-powered route optimization, real-time container tracking, and inclusive digital payments (Stripe, UnionPay, Fedapay). With partnerships including Africa Global Logistics and Auda-Nepad, it directly addresses high logistics costs, inefficiencies, and trade barriers. The model is designed for scalability across West Africa, with a sustainability lens through wind-powered feeder vessels and green supply chain practices.

Title: RuralNet Tanzania: Bridging the Digital Divide in Underserved Areas
Subtitle: Empowering rural communities in Tanzania through inclusive digital infrastructure and connectivity solutions.
Problem Statement: Rural and underserved regions in Tanzania lack reliable digital infrastructure, limiting access to digital services, education, entrepreneurship, and essential government and financial services. This results in deepening economic inequality and digital exclusion.
Solution Overview:
RuralNet Tanzania is an initiative that builds and manages affordable, community-focused digital infrastructure in rural and underserved areas across Tanzania.

How it works: RuralNet establishes last-mile fiber and wireless connectivity hubs, provides shared internet access points, and facilitates local training and digital literacy programs.

Technologies used: A mix of FTTH (Fiber to the Home), Wi-Fi mesh networks, and solar-powered base stations to ensure energy-resilient and scalable deployment.

Methodologies: A hybrid approach that includes needs assessment, local capacity building, and public-private collaboration.

Partnerships: We work with local ISPs, municipal councils, telecom hardware providers (e.g., Huawei, Ubiquiti), and international digital inclusion agencies.

Title: Digital Bridge: Empowering Rural Entrepreneurs with Tools & Marketplace Access
Subtitle: A mobile toolkit and digital marketplace empowering rural and township MSMEs—especially women and youth—with tools, mentorship, and access to grow their businesses online.
Problem Statement:
Problem Statement
In South Africa, structural inequality, digital exclusion, and high youth unemployment continue to hinder inclusive economic growth. As of Q1 2024, the country faces an alarming youth unemployment rate exceeding 60%, with young women disproportionately affected due to a combination of socio-economic barriers, limited access to education, and digital gender gaps (Stats SA, 2024). Despite the rise of the digital economy, many micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs)—especially those led by women and youth in rural and township areas—remain locked out of meaningful participation due to a lack of digital skills, poor infrastructure, and limited access to formal support systems.

Most township and rural entrepreneurs operate informally, without access to tools for business registration, inventory tracking, or online sales platforms. This perpetuates a cycle of exclusion, making it difficult for them to scale, access finance, or build resilient enterprises. Women-led cooperatives in agriculture and crafts, in particular, are unable to reach wider markets due to the absence of tailored digital solutions and support networks. Youth-led MSMEs also face barriers such as unreliable connectivity, high data costs, and a lack of mentorship or digital literacy training.

Without intervention, these disparities will continue to widen, excluding entire communities from the benefits of digital transformation. Addressing this gap is critical—not only for economic inclusion, but for achieving broader goals around gender equity, youth empowerment, and sustainable development in South Africa’s underserved regions.
Solution Overview:
Solution Overview
Digital Bridge is a mobile-first solution designed to empower youth and women in South Africa’s rural and township areas by equipping them with digital tools, a shared online marketplace, and mentorship support to grow sustainable MSMEs.

In marginalized regions, entrepreneurs often travel long distances—sometimes over 30km—to access help at municipal offices, CIPC registration centers, or SEDA hubs. Many return multiple times due to incomplete support, lack of digital literacy, or document issues, often leaving without solutions. These barriers prevent formalization, market access, and long-term growth.

Our solution addresses these systemic challenges through:

A multilingual, mobile digital toolkit (offline-capable) that guides users step-by-step through business registration, inventory tracking, online selling, and financial literacy—tailored for low-data environments.

A shared digital marketplace platform that connects women- and youth-led MSMEs to broader markets with mobile payments, product listings, and cooperative marketing tools.

A mentorship and infrastructure model, pairing local MSMEs with digital mentors while providing access to devices, data, and training clinics via schools and libraries.

We use Progressive Web App technology, human-centered design, and community-based partnerships to ensure adoption, scalability, and sustainability. This solution eliminates travel barriers, accelerates business growth, and digitally includes those most often left behind in South Africa’s economy.

Nkwane CTS focuses on empowering marginalized youth and women through technology, entrepreneurship, and skills development programs, especially in underserved rural and township areas. Sector: Civil Society / Non-Profit / Education & Digital Inclusion,  Technovation International – A global nonprofit that empowers girls and underserved youth to become tech leaders and entrepreneurs through hands-on mobile app development and AI programs. Sector: Education Technology / Youth Empowerment / Global Innovation,  The Centre for Project Innovation – A project-based learning hub that provides scholarships and training in Project Management, offering professional certification opportunities to disadvantaged youth and aspiring entrepreneurs. Sector: Professional Development / Education / Certification & Workforce Readiness,  Local TVET Colleges and Community Libraries (Eastern Cape and Gauteng) – Institutional partners supporting digital bootcamps, infrastructure access, and entrepreneurship support services. Desired impact:
Desired Impact of the Solution
Solution Objectives:
Our solution aims to break down the digital and economic barriers faced by youth and women entrepreneurs in South Africa’s marginalized rural and township areas. It seeks to:

Equip underserved MSMEs with practical digital skills and business tools.

Facilitate formal business registration and digital access to local and global markets.

Foster a culture of digital entrepreneurship, mentorship, and innovation at the grassroots level.

Key Expected Impacts:

500+ youth and women-led MSMEs empowered through access to a mobile-first digital business toolkit within the pilot phase.

Over 200 informal businesses formally registered through guided support, reducing legal and financial exclusion.

300+ entrepreneurs trained in digital business skills, inventory management, e-commerce, and online marketing.

Launch of a shared digital marketplace platform, enabling small enterprises to increase sales and reach beyond their local areas—targeting at least a 50% increase in visibility or income for active users.

50 trained digital mentors deployed to support and guide MSMEs through growth and problem-solving.

4 local digital access hubs activated using community libraries and schools, offering internet, devices, and training for entrepreneurs.

Improved productivity and reduced travel burden for MSMEs—who currently travel long distances and make multiple unsuccessful visits to centers like CIPC or municipal offices to register and access support.

By enabling inclusive access to digital infrastructure, knowledge, and markets, this solution will drive decent work, local economic resilience, and gender-equitable digital inclusion, aligning with SDGs 5, 8, and 9.
Key technologies:
Key Technologies Used in Our Solution
Our solution integrates accessible and scalable technologies that enable digital inclusion, enterprise formalization, and sustainable entrepreneurship for underserved communities:

🔹 1. Mobile Web and App-Based Platforms
We use lightweight, mobile-first digital interfaces that function on basic smartphones and low-bandwidth environments. This ensures accessibility for users in rural and township areas with limited digital infrastructure.

Purpose: Access to registration services, mentorship, training content, and marketplace integration.

🔹 2. AI-Powered Learning and Support Tools
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used to:

Personalize training content based on user needs (language, education level, business stage).

Offer automated business tips, financial literacy prompts, and goal tracking.

Enable a chatbot for 24/7 support in multiple South African languages.

🔹 3. Cloud-Based Data and Analytics
Cloud computing enables secure storage and real-time analysis of user data:

Tracks user progress and impact (e.g., registration, income growth).

Generates insights for community dashboards and potential policy use.

Ensures scalability and security of the platform.

🔹 4. Geolocation and Mapping Technology
Used to:

Connect users to nearby mentors, local cooperatives, or partner facilities.

Map informal business clusters for outreach and community-based scaling.

🔹 5. Digital Identity and Verification Tools
We incorporate API integrations for:

Verifying ID numbers with government systems.

Supporting business registration and compliance.

Facilitating access to digital wallets and mobile money services.

Together, these technologies form an integrated digital inclusion stack—empowering underserved entrepreneurs with the tools they need to succeed in the modern economy, while remaining low-cost, mobile-friendly, and easy to deploy in new regions.
Unique Characteristics:
Unique/Differentiated Characteristics of the Solution
What sets our solution apart is its deep localization, inclusive design, and ecosystem-based implementation that responds directly to the realities of women and youth in underserved South African communities.

🔹 1. Mobile-First, Offline-Capable Toolkit Designed for Low-Connectivity Areas
The digital toolkit is optimized as a Progressive Web App (PWA)—multilingual, data-light, and functional even without a consistent internet connection. It provides step-by-step business guidance, financial tools, and access to compliance resources (CIPC, SARS) in a format usable on basic smartphones.

🔹 2. Shared Digital Marketplace for Informal and Cooperative MSMEs
Unlike traditional e-commerce platforms, our marketplace is co-designed with informal entrepreneurs and cooperatives—especially in agriculture and crafts—and offers collective marketing, group profiles, and mobile-payment integration for communities often excluded from mainstream platforms.

🔹 3. Embedded Mentorship & Infrastructure Access Model
We go beyond tech deployment by integrating local mentorship, monthly digital clinics, and access to physical infrastructure through partnerships with schools, libraries, and public facilities—ensuring hands-on support where it's needed most.

🔹 4. Community-Led Implementation and Capacity Building
Through collaboration with local cooperatives, TVET colleges, and The Centre for Project Innovation, we offer project management training and leadership development, helping communities sustain and scale the solution independently.

🔹 5. Gender-Responsive and Scalable Design
Our approach integrates gender-sensitive content, AI voice support for low-literacy users, and flexible modules to adapt the platform for other geographies, languages, or development sectors—making it both inclusive and highly replicable.

This combination of human-centered design, grassroots partnerships, and digital innovation makes our solution not just a tech intervention—but a transformative, scalable pathway to inclusive economic empowerment.
Sustainable Change:
Theory of Change
If we provide underserved MSMEs with accessible digital tools, market access, mentorship, and infrastructure support,
then youth and women entrepreneurs will be able to formalize their businesses, increase their incomes, and participate in the digital economy—
which leads to more inclusive economic growth, reduced inequality, and greater community resilience.

Systemic & Sustainable Impact Pathways
🔹 1. Breaking the Informality Trap
By enabling business registration and access to financial systems via a mobile toolkit, the solution addresses the chronic informality that keeps township and rural entrepreneurs excluded from economic support, tax benefits, and growth opportunities.

🔹 2. Building Local Digital Ecosystems
Through partnerships with schools, libraries, cooperatives, and mentors, the project establishes community-led digital ecosystems that can continue operating beyond initial deployment—embedding digital entrepreneurship into local infrastructure.

🔹 3. Changing Mindsets & Skillsets
The mentorship and training components instill long-term entrepreneurial thinking, digital literacy, and confidence—particularly in young women—contributing to a new generation of digital-ready, locally rooted entrepreneurs.

🔹 4. Enabling Replication and Policy Influence
Our open, adaptable platform and localized data insights can support policy dialogues with local governments and influence broader strategies on MSME digital inclusion. The model can be scaled to other provinces or countries facing similar challenges.

Follow-on Effects May Include:

Increased female-led MSME representation in the digital economy.

Reduction in youth unemployment and underemployment in rural areas.

Stronger digital public-private partnerships at local levels.

Greater digital readiness and resilience across underserved communities.

In sum, our solution doesn’t just create access—it builds a sustainable foundation for generational change, shifting systems from exclusion to empowerment.
